summary: Research and fact-check the physics, coaching cues, visual style and tooling for a Kurzgesagt-style video on 3 soccer kicks

research.kick: Inside-foot curler: the bent finesse shot, the curled pass and the whipped cross
research.one_line_hook: Your foot touches the ball for about one hundredth of a second. In that instant, you program a flight that bends almost 3 metres around a wall, and the goalkeeper's brain cannot predict it.
research.mechanism_story:
1. Set-up. The player runs in at an angle and plants the standing foot beside the ball. That foot points where the ball must start, not at the target. The hip turns out, so the inside of the kicking foot faces the ball.

2. Contact. The foot touches the ball for only about 10 milliseconds (9 to 12 ms). It hits the back of the ball about 8 to 10 cm off centre, on the outer half, a little below the middle. The ball squashes to about 85% of its size and moulds itself to the foot. So it grips the foot like gear teeth, even when friction is low. The foot sweeps across the ball at about 45 degrees. Part of the push drives the ball forward. The other part twists it.

3. The trade-off. More offset gives more spin but less speed. A centre hit can give 26 m/s with almost no spin. An 8 cm offset gives about 18.5 m/s and 10 turns per second. Adults curl the ball at about 19 to 25 m/s (70 to 90 km/h). Good teenagers reach about 15 to 19 m/s. The ball spins 5 to 10 times each second.

4. The sideways push. The spinning ball drags a thin skin of air with it. On one side, this skin moves with the passing air and helps the air hug the ball longer. On the other side, the skin fights the air, and the air separates early. So the trail of air behind the ball goes to one side. Push air one way, and the ball moves the other way. The push starts at about 2 to 3 newtons, roughly half the ball's weight. A right-footer's curler spins anticlockwise from above and bends right to left. The ball bends the way its front surface turns.

5. The bend. The path is part of a huge circle, about 150 m across. The tightness depends on the ratio of spin to speed. So a teenager with less power but the same ratio bends the ball as much per metre as a pro.

6. Why the bend looks late. First, geometry. The gap between the curve and the start line grows with the square of distance. About three quarters of the drift happens in the second half. Second, air slows the ball by 20 to 25% over 20 m, but spin drops only about 2%. So the curve tightens a little, about 10 to 20% over 20 to 30 m. On long, fast, high-spin shots, this becomes a tightening spiral. Third, less than about 12 to 15 m/s, the airflow can change and add drag. Last, a goalkeeper's eyes read sideways acceleration badly.

7. Arrival. A 20 m curler takes about 1 second. After it clears the wall, the keeper has less than half a second.
plain_metaphors: Squashy gear: the ball squashes and moulds itself to the foot for 10 ms, so it grips like gear teeth, not like a slippery marble. This is why spin appears even with very low friction.
Energy budget: your foot brings a fixed amount of energy. Hit the centre and you spend it all on speed. Hit off centre and you spend part of it on spin. It is like cueing a pool ball off centre.

Coat of air: a spinning ball wears a thin coat of air that turns with it. On one side the coat helps the passing wind follow the ball. On the other side it rubs against the wind, and the wind separates early.
Skateboard push: throw air to the right, and you roll to the left. The ball throws its trail of air to one side, and the air pushes the ball the other way.
Nose rule: the ball bends the way its front surface turns, like a car goes where its front wheels point.
Crosswind cyclist: the same crosswind pushes a slow cyclist off line more than a fast one. The ball slows a lot, but its spin push fades much less, so the bend tightens a little near the end.

Ruler and circle: lay a ruler along the start of a big circle. The circle leaves the ruler slowly, then fast. At twice the distance, the gap is four times bigger. That is the late swerve most people see.
Leading a receiver: a quarterback throws to where the receiver will be. A curler aims to where the ball will return, 2 to 3 m outside the target at 20 m.
Door hinge: the plant foot is the hinge. The hip and kicking leg are the door that swings across the ball.
Windscreen wiper: the foot does not punch through the ball. It wipes across the back of it, at about 45 degrees.
Frisbee in the wind: our brains predict falling objects well, but sideways drift badly. Keepers read a curler like you read a frisbee in a gusty wind.

Water-tank spiral: French physicists fired tiny spinning balls into water. In a few centimetres, the balls spiralled like a snail shell. A football does the same thing, but the spiral is 50 to 75 m long, so you only see its first part.

jargon_map.plain_version: The spin push: the sideways shove that the air gives a spinning ball.
The thin skin of air that sticks to the ball and turns with it.
The place where the air leaves the ball surface.
The messy trail of swirling air behind the ball.
The air trail thrown to one side by the spin.
Push air one way, and the air pushes the ball the other way.
The air's brake. Cd is a number for how strong the brake is for a given speed. It is about 0.25 to 0.3 for a curled ball.
How good the ball is at turning spin into sideways push. It is about 0.2 to 0.3 for a football.
The spin-to-speed ratio: how fast the ball's surface turns compared with how fast the ball flies. A good curler is about 0.2.
How many times the ball turns each second (revolutions per second, rev/s). One rev/s equals 6.28 rad/s.
A number that tells if the air flows smoothly or messily around the ball. It grows with speed.
The speed band (about 12 to 15 m/s for a football) where the airflow suddenly changes and the air brake changes strength.
A rare case, seen in wind tunnels near the drag-crisis speed, where the spin push points the wrong way.
Hitting the ball away from its centre.
A twisting push.
Grip between boot and ball.
The angle at which your foot sweeps across the ball.
The ball squashing against the foot.
How long the foot touches the ball: about 10 ms, one hundredth of a second.
How tight the bend is: the size of the circle the ball is tracing. A curler traces a circle with a radius of about 70 to 80 m.
A bend that keeps getting tighter, like a snail shell.
The distance over which the air clearly slows the ball. It is about 50 to 75 m for a football.
The invisible pole the ball turns around. Straight up gives pure sidespin. A tilted pole mixes in backspin or topspin.
Spin that bends the ball left or right / lifts it / makes it dip.
The direction the ball leaves your foot: how far left or right, and how high.
The standing foot next to the ball.
Turning the leg out so the inside of the foot faces the ball, and swinging the leg across the body.
Letting the kicking leg keep moving after the kick instead of stopping it.
How well the eyes and brain notice that something speeds up or changes direction. Humans are bad at this.

claims.claim: Foot-ball contact in a curve kick lasts about 9 ms. The foot travels about 15 cm with the ball during contact, about 66% of the ball's diameter.
claims.value: 9.12 ± 0.28 ms; 147 mm; mean ball speed 25.4 m/s (92 km/h); 6 university players, 4500 fps video

claims.claim: High-speed video of curve kicks by experienced university players measured contact times of 9.6 to 12.0 ms. Ball speed was 19.8 to 24.3 m/s and spin was 3.4 to 12.5 rev/s.
During the kick, the ball squashes to about 85% of its original diameter.
claims.value: 85% in the finite element model, 86% on video (instep-type impact)

claims.claim: A speed-spin trade-off exists. Hitting further off centre adds spin but removes speed. Maximum spin occurs at an offset of about 10 cm. Past the ball's radius, both spin and speed collapse.
claims.value: Simulation, foot speed 25 m/s, friction 0.4: centre hit 26.0 m/s and near zero spin; 8 cm offset 18.5 m/s and 10.2 rev/s (64 rad/s); 12 cm offset 11.2 m/s and 16.2 rev/s (101 rad/s)

claims.claim: Offset affects spin more than boot-ball friction. Raising friction from 0 to 1 adds at most 13 rad/s (about 2 rev/s). The ball spins even at zero friction because it deforms around the foot.
claims.value: ≤13 rad/s (≈2 rev/s) from friction; doubling the offset roughly doubles the spin

claims.claim: In a validated model of real curve kicks, boot-upper stiffness and boot-ball friction had little effect on spin or speed. Foot speed before impact was the main factor. Marketing claims that a special boot adds big spin are not supported.
claims.value: Upper stiffness 5–50 MPa and friction 0.3–0.6 gave little change; friction mattered only at very low foot speed (5 m/s)

claims.claim: Spin grows with the attack angle (the angle at which the foot sweeps across the ball) up to about 55 degrees. At larger angles the foot slips and spin falls. A standard curve kick uses about 46 degrees.
claims.value: Optimum < ~55°; standard curve kick ≈46°; 'angle curve' ≈36° gave less spin

claims.claim: Foot-ball contact in kicking lasts less than 10 ms. Peak impact forces reach about 2200–2500 N. In a simulated inside-of-instep ('infront') curve kick, the sideways impact force was about 1140 N, compared with about 450 N in a straight instep kick.
claims.value: <10 ms; ~2200–2500 N peak; lateral force 1143 N vs 452 N (simulation)

claims.claim: Adult male side-foot kicks reach about 23.4 m/s, slower than instep kicks (about 28 m/s). The side-foot kick needs large hip rotation power to turn the foot sideways.
claims.value: Side-foot 23.4 ± 1.7 m/s (84 km/h); instep ≈28 m/s (101 km/h); hip rotation power ≈1000 W

claims.claim: Published curve kicks leave the foot at 15.1 to 25.4 m/s and spin at 25 to 59 rad/s. Maximal instep kicks reach 28.0 to 32.6 m/s.

Semi-professional players curling around a pole at 20 m produced 19.2 m/s and 36.4 rad/s, with 1.49 m of lateral deflection. Their straight kicks were 22.1 m/s. Faster balls had less spin (r = -0.81). More spin gave more deflection (r = 0.89). The spin axis tilted about 63 degrees from horizontal, not fully vertical, because contact was below the ball's midline.
claims.value: 19.2 m/s (69 km/h); 5.8 rev/s; 1.49 m; axis 62.6° from horizontal; n = 4 (pilot)

claims.claim: Real curve kicks rarely spin faster than 10 rev/s. Most curve kicks leave the foot at 20 m/s or more.

Wind-tunnel data: a ball flying at 26 m/s and spinning at 8 rev/s (spin parameter 0.21) gains about 4 m/s of sideways speed from the Magnus force. At spin parameter 0.18, both the drag and side-force coefficients are about 0.25.
claims.value: ≈4 m/s sideways; Cd ≈ Cs ≈ 0.25 at Sp 0.18

claims.claim: Smoke visualisation of a real curve kick (27 m/s, 7 rev/s) shows the wake behind the ball thrown to one side, like a downwash. The sideways force on the ball is the reaction to this deflected air.
claims.value: 27 m/s, 7 rev/s, Sp 0.18; vortex angle ≈128°

claims.claim: With spin, the air separates earlier on the side of the ball that moves into the airflow and later on the side that moves with it. This gives an uneven wake and a force at right angles to both the flight direction and the spin axis.
claims.value: Qualitative mechanism

claims.claim: Measured sidespin free kicks left the foot at 23.0 to 28.3 m/s and slowed to 17.9 to 20.4 m/s after 0.9 s, which covered about 20 m. The fitted drag coefficient was 0.25 to 0.30 and the lift (side) coefficient was 0.23 to 0.29.
claims.value: 83–102 km/h at launch, 64–73 km/h after ~20 m (≈25% speed loss); Cd 0.25–0.30; Cl 0.23–0.29

claims.claim: For a central free kick from 18.3 m at 25 m/s, over a 1.83 m wall at 9.14 m, the launch elevation must stay between 16.5 and 17.5 degrees with almost pure sidespin. Tilting the spin axis by 7 degrees (adding backspin) is as harmful as kicking 1 m/s harder. After the ball clears the wall, the keeper has about 0.45 s.
claims.value: 1° elevation window; 7° axis tilt ≈ +1 m/s error; 0.45 s

claims.claim: Soccer balls go through the drag crisis at a critical Reynolds number of 2.2 to 3.0 × 10^5, which is about 12 to 15 m/s of air speed. Below this band the drag coefficient of a non-spinning ball is about 0.43. Above it, the value is about 0.15.
claims.value: 12–15 m/s (43–54 km/h); Cd ≈0.43 sub-critical vs ≈0.15 super-critical

claims.claim: Powerful shots and free kicks (25 to 35 m/s) reach the goal before they slow into the drag-crisis band. So the drag crisis does not explain the late bend of fast shots. It can matter for slower, longer balls such as youth curlers, curled passes and crosses.
claims.value: Launch 25–35 m/s vs critical ≈12–15 m/s

claims.claim: In wind-tunnel tests at constant spin, the side-force coefficient falls as ball speed rises. So a slowing ball with the same spin bends more per metre.
claims.value: Qualitative: 'the rate of curvature decreased as the speed increased'

claims.claim: The spinning-ball spiral: when spin stays nearly constant, a spinning ball follows a tightening (exponential) spiral. The bending grows once drag has clearly slowed the ball. The cause: the spin force scales with speed, but drag scales with speed squared. For soccer, the paper gives a characteristic length of about 54 m, launch speed 30 m/s and spin parameter 0.21.
claims.value: L ≈ 54 m (soccer, Table 1); U0 = 30 m/s; S = 0.21 (≈9.5 rev/s). Bray & Kerwin speed data imply L ≈ 70 m.

claims.claim: The spiral authors explain Roberto Carlos's 1997 free kick against France with this effect. The kick came from about 35 m, which is close to the length L. DISPUTED DETAILS: other sources give about 30 m. The paper's lift model is also about 3 times weaker than measured soccer-ball side forces.
claims.value: ≈35 m (Dupeux) vs ≈30 m (Physics World)

claims.claim: Roberto Carlos struck that free kick with the OUTSIDE of his left foot, not the inside. The authors estimated 'probably over' 30 m/s and 'perhaps over' 10 rev/s from about 30 m. Press figures such as 136 km/h are unverified.
claims.value: >30 m/s (>108 km/h), >10 rev/s, ~30 m (author estimates)

claims.claim: Motion capture of real 23 m curve kicks (about 19 m/s, about 5.8 rev/s): ball speed fell about 22% in 1 s, but spin fell only about 2% in 0.8 s. The side force halved from about 2 N to 1 N. The trajectory's curvature peaked MID-flight, and no spiral appeared at about 6 rev/s. This conflicts with the simple 'it always bends hardest at the end' story.
claims.value: 18.8 → 14.7 m/s in 1 s; 5.8 → 5.7 rev/s; side force 2 N → 1 N; 2 players, 14 kicks

claims.claim: The side-force coefficient rises with the spin-to-speed ratio, but by less than the ratio itself.

Model estimate (my calculation from the published coefficients: Cs ≈ 0.5·√Sp fitted to Asai 2020, Cd 0.27, spin decay 2.5%/s, no gravity). A 25 m/s, 8 rev/s curler drifts from its launch line by 0.64 m at 10 m, 2.7 m at 20 m and 6.3 m at 30 m. The bend radius tightens from about 80 m to 66 m over 30 m (about 18%). A 16 m/s, 5 rev/s youth curler bends almost the same per metre (2.6 m at 20 m) because the spin-to-speed ratio is the same. It takes 1.5 s for 20 m instead of 0.9 s.
claims.value: Drift ≈ distance² / (2 × 75 m); 4× the drift at 2× the distance; radius tightening 10–20% over 20–30 m

claims.claim: Aiming estimate (geometry from the same model): to finish on target at 20 m, the ball must leave about 7 to 8 degrees outside the target line, which is about 2.5 m wide at the goal. The widest point of the bow is about 0.7 m from the straight line. At 25 m the numbers are about 10 degrees and 1.1 m. At 30 m they are about 12 degrees and 1.6 m. Real kickers do send the ball away from the target first and let the curve bring it back.

Simulated free kicks: a centrally struck ball (26 m/s, no spin) reaches the top corner in 0.9 s. An 8 cm offset strike (18.5 m/s, 10.2 rev/s) bends much more but must be launched higher and takes 1.6 s. This gives the keeper more time.
claims.value: 0.9 s vs 1.6 s; ball about 30% slower

claims.claim: One simulation suggests a wet boot and ball give about 2 rev/s (13 rad/s) less spin, so a curler misses by about one ball width. DISPUTED: a later validated model (Ishii 2014) found friction has little effect at match foot speeds.
claims.value: −13 rad/s → finish moves ≈ one ball diameter (22 cm) at ~20 m

claims.claim: Measured football lift or side coefficients level off at about 0.26 to 0.3. More spin past about 100 rad/s at 18 m/s adds drag but not much more bend.
claims.value: Cl rises to ≈0.26 by 100 rad/s, then flat; Cd rises from 0.2 to 0.5 at 240 rad/s

claims.claim: In wind-tunnel tests on a spinning soccer ball, a negative (reversed) Magnus effect appeared in the critical Reynolds-number range. It was not observed when the boundary layer was fully laminar or fully turbulent. I read only the abstract, and its role in real curlers is unproven.

Goalkeepers do not fully allow for spin-induced sideways acceleration. Novice keepers stopped only 6% of curved free kicks whose first heading pointed the opposite way to where they ended, against 56% of other kicks. Even the most experienced professional keeper could not fully account for the curve.
claims.value: Simulated 30 m kicks, 10 rev/s, ≈2 m deviation, 1.44 s flight; 10 novices + 2 pro keepers in VR

claims.claim: Curve-kick technique in international female players: a wide approach angle, the support foot pointed to the right of the target (for right-footers), the kicking leg swung across the face of the goal, and the foot moving upward and outward at impact. Peak knee angular velocity and peak ankle speed occur AT impact, which supports the 'kick through the ball' cue.
claims.value: 17 Vicon cameras, 250 Hz; foot speed at impact the same as the instep kick, but more from knee extension

claims.claim: Curve kicks from 20 m at a 1 m² target: the lateral launch angle and the tilt of the spin axis best predicted left-right placement. Launch angles had to stay within about 3 degrees to hit the target.
claims.value: ±3° launch window at 20 m; 15 international female players

claims.claim: National FA coaching advice for the curled pass: approach at an acute angle, plant the standing foot beside the ball angled towards its front, and wrap the kicking foot around the far side of the ball with the instep. The example given is Keira Walsh's pass around a defender in the Women's Euro 2022 final.
claims.value: Coaching guidance, not a measurement

claims.claim: Maximal instep ball speed in trained youth players rises with age: U13 66.7 km/h (18.5 m/s), U15 76.9 km/h (21.4 m/s), U17 81.4 km/h (22.6 m/s), U20 98.7 km/h (27.4 m/s). Kicking accuracy gets worse around the growth spurt (U13 to U15). Note: the abstract labels the youngest group differently from the table.
claims.value: 366 Brazilian players, 3D kinematics at 300 Hz

claims.claim: Estimate: good 11 to 16 year-olds probably curl the ball at about 13 to 19 m/s (47 to 68 km/h). This combines their maximal kick speeds with the 10 to 30% speed loss of curve kicks. No direct youth curve-kick measurement was found.
claims.value: ≈13–19 m/s, likely 4–7 rev/s

claims.claim: Isaac Newton described a curving, spinning tennis ball in a 1672 paper, about 180 years before Magnus studied the effect.
claims.value: 1672 (Newton) vs 1852–53 (Magnus); Robins studied musket balls in 1742

technique_cues: Approach from an angle of about 30 to 45 degrees to the line from ball to target, on a slightly curved run. Physics: this lets the foot sweep across the ball at the spin-making attack angle of about 45 degrees.

Plant the standing foot beside the ball, about a hand-width to the side and level with it or a little behind. Point its toes where the ball must START, outside the target (right of target for a right-footer). Physics: this sets the lateral launch angle, which must be right within about 3 degrees.
Turn the kicking leg out from the hip so the inside of the foot faces the ball. Physics: this gives a big, flat contact patch along the inner arch, so the ball can mould to the foot and grip it.
Lock the ankle, toes up and slightly out. Physics: a floppy foot absorbs energy and lowers ball speed. A firm foot passes more of the swing into the ball.

Contact with the inside of the foot, between the big-toe joint and the inner arch. Hit the back of the ball on its outer half, about 8 to 10 cm from the centre (halfway between the centre and the edge), a little below the middle. Physics: the off-centre push makes a twist (torque). About 10 cm gives the most spin before the foot starts to glance off.
Wipe across the back of the ball, do not slice its side. Physics: spin rises with attack angle up to about 55 degrees. Past that, the foot slips and you lose spin AND speed.

Keep your chest over the ball and do not lean back. Physics: leaning back tilts the spin axis and adds backspin. The ball lifts over the bar, and 7 degrees of tilt costs as much as 1 m/s of extra speed.
Kick THROUGH the ball: make your foot fastest at contact, not before. Physics: peak knee and ankle speed at impact is what elite curlers show. Ball speed and spin both grow with foot speed.
Follow through across your body towards the far side and land on your kicking foot. Physics: this keeps the foot wiping across the ball for the whole 10 ms contact, which is about 15 cm of travel.
Aim off: pick a spot about 2 to 3 m outside the target from 20 m, and 4 to 6 m from 30 m. Physics: the ball traces a circle with a radius of about 70 to 80 m, so it drifts back to the target late.

Use just enough curl on shots and more curl on passes around defenders. Physics: every extra turn per second costs speed. A heavily curled shot can take 1.6 s instead of 0.9 s, which gives the keeper time.

For crosses and long curled passes, add foot speed but keep the same wipe. Start the ball at the near post or at the defender's shoulder, so it bends away from the keeper and into the runner. Physics: the same spin-to-speed ratio gives the same bend per metre. More speed means less time for defenders.
Keep your head still and your eyes on the contact point through the kick. Physics: a 3 degree error at launch is enough to miss a 1 m² target from 20 m.
If your curlers get worse during a growth spurt, keep practising. Physics and biology: longer levers change your timing, and youth studies show accuracy dips around U13 to U15, then returns.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hitting the ball through its centre with the inside of the foot
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: No off-centre push means no twist. The ball flies straight (26 m/s, near zero spin in simulation), usually right at the keeper or the wall.
common_mistakes.fix: Move the contact point to the outer half of the back of the ball, about 8 to 10 cm off centre.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hitting too far round the side of the ball, or slicing across it very steeply
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: Past about 55 degrees of attack angle, or past the ball's radius, the foot glances off. Both spin and speed collapse (for example 11 m/s at 12 cm offset), and the ball dribbles wide.
common_mistakes.fix: Wipe across the BACK of the ball at about 45 degrees. Imagine the ball as a clock and hit about 4 to 5 o'clock (right-footer, top view).

common_mistakes.mistake: Aiming straight at the target
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The spin push moves the ball about 2.5 m from its launch line over 20 m, so the ball ends well past the target.
common_mistakes.fix: Pick an aim spot about 2 to 3 m outside the target from 20 m, and point the plant foot at that spot.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back and scooping under the ball
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The spin axis tilts, so part of the spin becomes backspin. The ball lifts and floats over the bar. A 7 degree tilt is as harmful as 1 m/s too much speed.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the chest over the ball. Contact a little below the middle, not the bottom.

common_mistakes.mistake: Floppy ankle at impact
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The foot bends back on contact and absorbs energy, so the ball leaves slower with less grip for spin.
common_mistakes.fix: Lock the ankle with toes up and out before contact. Practise short, firm side-foot passes first.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping the leg at contact (no follow-through)
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The foot slows during the 10 ms contact. You lose speed, and the wipe that creates spin gets shorter.
common_mistakes.fix: Swing through and across the body, and finish with the kicking foot crossing in front of the plant foot.

common_mistakes.mistake: Plant foot too close to the ball, or pointing at the target
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The hip cannot open and the leg cannot swing across, so the foot punches straight through the ball. The ball goes straight or lacks spin.
common_mistakes.fix: Plant a hand-width to the side, level with or a little behind the ball, toes pointing at the start line outside the target.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to put maximum spin on every shot
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: Speed and spin trade against each other (r = -0.81 in real kicks). A slow, big-bending ball gives the keeper 0.5 to 0.7 s more to react.
common_mistakes.fix: Use just enough curl to beat the wall or the keeper. Keep power as a goal even on curlers.

common_mistakes.mistake: Blaming or crediting the boots
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: A validated model shows that boot-upper stiffness and friction change spin very little at match foot speeds. Foot speed and contact point dominate.
common_mistakes.fix: Spend the effort on contact point, attack angle and foot speed, not on special boots.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting a youth curler to behave like a slow pro free kick on long balls
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: Youth curlers over 25 to 30 m can slow to 10 to 12 m/s, into the drag-crisis band. Drag, and possibly the side force, can change there, so the ball can die or behave oddly late.
common_mistakes.fix: Use curlers mostly from 15 to 22 m. For longer curled passes, add foot speed and keep the flight lower.

drills: Pole bend gate (physics: aim-off and bend radius): put a tall pole or mannequin on the straight line to a target 12 to 20 m away. Curl around it into a 1 m target square. Move back 2 m after 3 hits in 5. Log your aim spot for each distance.

Stripe test (physics: spin axis): draw one line around the ball's equator. Put the ball down with the line flat. Curl it 8 to 10 m to a partner. A flat, steady line means pure sidespin. A wobbling line means a tilted axis, usually from leaning back.

Offset ladder (physics: speed-spin trade-off): mark contact points on the ball with tape at the centre, 5 cm, 10 cm and 15 cm from the centre. Take 3 kicks at each from 15 m. Film from behind with a phone and compare how far each ball bends and how long it takes to arrive.

Slow-mo check (physics: 10 ms contact): film a curler at 240 fps from the side. Contact lasts only 2 to 3 frames. Check that the foot meets the outer-back quarter of the ball, the ankle stays locked, and the foot keeps moving after contact.

Plant-foot footprints (physics: launch direction): put a flat marker where the plant foot must land, a hand-width beside the ball, toes pointing at a flag 2 to 3 m outside the target. Take 10 kicks and only change the marker if the ball starts on the wrong line.

Aim-off flag (physics: circular path, radius 70 to 80 m): place a flag 2.5 m outside the post from 20 m and 5 m outside from 30 m. Aim at the flag, not the goal. Record where each ball crosses the goal line.

Wall-and-bar window (physics: 1 degree elevation window): set a 1.8 m high rope or mannequin wall 9 m from the ball and a crossbar at about 18 m. Score only curlers that clear the wall and go under the bar.

Curled pass around a defender (physics: same bend on a pass): passer, pole-defender and runner. The runner moves into space behind the pole. The passer curls the ball around the pole into the runner's path at 15 to 25 m. Swap feet.

Whipped cross into the zone (physics: out-swinger bends away from the keeper): a winger crosses from the right with the right foot. The target zone is between the 6-yard box and the penalty spot. A striker attacks the ball. Count crosses the keeper cannot reach before the striker does.

Same bend, less power (physics: spin-to-speed ratio sets bend per metre): kick one curler at 60% and one at 90% power. Try to match the bend by changing only the wipe. Discuss why the stronger kick reaches the goal sooner.
animation_ideas: Ultra slow-mo contact (10 ms stretched to 10 s): the foot wipes across the ball at about 45 degrees, the ball squashes to 85% and moulds itself to the foot, the foot travels 15 cm with the ball, then an equator stripe starts turning. Use a counter that reads 0 to 10 ms.

X-ray foot: transparent boot showing the bones. Highlight the contact zone along the inner arch (first metatarsal, navicular, cuneiforms), the locked ankle, and the hip turning out like a door on a hinge.

Top-down clock face on the ball: a slider moves the contact point from the centre to 16 cm. Two gauges react: speed (26 → 18.5 → 11 m/s) and spin (0 → 10 → 16 rev/s). Past the ball's edge, both drop to zero.
Energy budget bar: one bar of foot energy splits into a 'forward' part and a 'spin' part as the contact point moves off centre.

Airflow close-up from above: flat-vector streamlines pass a spinning ball. A thin glowing 'coat of air' turns with the ball. The air hugs one side longer and separates early on the other. The wake swings to one side (big arrow), and the ball gets an equal and opposite nudge (small arrow).
Nose rule gag: a cartoon face on the ball's front. The face turns left as the ball spins, and the ball follows its nose.

Force tug-of-war: drag arrow (backward) and spin-push arrow (sideways) on the ball as it flies. The drag arrow shrinks fast as speed drops 25%. The spin-push arrow shrinks more slowly, and a 'bend meter' creeps up.
Ruler vs circle: a dashed launch line and the real curved path. Labelled gaps appear: 0.16 m at 5 m, 0.64 m at 10 m, 1.5 m at 15 m, 2.7 m at 20 m. A pop-up reads '2× distance = 4× drift'.
Goalkeeper's-eye view: a ghost ball shows the straight-line path the keeper's brain predicts. The real ball peels away late. Stat cards: 6% saved vs 56% saved.

Stopwatch race: a straight 26 m/s shot (0.9 s) and a heavy curler (1.6 s) fly side by side, with the keeper's reaction bar filling in the background. A second clock shows 0.45 s from the wall to the goal line.

Shrinking pitch into a fish tank: zoom from a stadium to Dupeux's water tank, where tiny spinning plastic balls spiral like snail shells in centimetres. Zoom back out to show the same spiral stretched to 50 to 75 m. A 20 m curler uses only the gentle first part. A 35 m thunderbolt reaches the tighter part.
Same bend, different power: a 25 m/s pro ball and a 16 m/s youth ball with matching spin-to-speed ratios trace identical curves. The pro ball simply arrives 0.6 s sooner.
Wall window: side view of a free kick. The ball must clear a 1.83 m wall at 9.15 m and dip under a 2.44 m bar at 18 m. The allowed launch cone is highlighted as only 1 degree wide.
Plant foot as a compass needle: from above, the plant-foot toes point at a flag 2.5 m outside the post. The ball launches along that line, then curls back in.
Stripe-ball test split screen: a flat, steady stripe (clean sidespin, bends sideways) vs a wobbling stripe (tilted axis, ball floats upward).
Curled pass and whipped cross: a pass bends around a defender's outstretched leg into a runner's path. An out-swinging cross bends away from a reaching goalkeeper into a striker's run.
Wet-weather myth check: a boot polishes itself with a 'MAGIC GRIP' label, then a model readout shows spin barely changing, while a foot-speed dial changes spin a lot.
Historical cameo: Newton in 1672 watches a tennis ball curve on a Cambridge court, then a jump cut to a modern free kick.
misconceptions: 'The fast side of the ball has low pressure because of Bernoulli, end of story.' This is a simplified half-truth. The real cause is the thin skin of air on the ball (the boundary layer), which separates at different places on each side. The wake is thrown sideways and the ball is pushed the other way. This is why a reversed Magnus effect can occur in narrow lab conditions.

'The ball flies straight, then suddenly switches on its bend at the end.' Mostly false. The path is a smooth curve. Most of the visible drift comes late because of geometry (drift grows with distance squared) and because keepers read sideways acceleration badly. Real tightening is modest (about 10 to 20%), and one motion-capture study at about 6 rev/s found the curvature peaked mid-flight.
'The drag crisis causes every late swerve.' Disputed. Fast shots (25 to 35 m/s) reach the goal before slowing to the 12 to 15 m/s drag-crisis band. It can matter for slow, long balls.

'Roberto Carlos's free kick broke the laws of physics' or 'it was a fluke'. Folklore. The spiral explanation exists, but the exact distance (30 or 35 m) and speed are disputed. He also used the OUTSIDE of his foot, so it is not an inside-foot curler.
'More spin always makes a better curler.' False. Speed and spin trade against each other. Extra spin past about 100 rad/s adds drag but not much bend, and a slow ball gives the keeper time.

'You need a pro's power to bend it like a pro.' False. The bend per metre depends on the spin-to-speed ratio. A 16 m/s, 5 rev/s youth curler bends about as much per metre as a 25 m/s, 8 rev/s pro curler. Power only buys less flight time.
'Special boots or grippy uppers add lots of spin.' Not supported. A validated model found that upper stiffness and friction change spin very little at match foot speeds.

'A curler has pure sidespin around a vertical axis.' Rarely. Measured curlers have the spin axis tilted about 60 degrees from horizontal, which mixes in some backspin. That is why curlers float and why leaning back sends them over the bar.
'Hit the side of the ball to curl it.' Misleading. You hit the back of the ball about 8 to 10 cm off centre. A true side hit glances off and loses both spin and speed.
'Aim at the corner and the curl will do the rest.' False. You must aim 2 to 3 m outside the target from 20 m, or the spin carries the ball past it.

'The panels and seams make the ball curve.' False for curlers. Spin causes the curve. Panels and seams mostly change drag and the drag-crisis speed, and they matter more for non-spinning knuckle balls.

'The Magnus effect was discovered by Magnus.' Only partly true. Newton described a curving tennis ball in 1672, and Robins studied spinning musket balls in 1742. Magnus did the first careful experiment in 1852.

verdicts.claim: Foot-ball contact in a curve kick lasts about 9 ms. The foot travels about 15 cm with the ball during contact, about 66% of the ball's diameter.
verdicts.corrected_value: 9.12 ± 0.28 ms, 147 mm (66% of 223 mm), ball 25.4 m/s. These were INSTEP kicks at a mini-goal 4 m away. For real curve kicks, use Ishii 2014: 9.6–12.0 ms.
verdicts.note: The Methods section of Asai et al. 2002 says: 'The players kicked a ball with the instep toward a mini-football goal 4 m away.' One results sentence calls Fig. 1 a curve kick, so the paper is not consistent. Do not present 9 ms as a measured curve-kick value.

verdicts.claim: High-speed video of curve kicks by experienced university players measured contact times of 9.6 to 12.0 ms. Ball speed was 19.8 to 24.3 m/s and spin was 3.4 to 12.5 rev/s.
verdicts.note: Ishii, Sakurai & Maruyama 2014, Sci Rep 4:6067. Five players, 2500 fps, one kick each. Spins were 6.9, 8.6, 8.2, 12.5 and 3.4 rps, so three of five fall at about 7–9 rps. The FE model gave 10.0–12.0 ms.

verdicts.claim: During the kick, the ball squashes to about 85% of its original diameter.
verdicts.corrected_value: 85% (FE model) vs 86% (video), instep-kick model
verdicts.note: The value comes from the 'digitized 3D instep kick model' (Fig. 5). Nobody measured it for a side-foot curler. Say 'in a hard kick' and not 'in a curler'.

verdicts.claim: A speed-spin trade-off exists. Hitting further off centre adds spin but removes speed. Maximum spin occurs at an offset of about 10 cm. Past the ball's radius, both spin and speed collapse.
verdicts.corrected_value: Peak spin at 10–12 cm offset (Table 2 peak: 16.2 rev/s at 12 cm, 11.2 m/s). 8 cm: 18.5 m/s and 10.5 rev/s in Table 2 (paper II rounds this to 10.2 rev/s = 64 rad/s). 16 cm: 0 and 0.
verdicts.note: This is an FE simulation of an instep-shaped foot at 25 m/s foot speed with friction 0.4. The abstract says the optimum is 'around 100 mm'.

verdicts.claim: Offset affects spin more than boot-ball friction. Raising friction from 0 to 1 adds at most 13 rad/s (about 2 rev/s). The ball spins even at zero friction because it deforms around the foot.
verdicts.note: The abstract quotes these points word for word. 'Doubling the offset from the axis of the ball roughly doubles the spin' is also in the text.

verdicts.claim: In a validated model of real curve kicks, boot-upper stiffness and boot-ball friction had little effect on spin or speed. Foot speed before impact was the main factor. Marketing claims that a special boot adds big spin are not supported.
verdicts.corrected_value: Upper stiffness 5–50 MPa: little effect. Friction was tested from 0.2 to 0.6: little effect for 4 of 5 players. At 0.2, one player lost both speed and spin. At a 5 m/s foot speed, lower friction cut spin for 3 of 5 players.
verdicts.note: The authors say 'it cannot be concluded that the shoes do not influence the ball behaviour'. They did not test rubber or 3D upper elements. Say: 'the upper's stiffness and grip made little difference at match foot speeds'. Do not say 'boot marketing is false'.

verdicts.claim: Spin grows with the attack angle (the angle at which the foot sweeps across the ball) up to about 55 degrees. At larger angles the foot slips and spin falls. A standard curve kick uses about 46 degrees.
verdicts.note: Lees et al. 2010 review (J Sports Sci 28:805). It cites Asai et al. 2004 (FE model) for the approximately 55° limit and Ozaki & Aoki 2008 for 46° vs 36°. Attack angle = the angle between the foot velocity and the normal at the impact point.

verdicts.claim: Foot-ball contact in kicking lasts less than 10 ms. Peak impact forces reach about 2200–2500 N. In a simulated inside-of-instep ('infront') curve kick, the sideways impact force was about 1140 N, compared with about 450 N in a straight instep kick.
verdicts.corrected_value: Instep contact <10 ms (Nunome 2006). Curve-kick contact 9.6–12 ms (Ishii 2014). Peak force about 2200–2800 N: FE horizontal 2439 N instep and 2206 N infront; Shinkai 2008 estimated >2800 N for a maximal kick. Lateral force 1143 N vs 452 N (FE).
verdicts.note: The lateral-force figures come from Asai et al. 2002 paper I, not from the review. The infront model used only a 2 cm offset with the ankle turned out 45°.

verdicts.claim: Adult male side-foot kicks reach about 23.4 m/s, slower than instep kicks (about 28 m/s). The side-foot kick needs large hip rotation power to turn the foot sideways.
verdicts.corrected_value: Side-foot 23.4 ± 1.7 m/s, instep 28.0 ± 2.1 m/s. Hip external-rotation torque 56 vs 33 N·m. Hip rotation power close to 1000 W (Lees 2010 review).
verdicts.note: These were straight side-foot kicks, not curlers.

verdicts.claim: Published curve kicks leave the foot at 15.1 to 25.4 m/s and spin at 25 to 59 rad/s. Maximal instep kicks reach 28.0 to 32.6 m/s.
verdicts.corrected_value: Speed about 15–25 m/s. Spin about 21–79 rad/s (3.4–12.5 rev/s).
verdicts.note: Whiteside et al. (ISBS) state 15.1–25.4 m/s and 25–59 rad/s. The 25–59 rad/s range comes from one study (Griffiths 2005). Ishii 2014 later measured up to 12.5 rev/s (79 rad/s). The 25.4 m/s top value is the Asai 2002 mean, and those were instep kicks.

verdicts.claim: Semi-professional players curling around a pole at 20 m produced 19.2 m/s and 36.4 rad/s, with 1.49 m of lateral deflection. Their straight kicks were 22.1 m/s. Faster balls had less spin (r = -0.81). More spin gave more deflection (r = 0.89). The spin axis tilted about 63 degrees from horizontal, not fully vertical, because contact was below the ball's midline.
verdicts.note: Whiteside, Alderson & Elliott, ISBS proceedings. Pilot: n = 4, 250 Hz Vicon, 20.12 m. Curve-kick spin range 4.8–6.6 rev/s, axis 62.6 ± 3.9°. The paper says 'significant' but ran no inferential statistics. The authors give contact 'inferior to the midline and right of it' as the reason for the tilt.

verdicts.claim: Real curve kicks rarely spin faster than 10 rev/s. Most curve kicks leave the foot at 20 m/s or more.
verdicts.corrected_value: Usually 4–9 rev/s, up to 12.5 rev/s measured. Measured curve-kick speeds are about 15–25 m/s, often near 19–20 m/s.
verdicts.note: Asai 2007 writes both statements. But its '≥20 m/s' rests on Asai 2002, which measured instep kicks. Whiteside: mean 19.2 m/s (16.9–21.2). Asai 2020: about 19 m/s. Griffiths: 15–18 m/s. Ishii: one kick at 12.5 rev/s.

verdicts.claim: Wind-tunnel data: a ball flying at 26 m/s and spinning at 8 rev/s (spin parameter 0.21) gains about 4 m/s of sideways speed from the Magnus force. At spin parameter 0.18, both the drag and side-force coefficients are about 0.25.
verdicts.note: Quoted: 'when a soccer ball is in flight at 26 m/s and 8 rev/s, it is deflected at ~4 m/s due to the Magnus effect.' The paper gives no time window for this. Cd ≈ Cs ≈ 0.25 is for the 27 m/s, 7 rev/s smoke kick. Wind-tunnel spin tests covered only 22–30 m/s.

verdicts.claim: Smoke visualisation of a real curve kick (27 m/s, 7 rev/s) shows the wake behind the ball thrown to one side, like a downwash. The sideways force on the ball is the reaction to this deflected air.
verdicts.note: Titanium tetrachloride smoke, top view, 4500 fps. 'The vortex deviated and flowed like a downwash... The force acting in a lateral direction due to a counteraction to this vortex was a major reason for the curvature.' Vortex angle about 128°.

verdicts.claim: With spin, the air separates earlier on the side of the ball that moves into the airflow and later on the side that moves with it. This gives an uneven wake and a force at right angles to both the flight direction and the spin axis.
verdicts.note: Bray & Kerwin 2003, introduction: 'separation occurs earlier at points on the surface advancing into the flow and later for those that are receding... resultant force whose direction is normal to the plane containing the velocity vector and the spin axis.'

verdicts.claim: Measured sidespin free kicks left the foot at 23.0 to 28.3 m/s and slowed to 17.9 to 20.4 m/s after 0.9 s, which covered about 20 m. The fitted drag coefficient was 0.25 to 0.30 and the lift (side) coefficient was 0.23 to 0.29.
verdicts.corrected_value: 23.0–28.3 m/s at t = 0.1 s, and 17.9–20.4 m/s at t = 0.9 s. That is a 22–28% loss over 0.8 s of tracked flight. Cd 0.25–0.30, Cl 0.23–0.29.
verdicts.note: The speeds were measured 0.1 s after contact, not at foot contact. One left-footed player did 10 kicks with 'conventional instep kicking' and sidespin. The fitted spin axis was 61–96°.

verdicts.claim: For a central free kick from 18.3 m at 25 m/s, over a 1.83 m wall at 9.14 m, the launch elevation must stay between 16.5 and 17.5 degrees with almost pure sidespin. Tilting the spin axis by 7 degrees (adding backspin) is as harmful as kicking 1 m/s harder. After the ball clears the wall, the keeper has about 0.45 s.
verdicts.note: Simulation with Cd 0.28 and Cl 0.26. The wall blocks 75% of the goal line.

verdicts.claim: Soccer balls go through the drag crisis at a critical Reynolds number of 2.2 to 3.0 × 10^5, which is about 12 to 15 m/s of air speed. Below this band the drag coefficient of a non-spinning ball is about 0.43. Above it, the value is about 0.15.
verdicts.corrected_value: Re 2.2–3.0 × 10^5 ≈ 15–21 m/s (D = 0.22 m). Fevernova and Roteiro are about 15 m/s, and their drag starts to drop at about 12 m/s. Teamgeist is about 21 m/s. Across modern balls (Hong & Asai 2014), Re is 2.2–3.6 × 10^5 ≈ 15–25 m/s. Cd about 0.43 sub-critical and about 0.15 super-critical is correct.
verdicts.note: The '12–15 m/s' figure describes only the Roteiro drag drop. It does not convert 3.0 × 10^5 correctly. Lees 2010: for a rotating ball the critical Re is about 3 × 10^5 (≈20 m/s), and the coefficients change without a sudden jump.

verdicts.claim: Powerful shots and free kicks (25 to 35 m/s) reach the goal before they slow into the drag-crisis band. So the drag crisis does not explain the late bend of fast shots. It can matter for slower, longer balls such as youth curlers, curled passes and crosses.
verdicts.corrected_value: The critical band is about 15–25 m/s, depending on the ball. Typical curlers (17–25 m/s) start in or near it. For a spinning ball the drag change is gradual, not a switch.
verdicts.note: Asai 2007 does write the first sentence. But Lees 2010 (citing Asai 2007) says spinning balls show no sudden coefficient change. The claim that it matters for youth curlers is speculation, and nobody measured it. Carré 2002 found Cd RISING with speed from 15 to 35 m/s for a Mitre ball. So ball-to-ball variation is large.

verdicts.claim: In wind-tunnel tests at constant spin, the side-force coefficient falls as ball speed rises. So a slowing ball with the same spin bends more per metre.
verdicts.note: Asai 2007: 'When the number of revolutions was constant, the Cs decreased as the speed of the ball increased... the rate of curvature decreased as the speed increased.' Path curvature = ρACs/(2m), so it tracks Cs. CAVEAT: the only free-flight study (Asai 2020) found Cs FELL from 0.27 to 0.24 during flight, and the curvature peaked mid-flight. The wind-tunnel inference is not confirmed in real flight.

verdicts.claim: The spinning-ball spiral: when spin stays nearly constant, a spinning ball follows a tightening (exponential) spiral. The bending grows once drag has clearly slowed the ball. The cause: the spin force scales with speed, but drag scales with speed squared. For soccer, the paper gives a characteristic length of about 54 m, launch speed 30 m/s and spin parameter 0.21.
verdicts.corrected_value: L = 54 m, U0 = 30 m/s, S = 0.21 (Dupeux et al. 2011, Table 2). L = 54 m assumes CD ≈ 0.4. With measured in-flight Cd 0.25–0.30, L ≈ 60–75 m. The Bray & Kerwin speed decay gives about 60–65 m.
verdicts.note: 'Lift ∝ speed' is a MODEL assumption: F_L = 2Cn·ρπR³ωU, with Cn ≈ 0.1–0.13 from water tests with small balls. Measured soccer Cs rises less than linearly with Sp and levels off near 0.26–0.3. So the real side force scales about as U^1.5 at fixed spin, and the spiral is much weaker than the ideal model predicts. I read the NJP 2010 abstract and model. The site blocked its sports section, so I confirmed the table from the authors' 2011 J Fluids Struct paper.

verdicts.claim: The spiral authors explain Roberto Carlos's 1997 free kick against France with this effect. The kick came from about 35 m, which is close to the length L. DISPUTED DETAILS: other sources give about 30 m. The paper's lift model is also about 3 times weaker than measured soccer-ball side forces.
verdicts.corrected_value: 35 m (Dupeux) vs about 30 m (Asai et al., Physics World 1998). The Dupeux 2011 model used U0 = 38 m/s, ω0 ≈ 88 rad/s (14 rev/s) and a 12° launch angle. The lift model is 2–3 times weaker: CL = 4·Cn·S ≈ 0.08–0.11 at S = 0.21, vs a measured 0.21–0.29.
verdicts.note: The authors call their 88 rad/s 'difficult to extract from the movies, yet plausible'. They say a pure circle would have missed by about 1 m.

verdicts.claim: Roberto Carlos struck that free kick with the OUTSIDE of his left foot, not the inside. The authors estimated 'probably over' 30 m/s and 'perhaps over' 10 rev/s from about 30 m. Press figures such as 136 km/h are unverified.
verdicts.corrected_value: Outside of the left foot, anticlockwise spin seen from above, about 30 m, probably >30 m/s, perhaps >10 rev/s (Asai, Akatsuka & Haake 1998). A peer-reviewed paper (Dupeux 2011, Table 1) lists 38.1 m/s (137 km/h) for Brazil v France 3 June 1997, but it does not name the measurement source.
verdicts.note: The 136–137 km/h figure is in the literature, so do not call it unsourced. Its origin is still unclear, probably a broadcast speed estimate. The Physics World article explains the late bend with the drag crisis ('entered the laminar flow regime... around the 10 m mark').

verdicts.claim: Motion capture of real 23 m curve kicks (about 19 m/s, about 5.8 rev/s): ball speed fell about 22% in 1 s, but spin fell only about 2% in 0.8 s. The side force halved from about 2 N to 1 N. The trajectory's curvature peaked MID-flight, and no spiral appeared at about 6 rev/s. This conflicts with the simple 'it always bends hardest at the end' story.
verdicts.note: Asai et al. 2020, Proceedings 49:88 (ISEA). Two collegiate players did 7 kicks each, filmed by a 24-camera 100 Hz Vicon. Cs also fell from 0.27 to 0.24. The printed curvature values (1.1, 31.1, 0.9 m^-1) cannot be right physically (they are probably a unit error). The authors also assume a vertical spin axis. Treat 'peaked mid-flight' as the authors' conclusion from a small sample.

verdicts.claim: The side-force coefficient rises with the spin-to-speed ratio, but by less than the ratio itself.
verdicts.note: Free flight: Cs 0.21, 0.24, 0.29 at Sp 0.18, 0.22, 0.34. Sp rises 1.9 times, but Cs rises only 1.4 times. Wind tunnel: 0.20, 0.23, 0.24 at Sp 0.14, 0.18, 0.23. Cs ≈ 0.5·√Sp fits both sets.

verdicts.claim: Model estimate (my calculation from the published coefficients: Cs ≈ 0.5·√Sp fitted to Asai 2020, Cd 0.27, spin decay 2.5%/s, no gravity). A 25 m/s, 8 rev/s curler drifts from its launch line by 0.64 m at 10 m, 2.7 m at 20 m and 6.3 m at 30 m. The bend radius tightens from about 80 m to 66 m over 30 m (about 18%). A 16 m/s, 5 rev/s youth curler bends almost the same per metre (2.6 m at 20 m) because the spin-to-speed ratio is the same. It takes 1.5 s for 20 m instead of 0.9 s.
verdicts.corrected_value: The arithmetic reproduces: 0.64, 2.66 and 6.28 m, radius 80 → 66 m, youth 2.62 m, 0.94 s vs 1.47 s. But the ~18% tightening depends on the wind-tunnel Cs(Sp) trend. The only free-flight data (Asai 2020) show Cs falling in flight, so the true radius change could be anywhere from about −20% to +10%.
verdicts.note: A safe narration line: drift ≈ distance² / 150 m, so twice the distance gives four times the drift. Pure sidespin is assumed. With the measured axis tilt of about 60° from horizontal, the sideways part is about 10% smaller. The youth case extrapolates below the 19–30 m/s data range.

verdicts.claim: Aiming estimate (geometry from the same model): to finish on target at 20 m, the ball must leave about 7 to 8 degrees outside the target line, which is about 2.5 m wide at the goal. The widest point of the bow is about 0.7 m from the straight line. At 25 m the numbers are about 10 degrees and 1.1 m. At 30 m they are about 12 degrees and 1.6 m. Real kickers do send the ball away from the target first and let the curve bring it back.
verdicts.note: Derived, not measured. For R ≈ 75 m: angle = d/(2R), which gives 7.6°, 9.5° and 11.5°. Bow = d²/(8R), which gives 0.67, 1.04 and 1.5 m. Offset at goal = d²/(2R) ≈ 2.7 m at 20 m. Whiteside supports this in words ('direct the ball slightly away from the target area... let the curvature bring it back'). Alcock 2012 found the support foot points to the right of the target for right-footers.

verdicts.claim: Simulated free kicks: a centrally struck ball (26 m/s, no spin) reaches the top corner in 0.9 s. An 8 cm offset strike (18.5 m/s, 10.2 rev/s) bends much more but must be launched higher and takes 1.6 s. This gives the keeper more time.
verdicts.note: Carré et al. 2002, 'Kick a' vs 'Kick b'. The ball travels about 30% slower. Lees 2010 describes the flight as 78% longer, with a deviation of over 3 m.

verdicts.claim: One simulation suggests a wet boot and ball give about 2 rev/s (13 rad/s) less spin, so a curler misses by about one ball width. DISPUTED: a later validated model (Ishii 2014) found friction has little effect at match foot speeds.
verdicts.note: Kick b lands one ball radius inside the post and Kick c one ball radius outside, so the shift is about one ball diameter. The 13 rad/s is the MAXIMUM effect over friction 0–1, so this is a worst case. The dispute with Ishii 2014 is real.

verdicts.claim: Measured football lift or side coefficients level off at about 0.26 to 0.3. More spin past about 100 rad/s at 18 m/s adds drag but not much more bend.
verdicts.note: Carré 2002 used a horizontal spin axis at 18 m/s: Cl levels at about 0.26 above about 100 rad/s, and Cd goes from 0.2 to 0.5 at 240 rad/s. 'About 0.3 is the maximum... in a typical game situation.' Some wind-tunnel data are higher (Spampinato 2004: 0.31–0.39), so say 'about 0.25–0.35'.

verdicts.claim: In wind-tunnel tests on a spinning soccer ball, a negative (reversed) Magnus effect appeared in the critical Reynolds-number range. It was not observed when the boundary layer was fully laminar or fully turbulent. I read only the abstract, and its role in real curlers is unproven.
verdicts.note: Kray, Franke & Frank 2014, J Wind Eng Ind Aerodyn 124:46–53. A model soccer ball spun perpendicular to the flow at Re 96,000–462,000 (full-scale equivalent about 6.5–31 m/s). The positive effect appeared when the boundary layer was laminar or turbulent on both sides. I saw only the abstract text, through a search summary.

verdicts.claim: Goalkeepers do not fully allow for spin-induced sideways acceleration. Novice keepers stopped only 6% of curved free kicks whose first heading pointed the opposite way to where they ended, against 56% of other kicks. Even the most experienced professional keeper could not fully account for the curve.
verdicts.note: Dessing & Craig 2010, PLoS ONE 5:e13161. Ten recreational players and two keepers (aged 16 and 30) used a head-mounted display. Simulated 30 m kicks at 10 rev/s deviated about 2 m in 1.4375 s, with CL 0.2 and CD 0.33.

verdicts.claim: Curve-kick technique in international female players: a wide approach angle, the support foot pointed to the right of the target (for right-footers), the kicking leg swung across the face of the goal, and the foot moving upward and outward at impact. Peak knee angular velocity and peak ankle speed occur AT impact, which supports the 'kick through the ball' cue.
verdicts.corrected_value: The abstract says 'impact the ball with the foot moving upwards and in an abducted position'. That describes the foot's position (turned out), not an outward motion.
verdicts.note: Alcock et al. 2012, J Sports Sci 30:387–394. 17 Vicon cameras at 250 Hz. Foot speed at impact did not differ from the instep kick. Curve kicks used more knee angular velocity.

verdicts.claim: Curve kicks from 20 m at a 1 m² target: the lateral launch angle and the tilt of the spin axis best predicted left-right placement. Launch angles had to stay within about 3 degrees to hit the target.
verdicts.note: Alcock et al. 2012, J Appl Biomech 28:70–77, 15 elite female players. Vertical placement depended on vertical launch angle, forward speed and backspin.

verdicts.claim: National FA coaching advice for the curled pass: approach at an acute angle, plant the standing foot beside the ball angled towards its front, and wrap the kicking foot around the far side of the ball with the instep. The example given is Keira Walsh's pass around a defender in the Women's Euro 2022 final.
verdicts.note: Quoted: 'be at an acute angle to the ball', 'plant their non-kicking foot to the side of the ball while ensuring it's angled towards the front of the ball', 'wrap their kicking foot around the opposite side of the ball using their instep'. The Walsh pass set up Ella Toone.

verdicts.claim: Maximal instep ball speed in trained youth players rises with age: U13 66.7 km/h (18.5 m/s), U15 76.9 km/h (21.4 m/s), U17 81.4 km/h (22.6 m/s), U20 98.7 km/h (27.4 m/s). Kicking accuracy gets worse around the growth spurt (U13 to U15). Note: the abstract labels the youngest group differently from the table.
verdicts.note: Table 1: U9 48.54, U11 57.87, U13 66.70, U15 76.92, U17 81.35, U20 98.74 km/h. The abstract wrongly gives 48.54 as U11. These were 11 m penalty-style instep kicks aimed at a 1×1 m target. U9 and U11 used a size-4 ball.

verdicts.claim: Estimate: good 11 to 16 year-olds probably curl the ball at about 13 to 19 m/s (47 to 68 km/h). This combines their maximal kick speeds with the 10 to 30% speed loss of curve kicks. No direct youth curve-kick measurement was found.
verdicts.corrected_value: About 11–14 m/s at U11, 13–17 m/s at U13 and 15–19 m/s at U15–U17. Use 13–19 m/s only for ages 12–16.
verdicts.note: I found no direct youth curve-kick data. Adult curve kicks run 13–16% below straight kicks (Whiteside 19.2 vs 22.1 m/s, Nunome side-foot 23.4 vs instep 28.0). Present this as an estimate.

verdicts.claim: Isaac Newton described a curving, spinning tennis ball in a 1672 paper, about 180 years before Magnus studied the effect.
verdicts.note: Newton wrote it in his 1672 letter on light and colours, after he watched tennis at Cambridge. Robins explained musket-ball drift in 1742. Magnus demonstrated the effect in 1852 with a spinning BRASS CYLINDER, not a ball. The Chalkdust source does not mention Robins.

mechanism_errors: Step 2, '8 to 10 cm off centre': this offset comes from an FE model of an INSTEP-shaped foot at 25 m/s foot speed (Asai 2002). In that same model, 8–10 cm gives only 15–18.5 m/s. Step 3's adult 19–25 m/s would need about 4–6 cm (6 cm gives 20.7 m/s and 6.9 rev/s). Nobody has measured real curve-kick offsets. Say 'a few centimetres off centre, on the far half, slightly below the middle', or drop the number.

Step 2, 'ball squashes to about 85%' and 'about 9 ms': both figures come from instep kicks in Asai 2002. The paper's Methods say 'kicked a ball with the instep'. For a curve kick, use Ishii 2014: 9.6–12 ms. Present the 85% as 'in a hard kick'. The 'gear teeth' analogy is acceptable. Ishii shows the ball rolls on the foot without sliding for friction ≥0.3 at match speeds.

Step 4, 'push starts at about 2 to 3 N, roughly half the ball's weight': F = ½ρAv²Cs. At 19 m/s this gives about 2 N (Asai 2020 measured about 2 N), which is half the weight (4.2 N). At 25 m/s with Cs ≈ 0.25 it is about 3.3–3.6 N, about 80% of the weight. Say 'about 2 to 3.5 N, from half to most of the ball's weight'.

Step 4, direction and wake: CORRECT. The side that moves with the air separates later, the wake goes the other way, and the ball moves toward the with-flow side. A right-footer's inside-foot curler spins anticlockwise from above and bends right to left. 'Bends the way its front surface turns' is also correct.

Step 6, 'So the curve tightens a little, about 10 to 20%': this is only a model result from wind-tunnel Cs(Sp) data. The only free-flight measurement (Asai 2020, about 19 m/s and 5.8 rev/s) found Cs FELL from 0.27 to 0.24 and the curvature peaked mid-flight. So real curlers may not tighten at all. Say 'the bend stays about the same tightness; the drift looks late mainly because of geometry'.

Step 6, 'On long, fast, high-spin shots, this becomes a tightening spiral': the Dupeux spiral assumes a side force proportional to spin × speed (Cs linear in Sp) and CD ≈ 0.4. For real soccer balls, Cs rises less than linearly (about √Sp) and levels off near 0.26–0.3. So the spiral is much weaker than the ideal model, and nobody has measured it in air. Present it as a model idea for very long (30 m or more), very high-spin shots only.

Step 6, 'less than about 12 to 15 m/s the airflow can change and add drag': the numbers are wrong. Critical Re 2.2–3.6 × 10^5 corresponds to about 15–25 m/s, depending on the ball (Asai 2007; Hong & Asai 2014). For SPINNING balls the change is gradual, with no sudden jump (Lees 2010). The direction is right: below the critical speed Cd rises from about 0.15 to about 0.43.

Step 3, 'Adults curl the ball at about 19 to 25 m/s': measured curlers range 15–25 m/s (Griffiths 15–18, Whiteside 16.9–21.2, Asai 2020 about 19, Ishii 19.8–24.3). Say 'about 17 to 25 m/s (60 to 90 km/h)'.

Step 5, 'part of a huge circle, about 150 m across': this is correct for Cs ≈ 0.25 (R = 2m/(ρA·Cs) ≈ 75 m). For lower spin ratios (Cs ≈ 0.21), the circle is about 180 m across. A tilted spin axis (about 60° from horizontal) makes the sideways bend about 10% smaller and adds some lift.

Misconception 1 nuance: the pressure difference is real, and it is what pushes the ball. The error is to use Bernoulli alone to explain it, because Bernoulli does not hold across the boundary layer. Do not say that the pressure explanation is false.
Misconception 3 uses the same wrong band (12–15 m/s). Replace it with about 15–25 m/s, depending on the ball, and add that the change is gradual for spinning balls.

Misconception 7 is overstated: Ishii 2014 tested only upper stiffness and friction. The authors say other shoe features (rubber or 3D elements) may matter, and friction affected spin at a 5 m/s foot speed (short passes).
Misconception 12: Magnus demonstrated the effect in 1852 with a rotating brass cylinder, not a ball.
safe_numbers_for_narration: In a real curve kick, the foot touches the ball for only about 10 thousandths of a second (9.6 to 12 ms, measured at 2500 frames per second).
University players' curlers left the foot at about 20 to 24 m/s (70 to 87 km/h) and spun 3 to 12 times each second. Most spun about 7 to 9 times.
A computer model showed that a centre hit gives about 26 m/s with almost no spin. Moving the contact 8 cm to the side gives about 18.5 m/s and about 10 turns per second.
In that simulation, the curled free kick took 1.6 s to reach the top corner. The straight, centrally struck kick took 0.9 s.
Changing boot-ball friction from zero to very high adds at most about 2 turns per second. The ball spins even with zero friction, because it wraps around the foot.
Making the boot upper 10 times stiffer (5 to 50 MPa) made almost no difference to speed or spin.
In flight, a curler lost about 22% of its speed in one second, but only about 2% of its spin.
The sideways push on a 19 m/s curler is about 2 newtons, roughly half the weight of the ball.
A curler bends along a very large circle, about 150 m across. So a 20 m curler drifts about 2.7 m from the line it started on.
Drift grows with the square of distance. Twice the distance gives four times the drift, and about three quarters of the drift happens in the second half.
To land on target from 20 m, the ball must start about 7 to 8 degrees outside the target line.
For an 18 m free kick over a wall at 25 m/s, the launch angle must stay in a 1-degree window (16.5 to 17.5 degrees).
After the ball clears the wall, the keeper has only about 0.45 seconds.
In virtual reality, novice keepers stopped only 6% of curlers that first headed the wrong way, against 56% of other kicks.
Measured curlers do not spin about a vertical axis. The axis tilts about 63 degrees from horizontal.
Trained 12-year-olds kick at about 18.5 m/s at full power, 14-year-olds at about 21 m/s, and 16-year-olds at about 22.6 m/s.
Isaac Newton described a curving tennis ball in 1672, 180 years before Magnus studied the effect in 1852.

research.kick: Laces instep drive (the low, driven power shot)
research.one_line_hook: Your foot touches the ball for less than one hundredth of a second. In that time the ball goes from standing still to faster than your foot ever moved. How can the ball beat the thing that hit it?
research.mechanism_story:
1. Wind-up. You approach from an angle of about 45 degrees, in three or four steps, with a long last stride. Your hips turn away from the ball and your kicking-side arm swings out wide. Your body now works like a drawn bow.

2. Plant. Your standing foot lands beside the ball, toes to the target. That knee bends and your body brakes. The planted leg becomes the pivot for the swing.

3. Whip. Your hip pulls the thigh forward first. Then the thigh slows, and this slowing flings the shin forward, like the crack of a whip. At contact your knee moves at only about 5 m/s (17 km/h). Your toes move at about 22 m/s (79 km/h).

4. Lock. Your toes point down and your ankle stays rigid. The ball meets the hard, bony top of the foot, near the ankle. A loose ankle bends back like a hinge and absorbs energy. A locked ankle joins foot and shin into one heavier club. Thus more of your leg's mass takes part in the hit.

5. Squash. Foot and ball touch for only about 9 thousandths of a second. They move together about 15 cm. The ball flattens by several centimetres. The peak force is near 3000 N, the weight of a 300 kg motorbike. In the first half of contact, your foot shoves the ball. In the second half, the squashed ball rebounds from your foot like a trampoline. That rebound adds the last big part of the speed. Thus the ball leaves 1.2 to 1.5 times faster than your foot moved.

6. Aim. The point where your foot meets the ball sets the launch angle and the spin. A push straight through the centre gives the most speed and little spin. With your knee and chest over the ball, your shin is upright. The laces face forward and the foot moves level, so the ball stays low. If you lean back, or plant behind the ball, your foot meets the ball on the way up and under its centre. The ball climbs and gets backspin.

7. Flight. At 25 m/s the air pushes back on the ball with a force of about three-quarters of its weight. The ball loses about 6 m/s over 18 m. If the ball barely spins, the swirl of air behind it can flip from side to side. This effect is strongest at 15 to 25 m/s, near the "drag crisis". The ball can then wobble or dip. This is the knuckle effect.
plain_metaphors: Whip crack: the heavy handle (thigh) moves first and then stops. The stopping sends the energy down to the light tip (foot), which moves much faster.
Bowling ball hits a ping-pong ball: when something heavy hits something light and bouncy, the light thing flies away faster than the heavy thing was moving. Your leg is the bowling ball.
Hammer with a loose head: a floppy ankle is like a hammer head on a hinge. It folds on impact and wastes the hit. A locked ankle is a hammer head fixed tight to the handle.
Trampoline inside the ball: the ball squashes against your foot like a trampoline mat, then springs back. That spring-back does a big part of the work.
Crumple zone: a car's crumple zone absorbs crash energy on purpose. A floppy ankle is a crumple zone you do not want when you shoot.
Playground swing: your foot moves on an arc like a swing. It is lowest and moving level at the bottom of the arc. If the ball sits past the bottom, the foot meets it on the way up and the ball rises.
Pushing a shopping trolley: push it exactly through the middle and it goes straight and fast. Push one corner and it turns and goes slower. Hitting the ball off-centre gives spin and costs speed.
Motorbike on the ball: the peak force in a hard shot is close to 3000 N. That is like a 300 kg motorbike standing on the ball for less than a hundredth of a second.
Boat wake: a moving ball leaves a churned trail of air behind it, like the wake behind a boat. A bigger wake means more drag.
Flag in the wind: behind a ball with no spin, the wake can flap from side to side like a flag. Each flap nudges the ball sideways. That is the knuckle wobble.
Drawn bow: the wind-up (hips turned, arm out wide) stretches the front of the body like a bow string. The kick releases it.

jargon_map.plain_version: How long the boot and ball actually touch. For a hard laces shot it is about 9 ms, less than one hundredth of a second.
Ball speed divided by foot speed. It tells you how well your foot passes its speed to the ball. Good adult strikes reach about 1.2 to 1.5.
How heavy your foot 'feels' to the ball during the hit. A locked ankle makes more of the leg join the collision, so the foot acts heavier.
The bounciness of the collision. It measures how much of the squash energy comes back as speed. For foot on ball it is about 0.46 to 0.68.
Energy that turns into heat and wobble in the ball, boot and foot instead of into ball speed.
How much the ball squashes flat against the foot. In a hard kick it is several centimetres.
The size of the shove on the ball. The peak is close to 3000 N, more than four times the player's body weight.
Pointing the toes down. 'Forced' means the ball pushes the toes down further during the hit, which bends the ankle and wastes energy.
How firmly you hold the ankle so it does not bend when the ball hits it.
The whip order: hip first, then thigh, then shin, then foot. Each part speeds up the next part.
The fling effect: when the thigh slows down, it throws the shin forward faster without extra muscle effort.
The standing leg and foot next to the ball. It is the pivot for the swing.
Stretching the front of the body (hips back, opposite arm out wide) like a bow, then releasing it into the kick.
How far your hips and shoulders twist against each other in the wind-up, like wringing a towel.
How far from the ball's centre your foot hits it. Zero offset means straight through the middle.
How steeply the ball leaves the ground.
A spinning ball drags air around with it, and the air pushes the ball sideways, up or down. Backspin makes a ball float up.
Air resistance: how hard the air pushes back on the ball, and how 'slippery' the ball shape is.
The thin skin of air that hugs the ball's surface as it flies.
The speed at which the skin of air suddenly changes from smooth to turbulent. It then clings on longer, the wake shrinks and drag drops sharply. For a soccer ball this is at roughly 15 to 20 m/s.
The swirling trail of air behind the ball.
The wobble or sudden dip of a ball that barely spins, caused by the wake flipping from side to side.
The best place on the foot to hit the ball. For a laces drive it is the bony top of the foot, a few centimetres in front of the ankle.

claims.claim: In maximal instep kicks by 9 skilled adult players filmed at 1000 Hz, foot-ball contact lasted 9.1 ± 0.7 ms. Ball speed was 26.3 ± 3.4 m/s (range 19.2-32.6 m/s).
claims.value: 9.1 ms contact. Ball 26.3 m/s = 94.7 km/h (range 69-117 km/h)

claims.claim: In the same study, the ball-to-foot velocity ratio was 1.35 ± 0.09. The toe moved at 22.0 m/s at impact, but the knee moved at only 4.8 m/s. Shank angular velocity at impact was 35.8 rad/s (about 2050 degrees per second). Earlier studies report ratios from 1.06 to 1.29, and up to 1.65 when foot speed is measured at the ankle.
claims.value: ratio 1.35. Toe 22.0 m/s (79 km/h) vs knee 4.8 m/s (17 km/h)

claims.claim: At 4500 fps with 6 university players, mean contact time was 9.12 ms. Mean ball speed was 25.44 m/s and foot speed was 23.12 m/s. The foot moved 147 mm with the ball, about 66% of the 223 mm ball diameter.
claims.value: 9.12 ms. 147 mm travel. Ball 25.4 m/s (91.6 km/h)

claims.claim: With 5000 Hz video, ball deformation peaked at about 6 cm about 4 ms into contact. The foot is faster than the ball in the first half of contact and pushes it. In the second half the ball's recoil from the foot takes it to about 95% of its launch speed. The effective push lasts about three-quarters of the visible contact time.
claims.value: peak squash about 6 cm (about 27% of diameter)

claims.claim: Other studies measure less squash. Asai's finite-element model and experiment found the ball compressed to 85-86% of its diameter, about 3 cm. A review cites Shinkai et al. (2007) for deformation up to 68 mm. The values depend on how deformation is measured.
claims.value: about 3 cm to 6.8 cm

claims.claim: Peak ball reaction force reached 2926 N, more than four times the player's body weight. Earlier estimates were about 2500 N (Asai computer simulation) and 1610 N (Tol et al. 2002).
claims.value: 2926 N (about the weight of a 298 kg mass)

claims.claim: MYTH: 'longer contact = faster shot'. Shinkai/Nunome found only a weak NEGATIVE relationship between contact time and ball speed (r = -0.438, contact 8.2-9.8 ms). The authors call the longer-contact belief a myth among coaches and players.

With correct high-rate filtering, the shank is still speeding up at ball impact. Earlier studies that showed the leg slowing before contact had filtering errors. The authors say this supports the coaching advice to 'kick through the ball'.

The ball impact forces the ankle rapidly into plantar flexion (toes pushed down). Peak ankle angular acceleration comes mid-contact, and peak plantar-flexion velocity comes in the second half of contact.

A mechanical kicking limb compared a rigid ankle with a spring ankle, all else equal. The rigid ankle gave a higher effective mass (2.1 vs 1.7 kg), foot-to-ball ratio (1.16 vs 1.11) and ball speed (19.0 vs 18.3 m/s, about 4% more). The spring ankle bent 8.3 degrees and held 6.3 J of energy that never reached the ball. Caveat: the test used an Australian-football ball and a machine, not a soccer ball and a human.
claims.value: effective mass 2.1 kg vs 1.7 kg. Ball +0.7 m/s

claims.claim: In 51 junior-to-senior soccer players (Shinkai et al. 2013, as reported by Peacock), foot plus shoe mass was 84.0 ± 9.6% of the effective mass. Effective mass correlated with the foot-to-ball speed ratio (r = 0.89). Older, heavier players had both faster feet and more effective mass.
A review states that effective striking mass increases as muscle activation makes the limb more rigid. It is greatest when contact is closer to the ankle than to the metatarsals (toes).
The foot-ball coefficient of restitution ranges from 0.463 to 0.681. A rise from 0.5 to 0.65 would give about 10% more ball speed.

Ball speed and impact point show an inverted-U relationship. Projection speed was greatest when the impact point was about 6 cm in front of (distal to) the ankle joint (5 university players, 2500 fps, plus an impact-dynamics model). The model also shows foot speed at impact is the biggest single factor.
claims.value: sweet spot about 6 cm in front of the ankle

claims.claim: Asami & Nolte (1983, cited in the 2010 review) found that impact towards the far end of the foot forces more plantar flexion and reduces ball speed. Repeated impacts of this kind are linked to 'footballer's ankle'.

Finite-element model of an instep kick with a horizontal offset from the ball's axis. At 0 cm offset the ball left at 26.0 m/s with about 1.9 rev/s of spin. At 8 cm it left at 18.5 m/s with 10.5 rev/s. At 12 cm it left at 11.2 m/s with 16.2 rev/s. There is a clear trade-off between speed and spin.
claims.value: 0 cm: 26.0 m/s. 8 cm: 18.5 m/s and 10.5 rev/s

claims.claim: A finite-element skeletal foot model (Asai et al. 2005, cited in the review) varied the vertical offset. The fastest ball came from contact 20-40 mm below the ball's centre of mass. The highest projection angle, 16 degrees, came at 20 mm below. This is a simulation, so treat the exact numbers with care.
claims.value: best contact 2-4 cm below centre. Launch up to 16 degrees

claims.claim: Kicking is a proximal-to-distal motion. Angular velocity peaks first in the thigh, then the shank, then the foot. Knee extension velocity at ball contact is the strongest predictor of ball speed.

The hip is the main motor of the kick. Robertson & Mosher (1985) found about 2000 W at the hip and no more than 100 W at the knee. DISPUTED: Nunome et al. (2002) found knee power of more than 1000 W. The thigh's motion supplies about 20% of the knee-extension work through the 'fling' (motion-dependent) effect (Dorge 2002).
claims.value: hip about 2000 W

claims.claim: Skilled players choose an approach angle of about 43-45 degrees, and about 45 degrees gave maximum ball speed. Approach speed is only about 3-4 m/s. Professionals took a longer last step for a maximal kick (0.72-0.81 m) than for a submaximal kick (0.53-0.55 m).
claims.value: about 45 degrees. 3-4 m/s approach

claims.claim: Hip-shoulder separation reached 38-42 degrees in maximal kicks but only 6-12 degrees in submaximal kicks (2 professional players). The non-kicking arm goes out wide to make a 'tension arc' across the body that is released in the kick.
claims.value: 38-42 degrees vs 6-12 degrees

claims.claim: Skilled players leaned back 13 degrees for a low-trajectory kick and 17 degrees for a high-trajectory kick (Prassas et al. 1990). More backward lean goes with a higher ball.
claims.value: 13 degrees vs 17 degrees trunk lean

claims.claim: FOLKLORE / UNCONFIRMED: a common rule puts the plant foot 5-10 cm behind and 5-28 cm beside the ball (Hay 1993). The review states that experiments have not confirmed it.
claims.value: 5-10 cm behind, 5-28 cm beside

claims.claim: DISPUTED: in 13 players aged 13, a plant foot closer to the ball predicted faster shots. Mean distance was 14.1 cm, ball speed was 20.9 ± 2.5 m/s and foot speed 13.6 m/s. But a study of 366 Brazilian youth players found centroid-to-centroid distances of about 0.30-0.35 m at every age. It warns that too small a distance can slow kicks in U13-U17 players.
claims.value: 13-year-olds: 20.9 m/s = 75 km/h

claims.claim: Youth maximal instep penalty kicks (366 Brazilian players, 3D at 300 Hz). Ball speed: U9 48.5, U11 57.9, U13 66.7, U15 76.9, U17 81.4, U20 98.7 km/h. Foot speed: U11 53.8 to U20 78.2 km/h. Ball/foot ratio: U9 0.99, U11 1.07, U13 1.10, U15 1.18, U17 1.19, U20 1.26. Ball speed grows much faster than foot speed, so better strikes, not only stronger legs, explain the gain. Note: the abstract labels the 48.5 km/h group as U11, but the table and discussion give it as U9.

The same study cites Brazilian elite professionals at 99.7 ± 8.5 km/h ball speed (27.7 m/s) and 82.3 km/h foot speed (Vieira et al. 2016). Last stride length correlated with ball speed in all age groups (r = .36-.79). Accuracy got worse around the growth spurt (U13-U15).
claims.value: pros about 100 km/h

claims.claim: Prepubertal boys aged 11.7 ± 0.5 years reached a maximum instep ball speed of 17.3 ± 2.3 m/s.
Maximal instep ball speeds range from 18 to 35 m/s, depending on skill, age, approach angle and limb. Match shots at the 1990 World Cup reached 32-35 m/s (Ekblom 1994, secondary citation).
claims.value: 18-35 m/s = 65-126 km/h. World Cup 115-126 km/h

claims.claim: Guinness lists the fastest football kick as 129 km/h (35.8 m/s), set in a TV studio in Madrid in 2001. It lists the fastest shot in an English top-division game as 183 km/h (David Hirst, hit the crossbar). These are one-off radar readings, not lab data.
claims.value: 129 km/h (studio). 183 km/h (match)

claims.claim: FOLKLORE / DISPUTED: Ronny Heberson's 2006 free kick is often quoted at 210.9 km/h. No peer-reviewed or official measurement exists, and video analyses give lower speeds.
claims.value: 210.9 km/h claimed

claims.claim: FIFA Quality Pro size-5 ball: rebound 135-155 cm from a 2 m drop onto steel at 20 degrees C, and at least 125 cm at 5 degrees C (cold balls are less bouncy). Mass 420-445 g, circumference 68.5-69.5 cm.
claims.value: rebound 135-155 cm from 2 m

claims.claim: Law 2: circumference 68-70 cm, mass 410-450 g at the start of the match, pressure 0.6-1.1 atmosphere at sea level.

In robotic kicking tests, ball pressures of 0.6, 0.9 and 1.2 bar gave no difference in ball speed. Launch elevation was about 2 degrees higher at the lower pressure (Neilson & Jones 2005, cited in the review).
