Shoe weight does not change ball speed. Barefoot kicks were up to 1.5% faster than shod kicks, because the bare foot is already fully pointed at impact and bends less. But barefoot kicks were up to 20% less accurate. A higher toe box can cut ball speed by up to 2.0%.

Drag crisis: the drag coefficient of a non-spinning soccer ball falls from about 0.5 to about 0.1-0.2. The critical Reynolds number is 2.2-3.0 x 10^5, about 15 m/s for a non-spinning ball and about 20 m/s for a spinning one.
claims.value: critical speed about 15-20 m/s (54-72 km/h)

claims.claim: At a typical 25 m/s, drag on the ball is about 3.25 N. That slows the ball by about 6 m/s over an 18 m free kick.
claims.value: 3.25 N. About 6 m/s lost over 18 m

claims.claim: Wind-tunnel and robot tests of World Cup balls. Critical Re is about 2.2-2.5 x 10^5 for Brazuca and 3.3-3.6 x 10^5 for Jabulani (about 15-17 vs 22-25 m/s, my conversion with d = 0.22 m). Robot kicks at 30 m/s over 25 m with less than 1 rotation scattered by 0.20 m (Brazuca) up to 0.68 m (Cafusa), depending on ball and panel orientation.
claims.value: 30 m/s, 25 m, less than 1 rotation. Scatter 0.2-0.68 m

claims.claim: Knuckle physics: zigzag paths come from unsteady lift forces. The effect grows when launch speed falls in the drag crisis, which for soccer is 15-25 m/s. The zigzag length scale is about 13.5 m, so a 20-30 m shot has room for only about one or two sideways changes. Zigzags were seen with the Jabulani when kicked with no spin.
claims.value: 15-25 m/s (54-90 km/h). Wavelength about 13.5 m

claims.claim: Knuckling shots had the lowest spin, 0.9 ± 0.5 rev/s, compared with 4.0 ± 1.8 rev/s for a straight instep shot. The foot's angle of attack was 3.3 degrees for the knuckle, 19.3 degrees for straight and 32.6 degrees for curve shots. From the abstract only. I could not open the full text or check the direction of the spin.
claims.value: knuckle 0.9 rev/s vs straight 4.0 rev/s

claims.claim: Smoke visualisation of a kicked knuckleball showed a peak vortex lift of about 2.0 N, with the lift changing at about 3.5 Hz.
claims.value: about 2 N at about 3.5 Hz

claims.claim: Wind-tunnel work on the Teamgeist ball found that the knuckle effect comes from unsteady movement of the vortex wake in the supercritical Reynolds-number regime, not from spin.

Coaching sources for the laces drive: plant foot beside the ball, pointing at the target. Ankle 'locked'. Strike the centre of the ball so it stays low. Knee and chest over the ball. A plant foot behind the ball makes the ball rise. These are coaching sources, not biomechanics studies.

COACHING DISAGREEMENT: one national sport body teaches 'lean forward to keep your shot low, lock the ankle, strike the centre off your laces, long back lift but minimum follow through'. Other coaches teach a full swing through. The biomechanics (shank still speeding up at impact) supports not braking the leg before contact.

technique_cues: Toes down, ankle locked like a brick. This limits the forced toe-bend at impact, so the foot acts heavier and less energy is lost in the ankle.

Hit with the hard, bony top of the foot, a few centimetres in front of the ankle, not the toes. Contact near the ankle gives the most effective mass. Contact near the toes bends the ankle and slows the ball.

Plant the standing foot beside the ball, toes to the target, with a comfortable gap (about a boot-width to a hand-span). This puts the bottom of your swing arc at the ball, so the foot moves level at contact.
Knee over the ball, chest over the ball at contact. This keeps the shin upright so the laces face forward, not up. That gives a low launch angle.
Strike through the middle of the ball. Force through the centre gives the most speed and the least spin. Off-centre contact turns speed into spin.

Approach from an angle (about 30-45 degrees) in 3-4 steps with a longer last stride. This lets the pelvis wind up and unwind and lets you lean away so the toes can point down without hitting the ground.
Swing from the hip, snap from the knee. Keep the knee relaxed so the thigh leads and the shin whips. This is the proximal-to-distal whip that makes the foot fast.
Opposite arm out wide, then pull it across. This makes the tension arc, stretching the front of the body like a bow before the kick releases it.
Do not slow the leg down before contact. Swing through the ball towards the target. The foot must still be speeding up at impact, because the ball is gone in less than 10 ms.
Eyes on the ball at contact and head still. Small errors in the impact point change the speed, spin and direction.
Smooth, not wild. Hitting clean is worth more than hitting hard. The ball/foot ratio (strike quality) is what grows most from U11 to U20.

common_mistakes.mistake: Toes up or ankle floppy (the 'banana foot')
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The ankle folds on impact like a hinge. Less leg mass joins the collision and energy goes into bending the ankle, so the ball leaves slower. It can also hurt the front of the ankle.
common_mistakes.fix: Point the toes down and hold the ankle firm before the swing starts. Practise short laces volleys against a wall to feel the lock.

common_mistakes.mistake: Toe-poke or contact near the toes
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: Contact far from the ankle forces the foot to bend down more and gives a smaller effective mass. Ball speed drops and the strike is less repeatable.
common_mistakes.fix: Aim the bony top of the foot, just in front of the ankle, at the ball's centre.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning back at contact
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The foot meets the ball on the way up and under its centre. The launch angle rises and backspin adds lift, so the ball sails over the bar.
common_mistakes.fix: Chest and knee over the ball. Look down at the ball as you strike.

common_mistakes.mistake: Plant foot behind the ball
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The ball sits past the bottom of the swing arc, so the foot is already rising at contact. The ball climbs.
common_mistakes.fix: Plant the standing foot level with the ball. Put a disc marker where the plant foot must land.

common_mistakes.mistake: Plant foot too far to the side
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: You must reach, the leg tilts and contact goes off-centre. Off-centre contact turns speed into spin: in a model, an 8 cm offset cut ball speed from 26 to 18.5 m/s.
common_mistakes.fix: Plant a comfortable boot-width to hand-span from the ball. Check that you can swing through without stretching.

common_mistakes.mistake: Plant foot jammed too close
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The swing is cramped and the knee cannot extend freely, so foot speed falls. One youth study warns that too small a gap slows kicks in U13-U17 players.
common_mistakes.fix: Leave room for the kicking foot to pass cleanly beside the standing foot.

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging a stiff, straight leg from the hip only
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: No whip. The thigh never hands its speed to the shin, so the foot moves much slower than it could.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep the knee bent in the backswing. Let the thigh lead, then snap the shin through.

common_mistakes.mistake: Braking the leg at contact to 'control' the shot
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The foot slows exactly when speed matters. Ball speed depends mostly on foot speed at impact.
common_mistakes.fix: Swing through the ball towards the target and let the leg finish naturally.

common_mistakes.mistake: Running straight at the ball
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: Less hip rotation and no lean away from the ball. The pointed toes can catch the ground, so players lift the toes and lose the ankle lock.
common_mistakes.fix: Approach from an angle of about 30-45 degrees and lean slightly away from the kicking side.

common_mistakes.mistake: Looking at the goal instead of the ball at contact
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The impact point drifts off-centre, which changes speed, spin and direction.
common_mistakes.fix: Pick the target before the run-up, then keep your eyes on the ball through contact.

drills: Ankle-lock volleys: hold the ball in your hands, drop it and strike it with the laces into a wall 3-5 m away, toes pointed down. 3 sets of 10 each foot. The goal is a sharp 'thump' sound and a ball that comes back straight.

Knee-height target band: tape a line or hang a rope at about 50-60 cm across a wall or goal. From 8-12 m, drive stationary balls under the line. Knee-over-ball and plant-beside-ball show up at once as low shots.

Plant-foot marker: put a flat disc where the standing foot must land, level with the ball and about a hand-span beside it. Take 10 shots, then move the disc 5 cm closer or farther to find your personal best spot. Film it or use a speed app.
Three-step angle run: set a cone 3-4 steps back at about 45 degrees from the ball. Walk-through, jog-through, then full speed. Say 'long last step' before each shot.
Whip swings: hold a fence or partner for balance. Swing the kicking leg slowly with the thigh leading and the shin lagging, then snap. 10 slow, 10 medium, then 5 real shots.

Slow-motion check: film shots in phone slow-motion (240 fps). The 9 ms contact covers only about 2 frames (my calculation), so look at the frame just before and after. Check that the toes point down and the ankle has not folded, and that the knee is over the ball.
Speed ladder: measure shot speed with a radar or speed app. Compare with the age-group values: about 67 km/h U13, 77 km/h U15, 81 km/h U17. Track your best clean strike, not your wildest one.
Centre-strike gate: two cones 1 m apart at 11 m, with a bench or rope as the 'ceiling'. The ball must go through low and straight. Off-centre hits curve out of the gate.
Weak-foot mirror: repeat the ankle-lock volleys and target-band shots with the other foot at 50% speed.

Bonus knuckle experiment (older players): draw a thick stripe around the ball. Strike dead-centre with a short, firm, stabbing contact and a small follow-through. If the stripe does not visibly turn in flight, you made a low-spin shot. Watch for wobble from 20-25 m.
animation_ideas: Millisecond clock: a big stopwatch counts 0 to 9 ms while the ball squashes against the boot in extreme slow motion. Two speed bars (foot and ball) cross at the halfway mark. Label the phases 'foot pushes' and 'ball springs back'.
Foot outruns... no, ball outruns foot: the boot moves at 79 km/h and the ball shoots off at about 100 km/h. A big question mark appears, then a bowling ball hitting a ping-pong ball explains why.

X-ray foot: a see-through leg shows the bones. With a floppy ankle the foot hinges back 8 degrees and a small 'energy leak' puff escapes. With a locked ankle the foot and shin light up as one solid club, and a 'mass meter' rises from 1.7 kg to 2.1 kg.
Whip transformation: the leg morphs into a bullwhip. Speed tags ride on each joint: knee 17 km/h, toes 79 km/h. The thigh brakes and a pulse of energy runs down to the tip with a 'crack'.
Motorbike on the ball: for one frame, a 300 kg motorbike balances on the ball to show the 3000 N peak force, then vanishes.
Trampoline inside the ball: a cutaway ball shows a tiny trampoline that stretches as the boot presses in, then flings the ball forward.

Contact-point clock face: the ball shows a target with rings. Hits at the centre, below centre and to one side each show a launch arrow and a spin arrow. A speed gauge drops from 26 to 18.5 m/s as the hit moves 8 cm off-centre.

Swing-arc pendulum: side view of the leg as a pendulum with the lowest point marked. Slide the plant foot backward and the lowest point moves, so the foot meets the ball on the upswing and the ball rises over the bar.
Body-lean dial: a stick figure tilts back from 13 to 17 degrees and the ball path swings from a low line to a lob. Then the figure leans forward and the path flattens.
Drawn bow: the player's body becomes a bow. The opposite arm and kicking leg pull back as the string, then release into the kick.
Growth-chart bar race: bars for U11, U13, U15, U17 and U20 ball speeds grow from 58 to 99 km/h beside a pro bar at about 100 km/h. A smaller 'strike quality' bar grows from 1.07 to 1.26.

Air-flow tunnel: smoke lines stream around the ball. At slow speed the wake is wide and messy. Past about 15-20 m/s a switch flips ('drag crisis'), the smoke hugs the ball longer and the wake shrinks.

Knuckle top-down view: a spinless ball flies towards goal while its wake flaps side to side like a flag. The path shows one or two gentle zigzags about 13.5 m long. The goalkeeper dives the wrong way.
Spin stripe comparison: two balls with painted stripes fly side by side. The normal drive turns about 4 times per second, and the knuckle ball turns less than once per second.
Myth-buster stamps: 'Longer contact = more power' gets a red BUSTED stamp (r = -0.44). 'Heavier boots = harder shot' gets BUSTED. 'Kick through the ball' gets a green CONFIRMED stamp.
Cold-ball bounce test: two balls drop 2 m onto steel. The 20 degree C ball bounces 135-155 cm and the 5 degree C ball bounces lower. A thermometer pops up.
misconceptions: 'A longer contact with the ball gives more power.' False. In ultra-high-speed tests, longer contact went slightly WITH slower balls (r = -0.44). Contact is about 9 ms whatever you do.

'The ball can only go as fast as your foot.' False. A good strike sends the ball 1.2 to 1.5 times faster than the foot, because the leg is heavier than the ball and the ball springs back off the foot.

'Follow-through pushes the ball after contact.' Half true. The ball is gone in less than 10 ms, so the follow-through cannot touch it. But a full follow-through shows that the foot was still speeding up at impact, and that part matters.
'Heavier boots give harder shots.' False. Studies found shoe weight does not change ball speed, because a heavier foot also swings slower.
'Pump the ball rock-hard for faster shots.' Not supported. Robot tests at 0.6-1.2 bar found no change in ball speed, only about 2 degrees more launch at low pressure.
'Power comes from a strong thigh alone.' Incomplete. Strike quality (ball/foot ratio) grows from about 1.07 at U11 to 1.26 at U20. Better strikes, not only stronger legs, make the big gains.
'The plant foot must be exactly X cm from the ball.' Folklore. The common 5-10 cm behind and 5-28 cm beside rule has not been confirmed by experiment, and youth studies disagree. Find your own spot.

'Knuckleballs are magic or caused by the valve.' The wobble comes from the unsteady air wake behind a ball with almost no spin. It is strongest at 15-25 m/s. Ball panel design changes how much it happens.

'The fastest shot ever was 210 km/h.' Disputed. That number (Heberson, 2006) has no verified measurement. Guinness lists 129 km/h for a studio kick and 183 km/h for a Premier League shot. Lab tests of skilled adults give about 95-110 km/h.

verdicts.claim: Nunome 2006: 9 skilled adults, 1000 Hz, contact 9.1 ± 0.7 ms, ball 26.3 ± 3.4 m/s (range 19.2-32.6)
verdicts.note: Page 14 of the paper gives exactly these values: 9 male players, 1000 Hz ProReflex system. The paper has a typo ('9.1 ± 0.7 m/s'), but the context shows ms. 26.3 m/s = 94.7 km/h. The range is 69-117 km/h.

verdicts.claim: Ratio 1.35 ± 0.09. Toe 22.0 m/s, knee 4.8 m/s. Shank 35.8 rad/s. Earlier ratios 1.06-1.29, up to 1.65 at the ankle
verdicts.note: Table I (WGN column) gives these values. Important caveat: Nunome takes foot speed at the foot's centre of gravity (the midpoint of the toe and ankle markers). Ball/toe = 26.3/22.0 = 1.20. Ball/foot centre = 1.35. Ball/ankle (16.9 m/s) is about 1.56. The 'toe' marker is on the fifth metatarsal head, not the tip of the toe. 35.8 rad/s = 2051 deg/s. The earlier ratios are 1.06 (Asami & Nolte 1983), 1.29 (Plagenhoef 1971) and 1.65 at the ankle (Isokawa & Lees 1988).

verdicts.claim: Asai et al. 2002: 4500 fps, 6 university players, contact 9.12 ms, ball 25.44 m/s, foot 23.12 m/s, 147 mm travel = 66% of 223 mm
verdicts.note: Table 1 of Asai, Carré, Akatsuka & Haake (2002), Sports Engineering 5:183-192. Foot speed is taken at point 7 on the toe region. The HTTPS link fails, but the HTTP link works.

verdicts.claim: 5000 Hz: deformation peaks at about 6 cm at about 4 ms. Foot faster than ball in the first half. Recoil gives about 95% of launch speed. Effective push is about 3/4 of contact
verdicts.note: Nunome, Shinkai & Ikegami, ISBS 2012 keynote, Figure 5 and text. The deformation peaks at about 6.1 cm at about 3.9 ms. The foot is faster than the ball until the end of phase II. Ball decompression in phase III brings the ball to 95% of launch speed. Phase IV adds little. Caveat: the paper measures deformation as the change in distance from a fifth-metatarsal marker to the ball's geometric centre. Thus the value can include shoe and foot deformation.

verdicts.claim: Other studies measure less squash: Asai 85-86% of diameter (about 3 cm). Shinkai 2007 up to 68 mm
verdicts.note: Asai 2002: the model ball went to 85% of its diameter and the experiment to 86%. That is 3.1-3.3 cm. The Lees et al. (2010) review states 'as much as 68 mm after initial ball contact (Shinkai et al., 2007)'. A safe range for narration is 'about 3 to 7 cm'.

verdicts.claim: Peak ball reaction force 2926 N, more than 4x body weight. Earlier: about 2500 N (Asai simulation), 1610 N (Tol 2002)
verdicts.note: Page 40 of the ISBS 2012 paper states all three values. Asai's 2002 FE model gave 2439 N horizontal. Ishii & Maruyama (2007) estimated about 1200 N at 16.3 m/s. 2926 N is the weight of about 298 kg. This value is a model estimate from one lab.

verdicts.claim: Myth: longer contact = faster shot. Weak negative relation r = -0.438, contact 8.2-9.8 ms
verdicts.note: Figure 6 prints 'r = 0.438, P<0.05' with the negative fit y = -1.684x + 44.42. Contact times span 8.2-9.8 ms, and ball speeds were 26-33 m/s. The authors write: 'There is a myth among coaches/players that a longer contact time ... can produce a faster ball velocity.'

verdicts.claim: Shank still accelerating at impact. Earlier slowing was a filtering artefact. Supports 'kick through the ball'
verdicts.note: Nunome 2006 and ISBS 2012: 'the first to provide evidence that strongly supports the above practical advice'. The Lees 2010 review adds a nuance. The knee extensor moment reverses to a flexion moment just before impact. Thus 'kick through the ball' depends on the hip and trunk muscles, not the knee.

verdicts.claim: Impact forces the ankle into plantar flexion. Peak angular acceleration mid-contact. Peak plantar-flexion velocity in the second half
verdicts.note: Nunome 2006, p. 14: 'the ankle was rapidly forced into plantar flexion by ball impact and reached its peak angular acceleration at the middle of ball contact and its peak plantar flexion velocity during the latter half'. Shinkai 2008/2009 also saw a slight dorsiflexion first in some kicks.

verdicts.claim: Mechanical limb, rigid vs spring ankle: effective mass 2.1 vs 1.7 kg, ratio 1.16 vs 1.11, ball 19.0 vs 18.3 m/s, 8.3 deg, 6.3 J. Australian-football ball
verdicts.note: Peacock thesis, Table 5.1. The chapter abstract rounds the non-rigid ratio to 1.10. The machine used a Sherrin AF ball at 69 kPa in drop-punt kicking, recorded at 4000 Hz. The ball-speed gain is about 3.8%.

verdicts.claim: Shinkai 2013 (per Peacock): 51 players, foot+shoe = 84.0 ± 9.6% of effective mass, r = 0.89 with ratio
verdicts.note: Secondary citation only. Peacock gives both values. He attributes the age gain to higher foot speed and higher physical mass, not to effective mass directly. I did not open the original Shinkai 2013 paper.

verdicts.claim: Effective striking mass rises with limb rigidity. Greatest when contact is closer to the ankle than the metatarsals
verdicts.note: Kellis & Katis (2007) state this, citing Lees & Nolan 1998 and Asami & Nolte 1983.

verdicts.claim: Foot-ball COR 0.463-0.681. 0.5 to 0.65 gives about 10% more ball speed
verdicts.note: Kellis & Katis (2007), citing Bull-Andersen et al. 1999 and Dorge et al. 2002. The arithmetic checks: (1+0.65)/(1+0.5) = 1.10.

verdicts.claim: Ishii 2012: inverted-U, best impact point about 6 cm distal to the ankle. 5 players, 2500 fps. Foot speed is the biggest factor
verdicts.note: The PubMed abstract (PMID 21908898) confirms 5 players, 2500 fps, the model and foot speed as the dominant factor. The inverted-U and the 6 cm value come from Ravenscroft & Linthorne (ISBS 2015). They report about 15% less ball speed at the toe base or at the ankle. Caveat: Ishii changed tee height from 0 to 12 cm, with a one-step approach to a 4 m target. Ravenscroft & Linthorne then studied one player's penalty kicks and found no clear optimum.

verdicts.claim: Asami & Nolte 1983: distal impact forces plantar flexion and cuts ball speed. Linked to footballer's ankle
verdicts.note: The Lees 2010 review states both points. Tol et al. 2002 later backed the impingement link.

verdicts.claim: FE horizontal offset: 0 cm 26.0 m/s and 1.9 rev/s. 8 cm 18.5 m/s and 10.5 rev/s. 12 cm 11.2 m/s and 16.2 rev/s
verdicts.note: Table 2 of Asai 2002 labels the unit 'r/s'. The Lees 2010 review, co-written by Asai, converts the 16.2 peak to 101 rad/s. Carré 2002 uses 64 rad/s for the 8 cm case. Thus rev/s is correct. But the 2002 abstract gives the friction effect in rad/s, so the paper is not consistent about units. The 0 cm spin is signed -1.9. The model had a 25 m/s foot, a 4 kg leg and friction 0.4.

verdicts.claim: Asai 2005 FE vertical offset: fastest ball at 20-40 mm below centre. Max launch 16 deg at -20 mm
verdicts.note: The Lees 2010 review states exactly this. It is a simulation.

verdicts.claim: Proximal-to-distal sequence. Knee extension velocity at contact is the strongest predictor of ball speed
verdicts.corrected_value: Proximal-to-distal: confirmed by Kellis & Katis. 'Strongest predictor' comes from one different study: Sinclair et al. 2014 (22 academy players, 500 Hz, adjusted R2 = 0.39).
verdicts.note: The JSSM review does not name knee extension velocity as the strongest predictor. It stresses foot speed (r > 0.74) and COR. Sinclair 2014 found it the only significant joint-kinematic predictor. But in Nunome 2006, toe and ankle linear speed correlated more strongly (r = 0.80-0.85) than shank angular velocity (r = 0.61). Thus say 'foot speed matters most. Of the joint motions, knee extension speed predicts best.'

verdicts.claim: Hip is the main motor: about 2000 W hip vs 100 W or less knee (Robertson & Mosher). Disputed by Nunome 2002 (knee > 1000 W). Fling effect about 20% (Dorge 2002)
verdicts.note: The Lees 2010 review confirms all three. Precise wording: the motion-dependent moment from thigh motion did work equal to 20% of the work of the knee extensor muscle moment. It did not supply '20% of all knee-extension work'. Lees et al. 2009 found power profiles like those of Robertson & Mosher.

verdicts.claim: Approach about 43-45 deg. 3-4 m/s. Last step 0.72-0.81 m (max) vs 0.53-0.55 m (submax)
verdicts.note: Lees 2010 review: 43 deg self-selected (Egan 2007) and 45 deg for maximum speed (Isokawa & Lees 1988). It also gives 2-4 steps, 3-4 m/s, and the step values for 2 professionals (Lees & Nolan 2002).

verdicts.claim: Hip-shoulder separation 38-42 deg max vs 6-12 deg submax. Non-kicking arm makes a tension arc
verdicts.note: Lees & Nolan 2002 (2 professionals), and Shan & Westerhoff 2005 for the tension arc. It is the NON-kicking-side arm.

verdicts.claim: Trunk lean back 13 deg (low kick) vs 17 deg (high kick), Prassas 1990
verdicts.note: The Lees 2010 review states this. Other studies give 0-13 deg of lean, so values vary a lot between studies.

verdicts.claim: Folklore: plant foot 5-10 cm behind, 5-28 cm beside (Hay 1993). Not confirmed experimentally
verdicts.note: Kellis & Katis: 'this information has not been confirmed experimentally.' Lees 2010 also says no recent research reports support-foot data.

verdicts.claim: Disputed: 13 players aged 13, closer plant foot = faster (14.1 cm, 20.9 ± 2.5 m/s, foot 13.6 m/s) vs 366 Brazilians at 0.30-0.35 m
verdicts.note: Kapidzic 2014: 14.13 ± 7.43 cm, 20.95 ± 2.46 m/s, foot 13.60 ± 1.74 m/s, r = -0.446. Vieira Table 1: 0.30-0.35 m at every age. Its warning about U13-U17 is confirmed. Caveat: the Kapidzic values give a ball/foot ratio of about 1.54 at age 13. Vieira gives 1.10 for U13. Thus the Kapidzic foot speed is doubtful. The two studies also define the distance differently.

verdicts.claim: 366 Brazilian youth, 300 Hz: ball U9 48.5 to U20 98.7 km/h. Ratio 0.99-1.26. U9/U11 label error in the abstract
verdicts.note: Table 1 matches every value. Ball: U9 48.54, U11 57.87, U13 66.70, U15 76.92, U17 81.35, U20 98.74 km/h. Foot: 49.08, 53.79, 60.54, 65.17, 68.44, 78.24 km/h. Ratio: 0.99, 1.07, 1.10, 1.18, 1.19, 1.26. The abstract calls the 48.54 group U11. The U13-U20 conversions to m/s are correct.

verdicts.claim: Elite Brazilian pros 99.7 ± 8.5 km/h ball, 82.3 km/h foot. Last stride r = .36-.79. Accuracy dips U13-U15
verdicts.note: The Vieira paper quotes Vieira 2016: 99.74 ± 8.45 and 82.31 ± 7.93 km/h. The stride correlations and the growth-spurt accuracy dip are in the abstract.

verdicts.claim: Prepubertal boys 11.7 ± 0.5 y: max instep ball speed 17.3 ± 2.3 m/s
verdicts.note: Deniz & Kilci 2025, 31 prepubescent male players. 17.3 m/s = 62 km/h.

verdicts.claim: Max instep ball speed 18-35 m/s. 1990 World Cup 32-35 m/s (Ekblom 1994)
verdicts.note: Kellis & Katis quote both, as a secondary citation.

verdicts.claim: Guinness: fastest kick 129 km/h (Madrid studio, 2001). Fastest English top-division shot 183 km/h (Hirst, crossbar)
verdicts.note: 129 km/h: Francisco Javier Galan Marin, 29 Oct 2001. 183 km/h (114 mph): David Hirst for Sheffield Wednesday v Arsenal, 16 Sep 1996, from 13.5 m. 183 km/h = 50.8 m/s, far more than any lab value (35 m/s or less). Treat it as a doubtful radar reading.

verdicts.claim: Heberson 2006 free kick 210.9 km/h: no official measurement. Video analyses give lower speeds
verdicts.corrected_value: No verified or peer-reviewed measurement. Guinness does not list it. It is physically very unlikely.
verdicts.note: I found no credible video analysis that gives a lower speed. The web cites Reddit, and the Guardian's '16.5 m in 0.28 s' in fact implies about 212 km/h, from coarse frame timing. A better argument uses physics. 58.6 m/s at a ball/foot ratio of 1.35 needs a foot speed of about 43 m/s. That is about twice the 22-24 m/s measured in skilled adults.

verdicts.claim: FIFA Quality Pro size 5: rebound 135-155 cm from 2 m at 20 C, at least 125 cm at 5 C. 420-445 g. 68.5-69.5 cm
verdicts.note: The Oct 2022 testing manual gives all values in the first size-5 column. The drop is from 2.00 m onto a metal anvil. Lower tiers allow 125-155 cm and 410-450 g.
IFAB Law 2 text matches.

verdicts.claim: Robot kicks at 0.6/0.9/1.2 bar: no change in ball speed. About 2 deg higher launch at low pressure (Neilson & Jones 2005)
verdicts.note: The Lees 2010 review states this. Valve position also changed launch elevation.

verdicts.claim: Shoe weight does not change ball speed. Barefoot up to 1.5% faster, up to 20% less accurate. Higher toe box up to -2.0%
verdicts.note: The Lees 2010 review states all of these. The barefoot gain applies to players who can ignore the pain. A heavier shoe slows the foot, but the strike is more effective, so the effects cancel.

verdicts.claim: Drag crisis: Cd about 0.5 to 0.1-0.2. Critical Re 2.2-3.0 x 10^5, about 15 m/s non-spinning, about 20 m/s spinning
verdicts.note: The Lees 2010 review, Figure 6 and text, cites Asai 2006 (Re 220,000, about 15 m/s) and Asai 2007 (spinning Teamgeist, 300,000, about 20 m/s). Caveat: Carré 2005 found the transition much lower (Re 0.9-1.3 x 10^5). Values also depend on the ball (Hong & Asai 2014 give 2.2-3.6 x 10^5).

verdicts.claim: At 25 m/s drag is about 3.25 N and slows the ball about 6 m/s over 18 m
verdicts.note: The Lees 2010 review states both. Physics check: 3.25 N means Cd is about 0.23. With quadratic drag the speed loss over 18 m is about 5 m/s. It is about 6 m/s only with Cd near 0.28. Safer narration: 'about 5-6 m/s'. 3.25 N is about 0.77 of the ball's weight (4.2 N).

verdicts.claim: Hong & Asai 2014: critical Re Brazuca 2.2-2.5, Jabulani 3.3-3.6 x 10^5. Robot 30 m/s, 25 m, less than 1 rotation. Scatter 0.20 m (Brazuca) to 0.68 m (Cafusa)
verdicts.corrected_value: Impact-point SDs ranged from 0.13 m (Teamgeist 2, vertical) to 0.68 m (Cafusa, horizontal). Brazuca SDs were 0.20-0.45 m.
verdicts.note: The critical Re values, the 30 m/s launch, the 25 m distance, the less-than-1-rotation condition and the 20 kicks per orientation are all confirmed. The conversion to 15-17 vs 22-25 m/s is correct. But the claim cherry-picks Brazuca's smallest SD. Brazuca's vertical SD in orientation A was 0.45 m, more than several other balls. The values are standard deviations, not total scatter. The ball is Teamgeist 2.

verdicts.claim: Texier 2016: zigzags from unsteady lift, grow in the drag crisis (15-25 m/s for soccer). Wavelength about 13.5 m. Jabulani zigzags with no spin
verdicts.note: The paper gives 15-25 m/s for soccer and lambda = 2 pi D sqrt(4 rho_b / 3 rho) = 13.5 m for soccer. With Lshot = 30 m, Lshot/lambda = 2.2, so one full zigzag fits. Field observations (Table 1): soccer knuckling at 20-25 m/s, zigzag lengths 10-20 m, sideways shift less than 1.5 ball diameters. The Jabulani point is in the introduction.

verdicts.claim: Knuckle spin 0.9 ± 0.5 rev/s vs 4.0 ± 1.8 straight. Attack angle 3.3 / 19.3 / 32.6 deg
verdicts.note: The attack angles are in the abstract (Hong, Kazama, Nakayama & Asai 2012). The spin values are in the full text, per a search snippet: horizontal axis, straight -4.0 ± 1.8 r/s, knuckle 0.9 ± 0.5 r/s. Vertical axis: curve 7.4 ± 1.2, knuckle 0.6 ± 0.3. 'r/s' must mean rev/s, because 7.4 rad/s is far too low for a curve kick. The straight shot is signed negative. It is probably backspin, but I could not check the sign convention. ScienceDirect blocked access.

verdicts.claim: Smoke visualisation: peak vortex lift about 2.0 N, about 3.5 Hz
verdicts.note: Hong, Chung, Nakayama & Asai 2010, abstract. The lift and vortex frequencies correlated at r = 0.83. 2 N is about half the ball's weight.

verdicts.claim: Teamgeist wind tunnel: knuckle effect from unsteady wake movement in the supercritical regime, not from spin
verdicts.note: Murakami, Seo, Kondoh & Iwai 2012, Sports Eng 15:29-40. They tested a non-spinning Teamgeist and found 'unsteady movement of vortical wake structure in the supercritical Reynolds number regime'.

verdicts.claim: Coaching: plant foot beside ball pointing at target, ankle locked, strike centre, body over ball. Plant behind = ball rises
verdicts.note: The page says this almost word for word. It uses 'body over the ball', not 'knee and chest'. It also stresses a free follow-through.

verdicts.claim: Coaching disagreement: ActiveSG says lean forward, lock ankle, strike centre, long back lift, minimum follow-through
verdicts.note: ActiveSG Circle (Sport Singapore) gives these three points exactly. The biomechanics supports not braking before contact (Nunome 2006). What happens after the ball leaves (less than 10 ms) cannot change the ball.

mechanism_errors: Step 1 (Wind-up): 'your kicking-side arm swings out wide' is WRONG. It is the NON-kicking-side arm that goes out wide and back. It makes the 'tension arc' with the kicking leg (Shan & Westerhoff 2005, in Lees et al. 2010). The claims list itself says 'non-kicking arm'.

Step 4 (Lock): 'The ball meets ... the foot, near the ankle' is off. The best speed came from contact about 6 cm in front of the ankle joint, in the middle of the laces near the foot's centre of mass. Contact at the ankle or at the toe base gave about 15% less speed (Ishii et al. 2012, as reported by Ravenscroft & Linthorne 2015). Better: 'the middle of the laces'.

Step 4 (Lock): 'A loose ankle bends back like a hinge' can suggest the wrong direction. The ball forces the foot further into plantar flexion (the toes are pushed further down). It does not bend the foot up toward the shin. Also, no human ankle stays fully rigid. Even a 'locked' ankle gets forced down in the impact. A foot that is already fully pointed has less room to give (the barefoot finding). In a machine, a rigid ankle gave only about 4% more ball speed.

Step 5 (Squash): the 'Thus 1.2 to 1.5 times faster' chain is incomplete and depends on where foot speed is measured. The ball beats the foot only because the effective striking mass (about 1.7-2.1 kg) is several times the ball's mass AND the collision is partly elastic. With no rebound (e = 0), the ball would be slower than the foot. Ball/toe = 1.20, ball/foot centre = 1.35 and ball/ankle is about 1.56 in the same kicks (Nunome 2006). For young players the ratio is only 0.99 (U9) to 1.19 (U17).

Step 6 (Aim): 'A push straight through the centre gives the most speed' holds only side to side (Asai 2002, horizontal offset). For the vertical offset, the FE model found the fastest ball from contact 2-4 cm BELOW the centre, which also launches it up to 16 degrees (Asai 2005). The backspin direction for a low contact point is correct.

Step 7 (Flight): 'loses about 6 m/s over 18 m' is the review's round number. A drag force of 3.25 N means Cd is about 0.23, which gives about 5 m/s. Say 'about 5 to 6 m/s'. The rest of step 7 is correct: drag is about 3/4 of the ball's weight, and the knuckle window is 15-25 m/s. Note that a 25 m/s shot is at the top edge of that window.

Misconception 1: 'Contact is about 9 ms whatever you do' is overstated. Skilled kicks ranged from 8.2 to 9.8 ms. Other studies report 9-12 ms (Asami & Nolte: 12 ms), and faster feet give shorter contact (Peacock machine data). Say 'about 9 to 10 ms in a hard shot'.

Misconception 2: '1.2 to 1.5 times faster than the foot' is true for skilled adults only. For U9-U17 players the measured ratio is 0.99-1.19 (Vieira et al.). For a young audience, say 'up to about 1.3 times'.
safe_numbers_for_narration: Foot and ball touch for only about 9 thousandths of a second (9.1 ms at 1000 Hz, 9.12 ms at 4500 fps).
In that time foot and ball travel together about 15 cm, about two-thirds of the ball's width.
At impact the toe area moves at about 22 m/s (79 km/h), but the knee moves at only about 5 m/s (17 km/h).
A skilled adult sends the ball about 1.35 times faster than the centre of the foot moves.
Strike quality rises with age: the ball/foot speed ratio goes from about 1.0 at U9 to 1.26 at U20.
The ball squashes by about 3 to 7 cm, depending on how it is measured.
Peak impact force is estimated near 2900 N, more than four times the player's body weight (one ultra-high-speed study).
Longer contact did not help: slightly longer contacts went with slightly slower balls (r = -0.44).
Youth shot speeds: about 67 km/h at U13, 77 km/h at U15, 81 km/h at U17 and 99 km/h at U20. Elite pros average about 100 km/h.
The fastest spot is the middle of the laces, about 6 cm in front of the ankle joint. Contact at the toes or at the ankle gave about 15% less speed.
In a kicking machine, a locked ankle gave about 4% more ball speed than a springy one. The springy ankle kept 6.3 J that never reached the ball.
Barefoot kicks were up to 1.5% faster than kicks in boots, but up to 20% less accurate.
Ball pressures from 0.6 to 1.2 bar made no difference to ball speed.
At 25 m/s, air drag pushes back with about 3.25 N, about three-quarters of the ball's weight.
A knuckle shot spins about 0.9 turns per second. A normal laces drive spins about 4 turns per second.
Knuckling happens mostly at about 15 to 25 m/s (54 to 90 km/h). One zigzag needs about 13.5 m of flight.
The wobbling side force on a knuckleball peaks at about 2 N, about half the ball's weight, and flips about 3.5 times a second.
In max kicks, the hips and shoulders twisted apart by 38 to 42 degrees, but only 6 to 12 degrees in easy kicks.
Guinness lists 129 km/h for the fastest kick in a studio. The famous 210 km/h free kick has no verified measurement.

research.kick: Chip / lob with backspin (a short "stab" under the ball with little follow-through, to lift it over a goalkeeper who has come off the line)
research.one_line_hook: To lift a ball over a goalkeeper's head, you kick down into the grass. And the ball is gone in one hundredth of a second, before your leg has stopped moving.
research.mechanism_story:
Step 1: the stab. The player plants the standing foot close beside the ball. The kicking foot, toes pointed down, stabs forward and slightly down under the ball. It meets the ball only about 2-4 cm above the grass, far below the ball's middle.

Step 2: ten milliseconds. Foot and ball touch for about one hundredth of a second. The ball squashes. The push comes from underneath, so the ball shoots off upward, roughly along a line from the contact spot through the ball's centre. The foot also drags the underside of the ball forward, so the ball starts to turn backward. Some of the kick's energy goes into spin. The ball leaves slower than after a clean strike through the middle. For a chip, slow is good.

Step 3: the ball is already gone. After about 10 ms the ball leaves the foot. The follow-through happens in empty air. A short "stab and stop" matters only because it keeps the foot low and moving forward during those 10 ms. It also stops extra speed.

Step 4: launch. A good chip leaves at roughly 45-55 km/h and 40-55 degrees steep. It turns perhaps 5-10 times each second.

Step 5: the climb. The spinning ball drags a thin skin of air round with it. Behind the ball, this air gets flung downward. Push air down, and the air pushes the ball up. At launch this lift is about a quarter of the ball's weight. On the way up the lift leans slightly backward. So on a steep chip, backspin buys height and hang time, not distance.

Step 6: the hang. Near the top the ball is slow. Lift is much weaker, because it depends strongly on speed. Air resistance has eaten forward speed all the way up. A chip also flies in the speed zone (about 12-15 m/s) where football drag can suddenly triple.

Step 7: the drop. With little forward speed left, gravity wins. The ball falls more steeply than it climbed, at about 50-60 degrees.

Step 8: the landing. The ball arrives mostly downward. The turf swallows at least half of that downward bounce energy. The backspin makes the bottom of the ball scrub forward on the grass, so friction pushes back and removes more forward speed. In one lab test, a ball with backspin kept about 40% of its forward speed after the bounce. A ball with topspin kept 75%. The chip sits down instead of running away.

Step 9: the keeper. The ball passes over a rushing keeper in about half a second. It reaches the goal line 1.5-2.3 s after the kick. That is too soon for a keeper 8 m off his line to get back.
plain_metaphors: Snooker or pool 'screw/draw' shot: hit the cue ball below its middle and it spins backward. The chip is the same idea with a foot, and the backspin shows itself when the ball lands and brakes.
Golf wedge: golfers say 'hit down to make the ball go up'. The club face gets under the ball, the ball climbs steeply with backspin and stops on the green. A chip is a football wedge shot.

Tennis slice vs topspin: a high-to-low racket path makes backspin (slice), a low-to-high path brushes up the back of the ball and makes topspin. A chip foot path that rises and lifts through the ball acts like a topspin swing and kills the backspin.
Paddle wheel: a backspinning ball is like a paddle wheel that flicks the air behind it downward. Throw air down and the air throws you up.
Tumbling seed pods: some seeds tumble with backspin as they fall so they glide further (Bush, MIT). The chip borrows the same trick to 'hang'.
Car wheel: a chip spinning 6-8 times a second turns about as fast as a car wheel at 50 km/h in town.
Thumb-width sweet spot: the ball is about 22 cm tall, but the chip contact is only about a thumb's width (2-4 cm) above the grass.
Camera shutter: the picture is taken in the first 10 ms. The follow-through is what happens after the shutter closes. It cannot change the photo, but it tells you how the photo was taken.
Sticky vs slippery air: at high speed the air slides smoothly round the ball. When the ball slows to about 50 km/h the air 'lets go' early and the ball suddenly feels like it runs into thick air.
Fence and bucket: beating a rushing keeper is like tossing a ball over a fence into a bucket just behind it. It has to go up steeply to clear the fence and come down steeply to land in the bucket.
Backspin landing = skidding car wheel spinning backward: the bottom of the ball rubs forward on the grass and the friction acts like a brake.
A ball rolling toward you already turns backward relative to your kick direction, so it arrives with some free backspin. A ball rolling away from you arrives with topspin, which fights the chip.

jargon_map.plain_version: The ball turns backward while it flies forward. The top of the ball moves toward the kicker.
A spinning ball throws the air behind it to one side, and the air pushes the ball the other way. With backspin the air goes down, so the ball gets pushed up.
A number for how well spin turns into push. For a football it stays below about 0.3.
How fast the ball's surface spins compared to how fast the ball flies. A slow ball with the same spin feels the spin more.
Air resistance. The air pushes against the ball and slows it.
A number for how 'draggy' the ball's shape and surface are. About 0.15 when the air flows smoothly, about 0.4-0.45 when it does not.
The very thin skin of air that clings to the ball's surface and moves with it.
The point where the air skin peels away from the ball and leaves a messy trail behind.
The messy trail of air behind the ball. With backspin this trail is flicked downward.
A speed (about 12-15 m/s, 43-54 km/h, for a football) where the air skin changes behaviour. Below this speed the air peels off early and drag is about three times higher.
One number that combines ball size and speed (and air stickiness) to tell you how the air flows around the ball.
How steeply the ball leaves the foot, measured up from the ground.
How steeply the ball comes down. 90 degrees is straight down, 0 is rolling.
The highest point of the flight.
The path the ball draws through the air.
How long foot and ball touch: about 9-10 thousandths of a second.
The total push the foot gives the ball during that short touch.
Hitting the ball away from its middle. This is what makes it spin.
A turning push, like pushing a door far from its hinges.
The further from the middle you hit, the more spin you get and the less speed.
How many full turns the ball makes each second. 1 rev/s = 6.28 rad/s.
Bounciness: how much of its speed a ball keeps when it bounces.
Grippiness between ball and grass (or ball and boot).
The bottom of the ball scrubs along the grass instead of rolling. The scrub acts as a brake.
In some conditions spin pushes a ball the 'wrong' way. Shown on smooth balls. Not proven for real match balls.
A ball with almost no spin can wobble unpredictably because its air trail flips from side to side.
Toes pulled up toward the shin / toes pointed down.
What the leg does after the ball has left the foot.

claims.claim: Foot-ball contact in a full instep kick lasts about 9 ms. The measured value was 9.0 +/- 0.4 ms (11 skilled players, 5000 Hz cameras). Peak force on the ball was about 2,900 N. The ball is effectively accelerated only for about three quarters of the contact time. No study measured contact time for a chip. Expect a similar order, about 10 ms (inference).
claims.value: 9.0 +/- 0.4 ms contact; peak force 2926 +/- 509 N

claims.claim: Ball spin grows with the offset between the foot and the ball's centre line. Offset matters more than friction. Maximum spin came at about 100 mm offset. There is a trade-off: more offset gives more spin but less ball speed. Spin appears even with almost no friction, because the ball deforms around the foot.
claims.value: optimum offset ~100 mm for max spin

claims.claim: A foot at 25 m/s (90 km/h) hitting the ball centrally gives about 26 m/s (94 km/h) and no spin. The same foot 8 cm off-centre gives only 18.5 m/s (67 km/h) but 10.2 rev/s of spin. This shows the speed-for-spin trade-off. The simulated case used sidespin, but the same contact mechanics apply to an under-the-ball (backspin) hit.
claims.value: central: 26 m/s, 0 rev/s; 8 cm offset: 18.5 m/s, 10.2 rev/s (64 rad/s)

claims.claim: Machine-launched balls at 18 m/s (65 km/h), spin axis horizontal: the lift coefficient rose fast from 0 up to about 100 rad/s (16 rev/s) of spin, then stayed near 0.26. Drag coefficient rose steadily from 0.2 (no spin) to 0.5 at 240 rad/s (38 rev/s). With backspin up to about 100 rad/s 'the ball keeps its height because of increased lift'. More backspin than that gets cancelled by the extra drag. The authors say about 0.3 is the maximum lift coefficient in a typical game situation.
claims.value: C_L plateau ~0.26 above ~16 rev/s; C_D 0.2 -> 0.5; max C_L ~0.3

claims.claim: Wind-tunnel data: the soccer-ball drag crisis happens at about 12-15 m/s (43-54 km/h). Critical Reynolds number is 2.2-3.0 x 10^5. Drag coefficient is about 0.43 below the crisis and about 0.15 above it. A chip is launched at roughly this speed and slows below it, so it flies mostly in the high-drag regime (inference from these values).
claims.value: crisis 12-15 m/s; C_D ~0.43 subcritical vs ~0.15 supercritical

claims.claim: Real curve kicks spin at no more than about 10 rev/s. Powerful shots and free kicks leave the foot at about 25-35 m/s (90-126 km/h). A ball at 26 m/s and 8 rev/s is deflected sideways at about 4 m/s by the Magnus effect. At spin parameter 0.18, both drag and side-force coefficients were about 0.25.
claims.value: <=10 rev/s; 25-35 m/s shots; C_D ~ C_S ~0.25 at Sp 0.18

claims.claim: The same wind-tunnel study saw large irregular swings in the wake of a non-spinning ball. The authors suggest a 'knuckle-ball effect' that causes erratic movement. So a ball with real spin flies more predictably than one with almost none (inference for chips).
claims.value: ~50 vortices/s shed for a non-rotating ball at 25 m/s

claims.claim: A football goes through the drag crisis at about 12 m/s (43 km/h), 'comparable to that of a medium-range pass'. For a soccer ball, Re/10^5 is about V/(7 m/s). Different studies put the crisis speed anywhere from about 12 to 15 m/s.

When a football slows below about 15 m/s it crosses the drag crisis and its drag grows by about a factor of 3. On goal kicks this happens on the way down and makes the ball fall more steeply than it climbs. Experienced players know backspin extends a goal kick's range. The simple Bernoulli story of the Magnus effect is incomplete: the real cause is uneven air separation, which deflects the wake down for a backspinning ball.
claims.value: drag x3 below ~15 m/s

claims.claim: Reverse Magnus effect: as a ball slows through the drag crisis, the spin force can briefly change direction. This is shown clearly on smooth balls (a beach ball curves the 'wrong' way). A rubber band around the ball restores the normal curve. There is no direct evidence that this changes the flight of a real paneled match ball on a chip. Treat it as speculative for chips.
claims.value: sign reversal seen for smooth spheres above Re ~1.28 x 10^5

claims.claim: Lab bounce test on a rubber mat over a force plate. Backspin ball: 18.08 m/s (65 km/h) at 22.9 deg, backspin 58.4 rad/s (9.3 rev/s). It rebounded at 9.22 m/s at 46.5 deg and the spin flipped to topspin (77.8 rad/s). Topspin ball: 19.05 m/s at 29.6 deg rebounded at 14.94 m/s at 33.6 deg. Worked out from these numbers: the backspin ball kept about 38% of its forward (horizontal) speed, the topspin ball about 75%. The paper names a chip as a typical way to get backspin at landing. Caveat: not grass or 3G turf, and not a steep chip landing.
claims.value: horizontal speed kept: ~38% (backspin) vs ~75% (topspin); contact ~8.5 ms

claims.claim: Same study (Rezaei et al. 2011, J. Sports Sci. 29:1201-1213), simulation for a no-spin ball: raising ball-surface friction from 0.10 to 0.60 cut the rebound's forward speed from 15.89 to 10.53 m/s. Grippier surfaces brake the ball more.

A spherical ball normally bounces forward. It can bounce backward only when it lands near straight-down with backspin (as a superball does). A football chip landing at 50-60 deg with modest spin will normally just lose most of its forward speed, not reverse like a golf ball (inference).
claims.value: backward bounce only near normal incidence

claims.claim: FIFA artificial-turf standard: a ball dropped from 2 m must rebound 0.60-0.85 m (FIFA Quality Pro) or 0.60-1.0 m (FIFA Quality). So the turf keeps only about 30-50% of the drop energy (vertical bounciness about 0.55-0.7, worked out). The angled-ball test (ball at 50 km/h, 15 deg) must keep 45-60% (Pro) or 45-70% of its speed.
claims.value: vertical rebound 0.60-0.85 m from 2 m; angle rebound 45-60%

claims.claim: Instep kicks aimed high vs low (7 players, 2000 Hz video): contact was near the ball's centre for the low target and about 10 mm below it for the high target. The foot swung downward at impact in both cases. So a 1 cm change in contact height changes the launch clearly. A chip needs a much lower contact still.
claims.value: ~10 mm below centre for high target

claims.claim: In a straight (instep) kick, foot contact points were about 20 mm below the ball centre, which gave a backspin component (Kimachi et al.). Reported through a secondary summary. Full text not checked.
claims.value: ~20 mm below centre

claims.claim: A trajectory model found successful corner kicks for launch speeds of 24.6-29.1 m/s (89-105 km/h), backspin 3-9 rev/s and launch angles of 24-28 deg. This is a good reference for a lofted long kick, for comparison with a chip. Seen in search summaries only, full text blocked.

Drag data for soccer balls at chip speeds disagree between studies. Carre et al. (2002) found non-spinning drag coefficients rising from about 0.05 at 15 m/s to 0.35 at 35 m/s. Asai et al. (2007) found high drag (about 0.43) below 12-15 m/s and low drag (about 0.15) above. Flag this as disputed.
claims.value: C_D 0.05-0.45 at 12-18 m/s depending on study and ball

claims.claim: OWN MODEL (point-mass flight model using the Carre 2002 and Asai 2007 coefficients; not checked against measured chips). Chip at 14 m/s (50 km/h), 45 deg launch, 6 rev/s backspin, size-5 ball: carries about 15-17 m, stays in the air about 2.0-2.1 s, peaks at about 4.7-5.0 m, lands at about 52-55 deg with 10-11 m/s total and only about 6-7 m/s forward speed.
claims.value: range 15-17 m; 2.0-2.1 s; apex 4.7-5.0 m; landing 52-55 deg

claims.claim: OWN MODEL: the same chip without spin peaks about 0.3-0.5 m lower and lands about 0.15-0.2 s sooner, but carries almost the same distance (within about 0.5 m). On a steep chip, backspin buys height and hang time, not distance, because the lift leans backward while the ball climbs. At launch, spin lift is about 1.2 N, about 27% of the 4.2 N ball weight. Drag is about 1.1-1.4 N. Lift weakens with the square of speed, so it is strongest just after the kick.
claims.value: +0.3-0.5 m apex, +0.15-0.2 s airtime; lift ~27% of weight at launch

claims.claim: OWN MODEL, keeper geometry. Striker 14 m from goal, keeper rushed to 4-5 m from the ball, keeper reach 2.5 m, ball must cross the line under a 2.44 m bar. Workable chips are about 13-14 m/s (47-50 km/h) at 40-55 deg. The ball passes over the keeper after about 0.4-0.7 s and reaches the goal line after about 1.7-2.3 s. At a fixed angle the speed window is only about 1 m/s wide (about +/-0.5 m/s, +/-2 km/h, +/-4%). That is why a chip is a 'touch' kick. Steeper launches (60-70 deg) need more speed (15-23 m/s) and hang 2.5-3.8 s, which gives defenders time to recover.
claims.value: 13-14 m/s at 40-55 deg; 1.7-2.3 s to goal line; window ~1 m/s

claims.claim: OWN MODEL, comparison kicks. A lofted long pass at 24 m/s (86 km/h), 30 deg, 4 rev/s backspin carries about 40-45 m, is in the air about 2.8-3.0 s, peaks at about 7.5-8 m and lands at about 40 deg with about 11-12 m/s forward speed, so it runs on. A driven pass at 27 m/s (97 km/h), 12 deg covers about 30-33 m in about 1.4-1.5 s, peaks at about 2 m and lands at about 15 deg with about 17-19 m/s forward speed, so it skids. A chip hangs about as long as a 40 m lofted pass but travels about a third of the distance.
claims.value: chip ~6-7 m/s vs lofted ~11-12 m/s vs driven ~17-19 m/s forward speed at landing

claims.claim: Contact height worked out from ball geometry. A size-5 ball has a 68-70 cm circumference (radius about 11 cm) and weighs 410-450 g. To launch near 45 deg mostly from the push through the centre, the contact must be about 7-8 cm below the centre. That is only about 2-4 cm above the grass (inference, simple geometry).
claims.value: radius ~0.11 m; contact ~2-4 cm above ground

claims.claim: Full-size goal: 7.32 m x 2.44 m. FA-recommended youth goals: U11/U12 16 ft x 7 ft (4.88 x 2.13 m), U13/U14 21 ft x 7 ft (6.40 x 2.13 m, 24 x 8 ft also accepted), U15 and older 24 ft x 8 ft (7.32 x 2.44 m). A lower 2.13 m bar narrows the chip window.
claims.value: 2.44 m adult bar; 2.13 m U11-U14 bar

claims.claim: Official goal dimensions (Law 1): 7.32 m between the posts, 2.44 m from the lower edge of the crossbar to the ground.

Male youth soccer players run 10 m from a standing start in about 1.8 s (U13), 1.7 s (U15) and 1.6 s (U17). A keeper 8-10 m off the line who must turn and run back needs well over 1.6 s. A chip that reaches the line in 1.7-2.3 s is hard to catch up with. A chip that hangs 3 s or more gives him time (inference).

Standing reach is about 1.33 x body height (NBA Draft Combine median 1.335). By that rule a 1.70 m youth keeper reaches about 2.25 m standing, or about 2.6 m with a 30-40 cm jump. An adult 1.86 m keeper reaches about 2.5 m standing. This is a rough estimate from basketball data, not keeper data.
claims.value: reach ~1.33 x height

claims.claim: A simple blog model of a chip says the ball must leave at under about 20 m/s for gravity to dominate. Its example: 12.84 m/s at 45 deg over a keeper 6 m away, 1.56 s flight. Not peer-reviewed, and the text has a small number mismatch, but it agrees with the own-model range.

Coaching sources describe the chip as struck close to the ground with a downward jabbing motion, 'kick down, under the ball', standing straight or leaning back instead of over the ball. This gives a quick rise and a lot of backspin. A chip is approached straight on and does not go far, unlike a lofted drive.
claims.value: qualitative coaching cue

claims.claim: England Football Learning (The FA): a lofted pass needs players to 'strike underneath the ball with their instep'. A driven pass needs them to 'strike through the middle of the ball with their laces or instep'.
claims.value: qualitative coaching cue

claims.claim: Coaching opinions conflict on backspin for long passes. One coaching site says a lofted pass must have little or no backspin so it rolls forward on landing. Physics sources say backspin extends a long kick's range and holds it up. Flag this as a coaching choice, not a physics rule.
claims.value: disputed coaching preference

claims.claim: Golf analogy for stopping: a ball must come in steeply enough to stop. A ball that lands too shallow skips forward even with plenty of backspin. Pros aim for a landing angle just under 50 deg with about 6,200 rpm on iron shots. This supports the idea that a chip's steep landing does most of the braking and backspin adds to it.
claims.value: ~50 deg landing, ~6200 rpm (golf)

claims.claim: Folklore to flag: popular sources say chip backspin makes the ball 'lift sharply and drop quickly'. The lift part is right. The 'drop quickly' part comes mainly from gravity and drag after forward speed is lost, not from the backspin. Backspin by itself holds the ball up.
claims.value: folklore check

claims.claim: Seed pods and the box mite use backspin to extend their flight through Magnus lift. Useful as a nature example for the video.
claims.value: qualitative

technique_cues: Plant the standing foot close beside the ball, level with it or slightly behind. Physics: this lets the kicking foot reach the bottom third of the ball. The contact spot sets both launch angle and backspin.

Toes down, ankle locked, and slide the front of the laces/instep under the ball as if the foot goes into the grass. Physics: contact 2-4 cm above the ground means the push line points up through the centre (steep launch). The foot drags the underside forward (backspin).
Short backswing: 'stab, don't swing'. Physics: a chip needs only about 45-50 km/h of ball speed, and the working speed window is only about +/-2 km/h. Less leg speed means more control.

Stop the foot at contact. Finish low, not high. Physics: the ball is gone after about 10 ms. A foot that is still rising brushes up the back of the ball, which gives topspin and adds speed. A foot that keeps moving forward and slightly down keeps the backspin.
Stay tall or lean back slightly. Do not lean over the ball. Physics: leaning over tilts the foot and moves contact up toward the middle, which gives a low, fast, driven ball.
Keep the ankle firm. Physics: the foot is pushed around by about 3,000 N forces during a hard impact. A loose ankle soaks up energy and makes the contact point and spin random.
Swing straight along the target line, not across the ball. Physics: a sideways brush tilts the spin axis and adds sidespin, so the ball swerves instead of floating straight.

Look at the keeper before the kick and at the bottom of the ball during the kick. Physics: the keeper's distance sets the angle you need. About 4-8 m away and moving forward is ideal, because the ball passes him in about half a second.
Aim for the ball to peak just behind the keeper, not over the goal. Physics: 'just high enough' keeps flight time near 1.5-2 s. A 3 s moon ball gives the keeper or defenders time to recover.

Use a ball rolling toward you when you learn. Physics: a ball rolling toward the kicker already turns backward relative to the kick direction (about 4 rev/s at 3 m/s rolling speed). This helps it climb the foot with backspin. This point is plausible physics, not measured.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaning over the ball
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The foot meets the ball near its middle. The push goes straight forward, so the ball flies low and fast with little backspin, often straight at the keeper.
common_mistakes.fix: Stay tall or lean back a little. Look at the bottom of the ball.

common_mistakes.mistake: Big, lifting follow-through
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: It shows the foot was still speeding up and rising during the 10 ms of contact. This adds too much ball speed (over the bar) and brushes up the back of the ball (less backspin, even topspin).
common_mistakes.fix: 'Stab and stop': short backswing, freeze the foot low after contact.

common_mistakes.mistake: Contact too high (at or near the equator)
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The push line is almost horizontal. The launch is too flat to clear a keeper's 2.3-2.6 m reach a few metres away.
common_mistakes.fix: Aim for the bottom third of the ball, about a thumb's width above the grass.

common_mistakes.mistake: Digging the ground first (scuffing)
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The turf absorbs much of the foot's energy before the ball does. The ball pops up weakly, short and without a clean spin.
common_mistakes.fix: Plant foot close, toes down, 'brush' the grass while the foot slides under the ball.

common_mistakes.mistake: Toe-poke chip
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: A tiny, hard contact area gives an unpredictable push direction and little controlled spin.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the front of the laces/instep with the ankle locked.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chipping a keeper who stayed on his line
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The ball would need to rise over his reach and fall under the bar within 1-3 m. There is almost no workable arc.
common_mistakes.fix: Chip only when the keeper is well off the line and coming forward. Otherwise shoot low or pass.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chipping far too high
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: Steep 65-70 deg chips hang 3-4 s. A keeper or defender can run 15-20 m in that time.
common_mistakes.fix: Just high enough: peak about 3.5-5 m, flight about 1.5-2 s.

common_mistakes.mistake: Full-power lob instead of a chip
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: High speed, low spin and a shallow landing angle. The ball keeps forward speed after the bounce and runs out of play or over the bar.
common_mistakes.fix: Treat the chip as a touch kick at about half shooting speed (about 45-50 km/h).

common_mistakes.mistake: Swinging across the ball
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The spin axis tilts and adds sidespin. The ball curves away from the target and may lose its backspin 'check'.
common_mistakes.fix: Swing through the target line, square to the goal.

common_mistakes.mistake: Planting the standing foot too far from the ball
common_mistakes.physics_consequence: The kicking foot reaches for the ball, and contact height changes from kick to kick. A 1 cm change is enough to change the launch clearly.
common_mistakes.fix: Plant close, next to the ball, knee over the ball's back half.

drills: Stab-and-stop basics: ball still on grass, partner 5-6 m away. Chip so that the partner catches it above head height. Goal: high, soft, clear backspin. Progress to a ball rolled gently toward you.

See the spin: draw a thick stripe around the ball. Film on a phone at 240 fps. Count the frames for one full turn. 40 frames = 6 rev/s, 30 frames = 8 rev/s. The whole foot contact covers only about 2-3 frames.
Over the fence into the bucket: pole or mannequin (or a rope at 2.5 m) at 5 m, a hoop or 3x3 m box at 12-15 m. Points only if the ball clears the obstacle and lands in the box.
Check it: target box 5x5 m at 12-15 m. Score 2 points if the ball lands in the box AND stays in after bouncing (backspin plus a steep landing), 1 point if it lands in but rolls out.

Keeper-rush 1v1: attacker dribbles from 18-20 m. The keeper rushes out when the attacker passes a cone at 16 m. The attacker must decide: chip if the keeper is about 4-8 m away and moving forward, otherwise go round him or shoot low.

Goldilocks ladder: same distance (14 m to a small goal with a 2.13 m bar), keeper stand-in (coach with arms up) at 5 m. Do 10 reps and record 'too low', 'good' or 'over'. The aim is to feel the narrow speed window.

Rolling-ball progression: chip balls rolled toward you, then square balls, then balls rolling away from you (hardest, because the ball arrives with topspin). This builds feel for how incoming spin helps or fights the chip.

Compare kicks: from the same spot, hit a driven pass, a lofted pass and a chip to a target zone 15 m away. Watch how far each rolls after landing. This shows how the landing angle and spin control the stop.
animation_ideas: X-ray slow-motion side view of the 10 ms contact: foot wedges under the ball, ball squashes, stopwatch reads 0.009 s. A glowing arrow from the contact spot through the ball's centre shows the launch direction, and curved arrows show backspin appearing.

Ghost follow-through: the ball flies away at 10 ms while the leg keeps swinging as a dotted after-image. Caption: 'The ball never feels this part.' Then split screen: a foot rising through contact (brushes up the back, topspin arrows) vs a foot stabbing forward and down (backspin arrows).

Thumb ruler: a 22 cm ball next to a ruler. A small glowing band 2-4 cm above the grass marks the chip sweet spot, with a cartoon thumb for scale. Compare the bands for a driven ball (centre), a shot aimed high (1 cm below centre) and a chip (7-8 cm below centre).

Air-flow view: smoke lines around a backspinning ball. The thin air skin is dragged round, and the wake behind the ball bends downward. A big upward arrow shows the push. Next to it, a no-spin ball with a straight wake and no up arrow.

Shrinking force arrows: during the flight, three arrows (gravity: constant, lift: big at launch and small near the top, drag: shrinking) change size live. A label shows lift at about a quarter of the ball's weight at launch.

Air switch at about 50 km/h: as the ball slows through 12-15 m/s, the air skin peels off earlier, the wake balloons and the drag arrow jumps about 3x. A dial on screen reads 'slippery air' then 'thick air'.
Three ghost trajectories from the same kick: backspin (higher and about 0.2 s longer in the air), no spin, topspin (dips short). Stopwatches under each ball.

Keeper window: side view with a translucent keeper-reach bubble (about 2.5 m) and the crossbar (2.44 m, or 2.13 m for youth). The ball's arc threads the gap. A speed needle swings between 'keeper catches' and 'over the bar' with only about +/-2 km/h of green zone.
Race clock: the ball in the air (about 1.8 s to the goal line) vs a keeper turning and sprinting back 8 m (a 10 m sprint takes about 1.7 s for a 15-year-old). Show the ball winning by a few frames.

Landing comparison with skid marks: a backspin ball lands steeply, the bottom scrubs forward, a backward friction arrow flashes, and a speed bar drops to about 40%. A topspin ball lands and races on at about 75%. Overlay the driven, lofted and chip landings with their forward speeds (about 18, 12 and 6 m/s).
Analogy montage in flat vector style: snooker screw-back shot, golf wedge 'hit down to go up', tennis slice vs topspin racket paths, and seed pods tumbling with backspin to glide further.

Energy pie at contact: a central strike puts almost everything into speed. An off-centre strike splits the pie into a smaller speed slice and a spin slice (26 m/s with no spin vs 18.5 m/s with 10 rev/s).

Rolling-ball insight: a ball rolls toward the kicker with little rotation arrows. As the camera turns to the kicker's view, the arrows relabel as 'free backspin'. Then the ball rolls away and the arrows relabel as 'topspin, harder to chip'.
misconceptions: 'Backspin makes the chip drop sharply.' Backspin actually pushes the ball up (lift). The steep drop comes from gravity after air drag has removed most of the forward speed. Topspin, not backspin, makes a ball dip.
'The follow-through steers the ball.' The ball leaves the foot after about 9-10 ms. The follow-through cannot touch it. It is only a sign of what the foot did during contact.
'You need power to lift the ball over the keeper.' A good chip leaves at only about 45-50 km/h. Too much speed is the most common way to miss.
'Backspin makes a chip go further.' On a steep chip, backspin adds height and hang time but almost no distance (own model). On flatter long kicks, such as goal kicks, backspin does add range.
'Hit as low as possible for maximum spin.' Spin peaks at an offset of about 100 mm, but ball speed falls and the foot hits the ground first. Scuffing kills both speed and spin.
'Backspin alone makes the chip stop.' The steep landing angle does much of the work: the turf absorbs most of the downward speed. Backspin adds extra braking at the bounce, as with golf wedge shots.

'A football spins back like a golf ball on the green.' A football chip rarely bounces backward. It loses most of its forward speed and may pop up more steeply. A true reverse bounce needs a near-vertical landing with strong backspin.
'Spin lift is just the Bernoulli effect.' The simple Bernoulli story is incomplete. The real cause is that the air skin peels off unevenly, so the wake is thrown downward and the ball is pushed up.
'Air does not matter for slow kicks.' Chips fly exactly in the speed zone (about 12-15 m/s) where football drag is highest and can suddenly triple.
'Reverse Magnus makes chips do strange things.' The reverse effect is shown on smooth balls. It is not proven for paneled match balls, so treat it as speculation.

verdicts.claim: 1. Instep kick contact 9.0 +/- 0.4 ms, 11 players, 5000 Hz, peak force ~2,900 N, ball accelerated for ~3/4 of contact; no chip study
verdicts.note: Shinkai (ISB 2009): 22 maximal instep kicks by 11 skilled players, 5000 Hz, contact 9.0 +/- 0.4 ms, peak force 2926 +/- 509 N, and 'effectual duration to accelerate the ball is roughly three fourths of visually ball contact time'. Asai et al. 2002 found a mean of 9.12 ms, and Asami and Nolte found 12 ms. These were maximal kicks. I found no chip contact-time study. 'About 10 ms or a little longer' for a softer chip is a fair inference.

verdicts.claim: 2. Spin grows with foot offset; offset matters more than friction; max spin at ~100 mm; speed-spin trade-off; spin even with near-zero friction
verdicts.note: Asai et al. 2002 (Sports Eng. 5:183) abstract says all of this word for word. In their Table 2 the actual peak is at 120 mm (16.2 rev/s at 11.2 m/s). The model used a horizontal (sidespin) offset with friction 0.4. For a chip the ground limits a vertical offset: 100 mm below centre is only about 1 cm above the grass.

verdicts.claim: 3. Foot 25 m/s central gives 26 m/s, no spin; 8 cm offset gives 18.5 m/s and 10.2 rev/s
verdicts.note: Carré et al. 2002 p.198-199 state these exact values, with friction coefficient 0.4. The source table (Asai 2002 Table 2) lists 10.5 rev/s at 0.08 m, a small mismatch. Carrying this over to backspin is an inference.

verdicts.claim: 4. Machine balls at 18 m/s: C_L rises to ~100 rad/s then ~0.26; C_D 0.2 -> 0.5 at 240 rad/s; backspin to ~100 rad/s keeps height; ~0.3 max C_L in game
verdicts.note: All values and both quotes are in Carré 2002. The tested backspin range was only up to 224 rad/s. 100 rad/s (16 rev/s) is above real kick spins (10 rev/s or less), so a chip sits on the rising part of the curve. Goff and Carré 2012 later found C_L of about 0.35 at Sp 0.5 and 14 m/s, a little above the '0.3 max'.

verdicts.claim: 5. Drag crisis at ~12-15 m/s, Re_crit 2.2-3.0 x 10^5, C_D ~0.43 sub vs ~0.15 supercritical; chip flies mostly in high-drag regime
verdicts.note: Asai 2007 states all of these. But the paper does not agree with itself: Re_crit 2.2-3.0 x 10^5 (with D = 0.22 m) is about 15-20 m/s, not 12-15 m/s. Hong and Asai 2014 give 2.2-3.6 x 10^5 for modern balls, about 15-24 m/s. This makes the inference stronger: a chip launched at 12.5-15 m/s is at or below the crisis from the start.

verdicts.claim: 6. Curve kicks <=10 rev/s; shots 25-35 m/s; 26 m/s + 8 rev/s deflected ~4 m/s; C_D ~ C_S ~0.25 at Sp 0.18
verdicts.note: All values are in Asai 2007. Sp 0.18 was at 27 m/s and 7 rev/s. The 10 rev/s limit is what that study's real curve kicks reached. By design it tested only 2-10 rev/s.

verdicts.claim: 7. Irregular wake of non-spinning ball, possible knuckle-ball effect; ~50 vortices/s at 25 m/s; spinning ball more predictable
verdicts.note: Asai 2007 saw '~50 vortex s-1' for a non-rotating kick at 25 m/s and says a knuckle-ball effect 'possibly' plays a part. The authors call the cause unclear. They also saw the wake vary over time for some spinning balls. The chip inference is weak because knuckling was seen at 25 m/s, not at chip speeds.

verdicts.claim: 8. Drag crisis ~12 m/s 'comparable to a medium-range pass'; Re/10^5 ~ V/(7 m/s); studies range 12-15 m/s
verdicts.corrected_value: Crisis speed estimates span about 12-24 m/s, depending on ball design and panel orientation
verdicts.note: The Goff 2010 quotes are correct. But the claimed spread is too narrow. Goff and Carré 2012 say about 14 m/s, and Bush says about 15 m/s. The critical Re values convert (with Goff's own rule) to about 15-20 m/s for Asai 2007 and about 15-24 m/s for Hong and Asai 2014 (Brazuca lowest, Jabulani highest).

verdicts.claim: 9. Below ~15 m/s drag rises ~x3; goal kicks fall steeper than they climb; backspin extends goal kick range; Bernoulli story incomplete, wake deflected down
verdicts.note: All of this is in Bush (MIT, 2013 book chapter 'The aerodynamics of the beautiful game'). He puts Re_c about 1e5 using the radius, about 15 m/s, with 'a factor of approximately 3'. His Fig. 1b uses C_D 0.1 to 0.4. The goal-kick backspin point is player lore that he reports, not a measurement.

verdicts.claim: 10. Reverse Magnus: seen on smooth balls (sign reversal for smooth spheres above Re ~1.28e5), rubber band fix, no evidence for real ball
verdicts.corrected_value: Re 1.28 x 10^5 is for a smooth CYLINDER (Brown 1971). A wind tunnel measured a negative Magnus force on a real soccer ball at Re ~2.0-2.2 x 10^5 (~14-15 m/s) at low spin (Sp ~0.13-0.14, min C_L ~ -0.09)
verdicts.note: Bush's Re > 128000 figure is Brown's smooth-cylinder data. The beach ball and rubber band demo is correct. Kray, Franke and Frank 2014 (J. Wind Eng. Ind. Aerodyn. 124:46-53) found the effect on a real soccer ball in a wind tunnel, right in the chip speed band, but only at low spin. A chip at 6 rev/s and 14 m/s has Sp about 0.3, outside that zone. There is still no evidence from real ball flight. The Kray figures come from search summaries only.

verdicts.claim: 11. Rezaei lab bounce: backspin 18.08 m/s/22.9 deg/58.4 rad/s -> 9.22 m/s/46.5 deg/topspin 77.8; topspin 19.05/29.6 -> 14.94/33.6; horizontal kept ~38% vs ~75%; contact ~8.5 ms
verdicts.note: All the numbers match the paper. My computation: 6.35/16.66 = 38% and 12.44/16.56 = 75%. The 8.5 ms contact was for the topspin case. The paper names chips as a source of landing backspin. Caveats: a rubber mat with vertical restitution near 0.9-0.95 (much bouncier than turf), and unmatched angles. The backspin ball came in flatter, which alone would keep more forward speed, so the backspin effect is not overstated.

verdicts.claim: 12. Rezaei 2011 J Sports Sci 29(11):1201-13 simulation, no spin: COF 0.10 -> 0.60 cuts horizontal rebound 15.89 -> 10.53 m/s
verdicts.note: Confirmed in the full text (sec. 5.4) and the PubMed record. Above COF 0.6 the trend reverses because the ball starts to roll during contact.

verdicts.claim: 13. Ball bounces backward only near normal incidence with backspin; chip at 50-60 deg just loses forward speed
verdicts.corrected_value: Backward bounce needs the spin surface speed to exceed about 1.5x the forward speed (hollow ball, friction enough to reach rolling). It is not limited to near-normal incidence.
verdicts.note: Cross 2005 shows a spinning ball dropped straight down bounces off at an angle. 'Only near normal incidence' is too strong. My rigid-ball estimate: a chip landing with about 6.5 m/s forward and 6 rev/s backspin keeps about 2.2 m/s (about 35%), close to Rezaei's 38%. Reversing it would need about 14 rev/s. So the chip inference holds.

verdicts.claim: 14. FIFA turf: 2 m drop must rebound 0.60-0.85 m (Pro) / 0.60-1.0 m; turf keeps 30-50% energy; angle ball 50 km/h 15 deg keeps 45-60% / 45-70%
verdicts.corrected_value: Values are right, but the cited 2006 handbook calls the levels 'FIFA Two Star / One Star', and the 30-50% is for ball plus turf, not turf alone
verdicts.note: The FIFA test methods confirm a 2.00 m drop and a ball at 50 +/- 5 km/h and 15 +/- 2 deg, with radar on horizontal speed. On a steel plate, a FIFA-approved ball rebounds 135-155 cm from 2 m (keeps 68-78%), so part of the loss is in the ball. The angle test is a shallow 15 deg shot, not a 50-55 deg chip landing.

verdicts.claim: 15. High vs low instep target: contact ~10 mm below centre for high, near centre for low; foot swung downward in both
verdicts.note: Inoue, Smith and Nunome, ISBS 2025: 7 players, 42 trials, 2000 Hz. The abstract quote matches, including 'foot swung downward in both cases, its direction was more horizontal for the high target'.

verdicts.claim: 16. Kimachi et al.: straight kick contact ~20 mm below centre giving backspin
verdicts.note: The Kimachi abstract (Proc IMechE P 238(3):232-241, online 2022) gives no 20 mm value. Its 'impact points' are spots on the foot, not on the ball. The 20 mm figure appears only in a secondary summary, which I could not open (403).

verdicts.claim: 17. Successful corner kicks: 24.6-29.1 m/s, backspin 3-9 rev/s, 24-28 deg (cited as Goff and Carré 2009 AJP)
verdicts.corrected_value: Source is Cook and Goff 2006, Eur. J. Phys. 27:865-874 'Parameter space for successful soccer kicks'
verdicts.note: The numbers match as quoted in a thesis that cites Cook and Goff: 24.6 < v < 29.1 m/s, 3 < omega_right < 9 rev/s, 24 < psi < 28 deg. These are simulated success windows, not measurements. The spin component is 'omega_right', which is probably backspin, but I could not check the axis in the full text.

verdicts.claim: 18. Drag data disagree: Carré 2002 C_D 0.05 at 15 m/s to 0.35 at 35 m/s vs Asai 2007 0.43/0.15
verdicts.note: Carré 2002 states 'from 15 to 35 m/s ... from around 0.05 to 0.35', fitted to launches at 17-31 m/s. A third estimate, Goff and Carré 2012, gives C_D about 0.17 at 15.6-19.3 m/s. So the dispute is real.

verdicts.claim: 19. OWN MODEL chip 14 m/s, 45 deg, 6 rev/s: 15-17 m, 2.0-2.1 s, apex 4.7-5.0 m, lands 52-55 deg, 10-11 m/s total, 6-7 m/s forward
verdicts.note: My own point-mass run (C_D 0.25-0.45 or a drag-crisis curve, C_L from Sp per Goff and Carré 2012) gives 15.5-17.8 m, 2.1-2.2 s, apex 5.0-5.4 m, landing 50-53 deg, 10.7-11.8 m/s and 6.4-7.6 m/s forward. That is close enough. No measured chip trajectories exist to check against.

verdicts.claim: 20. OWN MODEL no-spin chip: apex 0.3-0.5 m lower, 0.15-0.2 s sooner, range within 0.5 m; lift ~1.2 N (27% of 4.2 N); drag 1.1-1.4 N; lift weakens with v^2
verdicts.corrected_value: Backspin adds about 0.3-0.8 m apex, 0.15-0.3 s airtime and up to about 1 m range; drag at launch about 1.1-1.9 N; lift falls more slowly than v^2
verdicts.note: Lift at launch: Sp 0.30 and C_L about 0.27 give 1.19 N, 28% of weight. Confirmed. Drag of 1.1-1.4 N assumes C_D 0.25-0.3. With the subcritical C_D 0.43 it is 1.9 N. C_L rises as the ball slows because Sp goes up, so lift falls between v and v^2. It is still largest at launch. The main message (height and hang time, little distance) holds.

verdicts.claim: 21. OWN MODEL keeper geometry: 13-14 m/s at 40-55 deg; over keeper 0.4-0.7 s; goal line 1.7-2.3 s; window ~1 m/s; 60-70 deg needs 15-23 m/s and 2.5-3.8 s
verdicts.note: My re-run (keeper 4-5 m out, reach 2.5 m, ball centre under the 2.44 m bar at 14 m) gives 12.3-15.2 m/s at 40-55 deg depending on C_D. The line comes at 1.64-2.38 s, the keeper is passed at 0.40-0.74 s, and the window is 0.75-1.25 m/s. At 60-70 deg: 14.7-23 m/s and 2.55-3.86 s. Caveat: if the ball may bounce once before the line, the window becomes much wider (about 10-14 m/s at 45 deg).

verdicts.claim: 22. OWN MODEL: lofted 24 m/s 30 deg 4 rev/s -> 40-45 m, 2.8-3.0 s; driven 27 m/s 12 deg -> 30-33 m in 1.4-1.5 s, apex ~2 m; chip hangs about as long as the lofted pass
verdicts.corrected_value: Driven pass with no spin: ~23-26 m, ~1.1 s, apex ~1.5 m (30-33 m and 1.4-1.5 s need ~3-4 rev/s backspin). Chip hangs ~2.0-2.2 s, about three quarters of the lofted pass's ~2.7-3.0 s
verdicts.note: Lofted pass: my run gives 38-44 m, 2.7-2.85 s, apex 7.3-8.0 m, landing 39-42 deg and 11-12.8 m/s forward. That agrees. But even with no drag, 27 m/s at 12 deg flies only 1.14 s and 30.2 m. So 1.4-1.5 s is impossible without backspin lift. 'About as long as a lofted pass' is wrong. 'About a third of the distance' is about right (0.35-0.4).

verdicts.claim: 23. Size-5 ball 68-70 cm, 410-450 g, radius ~11 cm; 45 deg launch needs contact ~7-8 cm below centre, ~2-4 cm above ground
