verdicts.note: IFAB Law 2 confirms 68-70 cm and 410-450 g, so the radius is 10.8-11.1 cm. The geometry is right: R sin 45 = 7.8 cm, about 3.2 cm above the ground. Physics caveat: foot friction drags the ball forward and down along its surface, which flattens the launch below the contact normal. So a 45 deg launch needs a contact at or below this height, or a rising foot path. Ground reaction on a resting ball is also ignored.

verdicts.claim: 24. FA youth goals: U11/12 16x7 ft, U13/14 21x7 ft (24x8 also accepted), U15+ 24x8 ft
verdicts.note: FA Handbook 2025-26, section 38 table and note: 'If a pitch is to be provided for U13/14 it is recommended that 7 x 21 goalposts are provided... 8 x 24 would also be acceptable'. 7 ft = 2.13 m.

verdicts.claim: 25. Law 1 goal 7.32 m x 2.44 m
verdicts.note: IFAB Law 1.10: 7.32 m (8 yds) between posts, 2.44 m (8 ft) from the lower edge of the crossbar to the ground.

verdicts.claim: 26. Youth 10 m sprint ~1.8 s (U13), 1.7 s (U15), 1.6 s (U17); chip at 1.7-2.3 s hard to catch
verdicts.note: Martins et al. 2021 (IJERPH), standing split start: 1.8 +/- 0.1, 1.7 +/- 0.1 and 1.6 +/- 0.1 s (n = 14, 25, 23). Caveat on the inference: add about 0.2-0.3 s for reaction and turning. A keeper 8 m out may then reach the line in about 1.8-2.1 s. So only the faster chips (about 2 s or less) clearly beat him. A 2.3 s chip may not.

verdicts.claim: 27. Standing reach ~1.33 x height (NBA combine median 1.335)
verdicts.note: The site says 'about 1.335 times', and about half of players fall at 1.32-1.35. The data are basketball draft prospects, not keepers. It is a rough estimate only.

verdicts.claim: 28. Chalkdust blog: <20 m/s; 12.84 m/s at 45 deg over keeper 6 m away, 1.56 s
verdicts.corrected_value: The self-consistent example is 10.84 m/s at 45 deg (no drag): 12 m range, 3 m apex, 1.56 s
verdicts.note: With no drag, v = sqrt(12 x 9.81) = 10.85 m/s, and T = 2 v sin45 / g = 1.56 s. So 12.84 is the typo, not 10.84. The blog ignores drag. My drag model needs about 12.5-14 m/s for the same kind of chip, 15-25% more.

verdicts.claim: 29. Coaching: chip struck close to ground, downward jab 'kick down, under the ball', lean back, quick rise, lots of backspin, approached straight, short
verdicts.note: All of these phrases are on the SoccerHelp page.

verdicts.claim: 30. England Football: lofted pass 'strike underneath the ball with their instep'; driven pass 'strike through the middle of the ball with their laces or instep'
verdicts.note: Both quotes are exact.

verdicts.claim: 31. Coaching conflict: lofted pass should have little or no backspin vs physics backspin extends range
verdicts.note: The quote is exact: 'There should be little or no backspin on a lofted pass... the ball should roll forward when it lands instead of dying due to backspin'. Bush and Carré back the physics side. It is a coaching choice about the landing, not a rule about flight.

verdicts.claim: 32. Golf: steep landing needed to stop; shallow ball skips even with backspin; pros ~50 deg with ~6,200 rpm on irons
verdicts.note: The quotes match: 'just shy of 50 degrees on their irons, with backspin in the 6,200 RPM range'. This is a popular article, not research data.

verdicts.claim: 33. Seed pods and box mite use backspin Magnus lift to extend flight
verdicts.note: Bush 2013, Fig. 5: seed pods 'tumble with backspin as they fall, thus extending their range via Magnus lift', and 'the box mite leaps with backspin' (images from Vogel 2003).

verdicts.claim: 34. Folklore: backspin makes the ball 'lift sharply and drop quickly' (cited to Wikipedia)
verdicts.corrected_value: The phrase comes from modern-physics.org, not Wikipedia. Backspin also raises drag, which helps steepen the fall.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia says only that 'Chip shots usually have backspin'. The folklore check needs one fix: Carré 2002 and Asai 2007 show drag rises with spin. So backspin helps the steep drop through extra drag, even though its lift holds the ball up.

mechanism_errors: Step 2: 'Some of the kick's energy goes into spin. The ball leaves slower' suggests spin energy is why the ball is slow. It is not. Spin holds only about 5-10% of the lost energy. In Asai 2002 Table 2, the 8 cm offset loses about 72 J of forward energy but spin holds only about 8 J. The main causes are the glancing off-centre contact and the softer swing.

Step 2 and step 1: the ball does not leave along the line from the contact point through the centre. Foot friction drags the ball forward and down along its surface, and this flattens the launch. A downward foot path flattens it more. A 45 deg launch thus needs a contact at or below about 3 cm, or a rising foot. The ground under a resting ball also pushes back up, which the simple picture ignores.

Step 5: 'On the way up the lift leans slightly backward' is wrong in size. Lift is at right angles to the flight path. On a 45 deg climb it leans about 45 deg backward, and on the way down it leans forward. This is why the net effect on distance is small.

Step 5 and claim 20: lift does not simply 'weaken with the square of speed'. As the ball slows, its spin parameter rises, and so does C_L (Goff and Carre 2012). Lift thus falls more slowly than v^2. It is still largest just after the kick.

Step 6 and misconception 9: a chip does not meet a 'sudden tripling' of drag in mid-flight. It is launched at 12.5-15 m/s, which is at or below the drag crisis for modern balls (critical Re gives about 14-24 m/s). So it flies almost all the way in the high-drag regime. The tripling happens to faster kicks, such as shots and goal kicks, as they slow down. 'Drag is highest' is true of the coefficient, not of the force.

Misconception 1: backspin also increases drag (Carre 2002: C_D 0.2 -> 0.5 with spin; Asai 2007: C_D rises with Sp). This extra drag removes forward speed faster and steepens the descent. So backspin does help the steep drop, through drag and not through lift. Better wording: 'backspin holds the ball up, but it also brakes it'.

Misconception 6: 'the turf absorbs most of the downward speed' does not explain forward braking. Losing vertical energy only keeps the next hop short. Forward speed is removed by friction, and the most friction can remove is set by the vertical impact. A steep landing brings little forward speed and a big vertical impact, so friction can bring the ball to rolling. Backspin increases the slip, so friction removes more.

Misconception 10: the reverse Magnus effect has been measured on a real paneled soccer ball in a wind tunnel (Kray et al. 2014). It appeared at Re about 2.0-2.2 x 10^5 (about 14-15 m/s) at low spin (Sp about 0.13-0.14). Better wording: 'seen on real balls only at low spin; a well-struck chip (Sp about 0.3) spins too fast for it'. Also, Bush's Re 1.28 x 10^5 value is for a smooth cylinder, not a sphere.

Step 9: 1.5-2.3 s conflicts with claim 21's 1.7-2.3 s. An in-air crossing under the bar takes about 1.6-2.4 s in an independent run. Also, 'too soon for a keeper 8 m off his line' holds only for the faster chips. Youth players need 1.6-1.8 s for 10 m, plus about 0.2-0.3 s to react and turn. A 2.3 s chip may be caught.

Step 8: 'the turf swallows at least half of the downward bounce energy' describes ball plus turf. A FIFA-approved ball on steel already loses 22-32% (135-155 cm rebound from 2 m). The 40%/75% lab result was on a rubber mat with vertical restitution near 0.9, at unmatched angles.

Misconception 3: 'Too much speed is the most common way to miss' has no source. My model does show the window is narrow (about +/-0.5 m/s at a fixed angle), but no data show which miss is most common.
Step 4 and claim 19: '5-10 rev/s' of chip spin is an assumption. No measured chip spin rates were found. Real curve kicks reach about 10 rev/s or less (Asai 2007).

Misconception 7: a reverse bounce does not strictly need a near-vertical landing. It needs the spin surface speed to exceed about 1.5x the forward speed (hollow ball, enough friction). For a chip at 6-7 m/s forward speed, that is about 14 rev/s or more, above typical kicks. So the conclusion stands, but the reason must be stated this way.
safe_numbers_for_narration: In a full-power instep kick, foot and ball touch for only about 9 milliseconds (Shinkai 2009, 11 skilled players filmed at 5,000 frames per second).
At peak, the foot pushes on the ball with about 2,900 newtons, roughly the weight of a 300 kg mass (Shinkai 2009).
During contact the foot travels only about 15 cm with the ball (Asai et al. 2002: 147 mm).
Hit the ball 8 cm off-centre with the same swing, and ball speed drops from 26 to 18.5 m/s while spin jumps from zero to about 10 turns per second (Asai 2002 and Carre 2002 simulation).
Spin peaks when the foot meets the ball about 10 cm off its centre line, and speed keeps falling as the offset grows (Asai et al. 2002).
Even real curve kicks spin at no more than about 10 turns per second (Asai et al. 2007).
Below its drag crisis, a football's drag coefficient is about 0.43. Above it, the coefficient is about 0.15, nearly three times lower (Asai et al. 2007 wind tunnel).
For a 50 km/h chip with 6 turns per second of backspin, the lift at launch is about 1.2 N, roughly a quarter of the ball's 4.2 N weight (model with measured coefficients).
To lob a keeper from 14 m, the ball needs only about 45-55 km/h, and at a fixed angle the working speed window is only about plus or minus 2 km/h (model).
In one lab bounce test, a ball landing with backspin kept only about 38% of its forward speed. A ball with topspin kept about 75% (Rezaei et al. 2011, rubber mat).
A beach ball curves the wrong way when you spin it. Wrap one rubber band around it, and it curves like a real football (Bush 2013).
Some seed pods and the box mite use backspin to stretch their flight, the same lift a chip uses (Bush 2013).
On FIFA-certified artificial turf, a ball dropped from 2 m may bounce back only 0.60-0.85 m (FIFA turf requirements).
A full-size goal is 7.32 m wide and 2.44 m high. English U11-U14 goals have a lower 2.13 m bar (IFAB Law 1, FA Handbook).
Youth players cover 10 m from a standing start in about 1.6-1.8 seconds (Martins et al. 2021).

candidates.reason: KEEP. Science: foot-ball contact lasts only 9-12 ms (Nunome, Shinkai, Ikegami 2012, https://ojs.ub.uni-konstanz.de/cpa/article/view/5153/4730). Peak force is about 2500-2800 N and the ball squashes by up to 68 mm (Lees et al. 2010 review, https://numerik.mi.fu-berlin.de/wiki/WS_2020/CoMaI_Dokumente/FTVS-2332-version1-the_biomechanics_of_kicking_in_soccer_a_review.pdf). The ball leaves 1.06-1.65 times faster than the foot (Kellis & Katis 2007, http://www.jssm.org/hfpdf.php?volume=06&issue=2&page=154). Contact through the centre gives the most speed. A strike 20-40 mm below centre keeps launch at 16 degrees or less, which suits a low shot (Asai 2005, cited in Lees 2010). Visual hook: the drag crisis. Drag on a ball falls sharply from about 0.5 to 0.1-0.2 near 12-15 m/s (Goff 2010, https://physicstoday.aip.org/quick-study/power-and-spin-in-the-beautiful-game ; Lees 2010). Youth shots are fast enough for this: 11-12-year-olds reach 17.3 m/s (Deniz & Kilci 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12357547/) and 13-year-olds reach 20.9 m/s (Kapidzic 2014, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4234773/). Effective: 81% of Premier League 2015/16 goals came from the foot. Inside-box foot shots scored 14.1% of the time (my count from StatsBomb open data, 380 matches, 988 goals, https://github.com/statsbomb/open-data). Caveat for the script: 'low beats high' is not proven. On-target shots to the low post-third scored 34%, and shots to the high post-third scored 45.5%. Shots to the centre did worst at every height. Thus the lesson is 'low AND wide of the keeper'. The low part buys on-target reliability. This is my own analysis, and saved-shot locations mark the save point, so confidence is medium. Achievable: US Youth Soccer teaches the instep drive at U10 (https://www.usyouthsoccer.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/160/2023/09/2017-Skills-School-Manual.pdf).

KEEP. Science: Magnus force. Asai et al. 2002 filmed impact at 4500 fps. Spin grows with foot offset from the ball axis and with friction, but ball speed drops. At maximum offset, spin was 101 rad/s and speed fell from 26 to 11 m/s. That trade-off makes a good visual (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1046/j.1460-2687.2002.00108.x). Carre et al. 2002 modelled a strike 8 cm off-centre: 18.5 m/s and 64 rad/s (about 10 rev/s). The ball bent more than 3 m over 18 m. Lift coefficient peaked at about 0.26 near 100 rad/s (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1046/j.1460-2687.2002.00109.x). Goff says the Magnus force on a free kick is comparable to the ball's weight, with about 600 rpm sidespin (https://physicstoday.aip.org/quick-study/power-and-spin-in-the-beautiful-game). Bray & Kerwin 2003: to curl over a wall from 18 m at 25 m/s, launch must stay in a 16.5-17.5 degree window (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/0264041031000070994). Bush (MIT) calls the instep bend the easiest free-kick style to do (https://thales.mit.edu/bush/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/Beautiful-Game-2013.pdf). Effective: outside-box goals were 14.5% of PL 2015/16 goals (StatsBomb). Direct free kicks were 2.5% of goals at 6.2% conversion. Opta: 11.7% of PL 2024-25 goals came from outside the box, at 4.2% conversion (https://theanalyst.com/articles/premier-league-2024-25-shot-data). The same skill makes every bent cross and corner. Achievable: US Youth teaches bending shots at U12 and bending passes at U14. The FA gives curl coaching points (https://learn.englandfootball.com/articles-and-resources/coaching/resources/2023/Different-passing-techniques-in-football).

SWAP IN for the chip. Effective: in PL 2015/16, 69 volley goals and 122 half-volley goals made 19.3% of all goals. Conversion was 10.6% for volleys and 9.4% for half-volleys, about the same as normal shots (9.8%). At World Cups 2018 and 2022 the share was about 15% (55 of 378 goals, with shoot-out penalties in the total). Source: my count from StatsBomb open data (https://github.com/statsbomb/open-data). Lobs made only 1.6% of goals. Science: this is the only pick where the ball is already moving. It is a collision problem. Tani et al. 2013 fired balls at 9, 11.5 and 15 m/s at players. Ball speed tracked foot speed. The ball-foot speed ratio was highest when the ball hit near the midline of the foot (https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1390282680878612992). Timing hook: contact lasts about 10 ms. A 10-15 m/s ball crosses its own width in about 15-20 ms (my arithmetic from the numbers above). Keeping it down: a strike above the ball's midline drives it downward (US Youth manual). Topspin adds a downward Magnus force. Bush notes that 'volleying a ball with topspin is relatively straightforward', unlike topspin from a dead ball (https://thales.mit.edu/bush/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/Beautiful-Game-2013.pdf). Achievable: US Youth introduces volley and half-volley shooting at U12 and refines it at U14 (https://www.usyouthsoccer.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/160/2023/09/2017-Skills-School-Manual.pdf). The FA lists volleys as a finishing technique (https://learn.englandfootball.com/articles-and-resources/coaching/resources/2026/What-are-the-ten-core-skills-in-football). It scores 3, not 4, because players need a feeder and timing practice.

DROP as a main pick. Keep it as a short 'flip side' moment. Science: the stab technique wedges the foot under the ball and stops with no follow-through. This gives backspin (US Youth manual: 'to get backspin hit the ball under line A', 'squeeze the ball between the foot and ground', https://www.usyouthsoccer.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/160/2023/09/2017-Skills-School-Manual.pdf). Backspin gives an upward Magnus lift. Slow balls stay in the high-drag regime below the drag crisis, so they drop more steeply than they climb (Bush, MIT, https://thales.mit.edu/bush/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/Beautiful-Game-2013.pdf). I found no peer-reviewed paper on chip-shot flight. The backspin physics comes from general spin data (Carre 2002), so confidence is medium. Effective: rare but deadly when the keeper is off his line. Lobs were 16 of 988 PL 2015/16 goals (1.6%), but 25% of lobs scored. At the 2018 and 2022 World Cups, 10 of 24 lobs scored (StatsBomb open data). Achievable: US Youth introduces 'chipping to shoot' only at U14, later than volley shooting (U12). Its backspin physics repeats the curler's Magnus idea on a different axis. Thus it adds less new science than the volley.

Use as the reference kick in the intro, not as a deep segment. Science: a large, flat contact area trades speed for accuracy. Side-foot ball speed is about 23.4 m/s in adult males (Nunome et al. 2002, MSSE, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/11001093_Three-dimensional_kinetic_analysis_of_side-foot_and_instep_soccer_kicks). That is slower than the instep. The speed-accuracy trade-off is well documented (Lees 2010 review). Effective: the most-used kick in the game. The FA calls it 'traditionally the technique players master first' (https://learn.englandfootball.com/articles-and-resources/coaching/resources/2023/Different-passing-techniques-in-football). Achievable: US Youth teaches inside-foot shooting at U8. Good youth players already own it, so it gives little new science to explore.

Good support material but overlaps the drive and the chip. Science: a 30 m/s goal kick would travel about 120 m with no air, but real kicks go about half that. Backspin extends range, and the ball falls more steeply than it climbs (Bush, MIT, https://thales.mit.edu/bush/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/Beautiful-Game-2013.pdf). Effective: the FA says a lofted ball 'could sail over the defence' against a high line (https://learn.englandfootball.com/articles-and-resources/coaching/resources/2023/Different-passing-techniques-in-football). I found no match statistic that isolates long-pass value, so confidence in the effectiveness score is lower. Achievable: US Youth covers the instep and lofted pass and 'chipping to pass' at U12-U14.

A fun 'myth-buster' option. Science: Andersen, Kristensen & Sorensen 2008 found a higher coefficient of restitution for toe kicks than instep kicks at foot speeds under about 15 m/s. That is, a small, stiff contact wins on quick, short swings (execution 0.25-0.34 s). The advantage disappears at high speed because the foot cannot stay aligned (https://www.shobix.co.jp/jssf/tempfiles/journal/2008/019.pdf). Effective: a quick, no-backswing finish in crowded boxes. One futsal study reports toe-poke was a more successful scoring action than instep (abstract only, https://ejournal.upsi.edu.my/index.php/JSSPJ/article/view/3900). I could not read the full text, so confidence is low. The FA lists 'toe pokes' as a finishing technique (https://learn.englandfootball.com/articles-and-resources/coaching/resources/2026/What-are-the-ten-core-skills-in-football). Achievable: US Youth teaches the 'toe pass & shot' at U8.

Strong physics story, but it is the curler's physics mirrored. Science: same Magnus effect with opposite spin. Roberto Carlos's 1997 goal (a trivela per Bush) was struck from 35 m at 136 km/h with about 14 rev/s. It followed a tightening spiral (Dupeux et al. 2010, https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1367-2630/12/9/093004 ; summary https://phys.org/news/2010-09-carlos-free-fluke-french-physicists.html). Bush says the smaller contact area makes it 'more difficult to control' (https://thales.mit.edu/bush/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/Beautiful-Game-2013.pdf). Effective: disguise and quick release. The FA says it is 'quicker and more deceptive' but 'more advanced' and needs 'a lot of practice' (https://learn.englandfootball.com/articles-and-resources/coaching/resources/2023/Different-passing-techniques-in-football). US Youth teaches the outside-foot pass at U12 and the outside-foot shot at U14. I found no peer-reviewed biomechanics study of the outside-foot kick, so confidence is lower. Use it as a 10-second extra in the curler segment.

Best BONUS TEASER, poor main pick. Science: with almost no spin, unsteady lift near the drag crisis makes the ball zigzag. Texier, Cohen, Quere & Clanet 2016 give the soccer window as 20-25 m/s. One zigzag takes 10-20 m, and lateral shift is only about one ball diameter after 30 m (https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1367-2630/18/7/073027). Hong & Asai 2014 kicked balls with a robot at 30 m/s with less than one rotation. At 25 m, landing spread (SD) was 0.2-0.7 m, depending on ball model and panel direction (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4038026/). Asai & Kamemoto 2011 link it to large wake undulations (https://sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0889974611000557). Bush says the cause 'remains an open question' (https://thales.mit.edu/bush/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/Beautiful-Game-2013.pdf). Achievable: 11-12-year-olds average 17.3 m/s and 13-year-olds 20.9 m/s. That is below or at the bottom of the window. Near-zero spin is hard to repeat. Effective: the effect is unreliable and depends on the ball.

Great physics, too hard from a dead ball. Bush: 'imparting pure topspin is extremely difficult to do from a dead ball, and only a few players have truly mastered it' (https://thales.mit.edu/bush/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/Beautiful-Game-2013.pdf). The same topspin-dip idea is easy to show inside the volley segment instead. I found no match statistic for dipping shots.

Its science is psychology, not physics. In 286 penalties, keepers almost always dove, but staying in the centre was optimal (Bar-Eli et al. 2007, https://pluto.huji.ac.il/~msiritov/BarEliAzarRitovKeidarSchein.pdf). Shots to the upper third were 13% of kicks and all scored (Bar-Eli & Azar 2009, https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/routledg/sas/2009/00000010/00000002/art00003). Penalties were 7.5% of PL 2015/16 goals (StatsBomb). A failed Panenka is costly, and it only applies to one set piece.

Spectacle only. In PL 2015/16, 3 of 63 overhead kicks scored (4.8%, 0.3% of goals). At the 2018 and 2022 World Cups, 0 of 20 scored (StatsBomb open data). Shan et al. 2015 treat it as a high-risk skill with landing danger and ask whether it can be trained at all (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2095927316304455). Do not teach it to 11-16-year-olds without mats and supervision.

No biomechanics or match-frequency source found. Shan & Zhang 2022 list acrobatic scoring techniques as under-researched and 'high-risk and low-reward' (https://www.mdpi.com/2306-5354/9/8/333). I could only read a search snippet, not the full text, so confidence is low. The physics adds nothing new, because it is a normal instep or outside strike with crossed legs.

choice.swap_advice: Swap the chip for the volley/half-volley. Keep the drive and the curler. First reason: match value. Volleys and half-volleys made 19.3% of Premier League 2015/16 goals and about 15% of World Cup 2018 and 2022 goals. Lobs made 1.6% (my count from StatsBomb open data). Second reason: new science. The chip's backspin lift is the curler's Magnus effect on a different axis. The volley adds a moving-ball collision, a tiny timing window, and topspin that pulls the ball down. Third reason: age fit. US Youth Soccer introduces volley shooting at U12 but 'chipping to shoot' only at U14. The new spine works well without equations: drive = no spin plus the drag crisis (the fast ball slips through the air), curler = sidespin (Magnus sideways), volley = topspin (Magnus down) on a moving ball. Keep a 20-30 second chip moment inside the volley segment as the mirror image: backspin floats the ball up, topspin dives it down. One case favours keeping the chip: the producer wants only dead-ball kicks that a child can practise alone. The chip is easier to practise solo than the volley. Present the 'keep it low' advice as 'low and away from the keeper'. My on-target analysis does not show that low shots beat high corners. Confidence: high for the biomechanics and aerodynamics numbers (peer-reviewed). Medium for my StatsBomb counts (one season plus two World Cups, reproducible). Low for the toe-poke futsal claim and the rabona (no full text found).
choice.bonus_teaser: Knuckleball (the no-spin shot). It closes the arc as the drive's extreme. Remove all spin and the air itself makes the ball dance. A 20-25 m/s strike with almost no rotation can zigzag, with one wiggle every 10-20 m (Texier et al. 2016, New J. Phys.). Lab robots show 0.2-0.7 m of random scatter at 25 m (Hong & Asai 2014, Sci. Rep.). Bush (MIT) says the cause 'remains an open question', which suits a Kurzgesagt-style cliffhanger. It is honest to tease it as 'try this at 15-16'. Younger players kick at about 17-21 m/s, at or below the speed the effect needs, and repeating near-zero spin is hard. Runner-up teaser: Roberto Carlos's 1997 outside-foot spiral (Dupeux et al. 2010). Avoid the bicycle kick as the teaser because it invites unsafe copying.

visual_rules: SCOPE NOTE: This is a style guide, not physics research. The peer-reviewed kick papers (Asai, Carre, Bray and Kerwin, and so on) are out of scope here. Primary sources for style are Kurzgesagt's own making-of video, their site, and the Skillshare class their animators teach. Rules marked 'own measurement' come from caption and frame data I read from YouTube streams in memory. I saved no files.

V1 MOOD FIRST: Make 3 to 5 colour 'mood' frames before the storyboard. Take the dominant colours of each chapter from them, then build a rough palette. A former Kurzgesagt art director says a mood is 'completely exaggerated with too much saturation and little black'. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_VrNiya8kLg (third-party tutorial that quotes the art director). Confidence: medium.

V2 NO OUTLINES: Do not use black line art. Separate shapes only by fill colour and tone. In 2 sampled 2025 videos, near-black pixels (HSV V<0.06) were about 0% of the frame at the median. Own measurement: 1 frame every 8 s at 144p from https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Cyl3X88KEgg and https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qQW4LTWgtc. Confidence: high that there is no black line art, medium for the number.

V3 ROUNDED GEOMETRY: Round every corner on the main objects. One trick: add a thick stroke in the same colour as the fill. Then the corner radius stays the same when you scale. Give all detail strokes in one scene the same width. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rs_BiKgpSPM (third-party, medium). My own numbers for 1920x1080: detail strokes 6-8 px, and a corner radius of at least 15% of the shape's short side (low).

V4 SATURATED BACKGROUNDS: The background is always a saturated colour, never grey and never pure black. Measured median saturation of the dominant (background) colour was 0.90 to 0.91. The space-themed video sat dark: median brightness V=0.30, with hues at 210-270 deg (blue to indigo). The planet/nature video sat brighter: median V=0.51. Own measurement (same 2 videos). Confidence: medium.

V5 LIMITED PALETTE, SMALL ACCENT: Use about 3 hue families per frame. Measured median was 3 families of 30 deg each, each holding more than 5% of coloured pixels, with an interquartile range (IQR) of 2-5. Keep the bright contrasting accent small. It covered 1.5-4% of pixels at the median and 4-10% at the upper quartile. Put the accent on the subject of the current sentence. Own measurement. Confidence: medium.

V6 CONTRAST DIRECTS THE EYE: Make the background darker or lighter than the foreground. Give the subject the highest contrast in the frame. Separate foreground from background with a complementary pair, such as blue against orange. Show form with tints and shades of one hue. The art director's advice: work in HSB with all 3 parameters and treat contrast as tonal value. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_VrNiya8kLg. Confidence: medium.

V7 SIMPLIFIED SHADING: Draw a rim light as a lighter stroke along the lit edge. Draw the shadow as 1-3 darker shapes of the same hue that wrap around the far side. For a darker shadow, stack more shadow layers. Use a light-to-dark gradient only on low-detail or background objects. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ByYNLEl160M (third-party). Confidence: medium.

V8 GLOWS: Show a light source (a floodlight, the sun, the impact point) with low-opacity concentric circles around it, or a soft glow on the emitter. Technique source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ByYNLEl160M (medium). My own numbers: 3-4 rings, each radius x1.5 the one before, opacity 20% / 12% / 6% / 3% (low).

V9 LONG SHADOWS: I found no source that confirms long cast shadows as a Kurzgesagt rule. If you use them, keep them flat: the ground colour 10-15% darker, no blur, all at one angle per scene. Confidence: low.

V10 DEPTH WITH PARALLAX LAYERS: Build each scene in 3-5 depth layers that move at different speeds. Kurzgesagt calls its work 'classic 2D flat animation with 3D elements'. Its class has a lesson on 'Fake 3D Depth + Secondary Action'. Sources: https://kurzgesagt.org/what-we-do?visit=videos and https://www.skillshare.com/en/classes/motion-graphics-with-kurzgesagt-part-3/140140401 (high). My own speed ratios: far layer 0.2x, mid 0.5x, subject 1x, foreground 1.3x, with the foreground darker (low).

V11 STARS AND PARTICLES: For night sky and x-ray scenes, add a star or dust field in 3 layers: 1-2 px far, 2-3 px mid, 3-4 px near. Twinkle them with a looped opacity animation and offset phases. No primary source states a star rule. Confidence: low (my observation only).

V12 SIMPLE CHARACTERS: Build characters from rounded primitives and keep faces minimal (dot or oval eyes). Rig limbs with Duik IK or Rubberhose. The class exaggerates with scale: parts shrink to 80% or start at 52%, then return to 100%. Eyes grow about 10% to show shock. Sources: https://www.skillshare.com/en/classes/motion-graphics-with-kurzgesagt-part-3/140140401 and https://www.classcentral.com/course/skillshare-motion-graphics-with-kurzgesagt-part-2-82026. Confidence: medium. Design an original mascot, such as a young player made of rounded rectangles. Never use a bird.

V13 VISUAL METAPHOR BEFORE PIXELS: Sketch the visual metaphors and the transitions between ideas before you illustrate. Kurzgesagt aims to find 'the right images to the words in the script'. They illustrate about 200 panels per video, mostly from scratch. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uFk0mgljtns (Kurzgesagt's own making-of). Confidence: high. Budget about 20 new illustrations per minute.

V14 ABSTRACT OVER LITERAL: Use an abstract diagram instead of a realistic picture when it explains better. For example, show the foot, the ball and the airflow as simple shapes on a clean field. The style moved from literal detail to abstract images joined by seamless transitions. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rs_BiKgpSPM. Confidence: medium.

V15 TEXTURE: Keep texture minimal. Kurzgesagt lists 'vector illustration, pixel-based illustration and infographics'. If you add grain, keep it at 2-4% opacity and static for each shot. Source: https://kurzgesagt.org/what-we-do?visit=videos. Confidence: low for any grain rule.

V16 SOCCER STAGING (own rule): Give each kick 3 recurring views, each with its own palette. The PITCH view is side-on or top-down on the night pitch. The X-RAY view shows foot, ankle and ball contact. The SKY view shows the full ball flight. The ball keeps the same motif colour, #FF7A3D, in every view.
motion_rules: M1 FRAME RATE: The Kurzgesagt class says 'We will be animating at 60 frames per second'. I measured the published videos at 25 fps (2014) and 30 fps (2025). Animate at 60 fps and deliver at 30 or 60 fps. Sources: https://www.skillshare.com/en/classes/motion-graphics-with-kurzgesagt-part-1/631970755, plus my own frame counts of https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zQGOcOUBi6s and https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PqtggjVAi8M. Confidence: high.

M2 STANDARD MOVE = 50 FRAMES @60fps (0.83 s): The class animator says 'Generally, I use 50 frames for most of my animation'. The class uses a 90 deg rotation over 50 frames as an example. Source: https://www.skillshare.com/en/classes/motion-graphics-with-kurzgesagt-part-1/631970755 (transcript read through a proxy). Confidence: high.

M3 STANDARD EASE = 75% INFLUENCE: The class sets keyframe velocity to 75% ('If you change this to 75 percent, you can see how the curve changed'). With speed 0 on both keys, 75/75 influence equals cubic-bezier(0.75, 0, 0.25, 1). That is almost the same as easeInOutQuart, cubic-bezier(0.76, 0, 0.24, 1). The mapping is that influence sets the control point's x value: https://creativecow.net/forums/thread/converting-keyframe-velocity-to-bezier-curves/ and https://easings.net/. Confidence: medium (derived).

M4 POP-UPS = 5-10 FRAMES @60fps (0.08-0.17 s): Class quote: 'Ten or five frames are usually used for a pop-up, like popping up a sign or a speech bubble.' Add a small overshoot, then settle, with easeOutBack or a spring (see easing). Source: https://www.skillshare.com/en/classes/motion-graphics-with-kurzgesagt-part-1/631970755. Confidence: high for the timing.

M5 ANTICIPATION, HOLDS, OVERLAP: Before a big action, hold the key pose for about 20 frames at 60 fps (0.33 s). Start a small counter-move about 10 frames before the main move. Offset linked body parts by 3-5 frames so they follow through. These are examples from the class's character lessons, which cover timing, exaggeration and overlapping action. Source: https://www.skillshare.com/en/classes/motion-graphics-with-kurzgesagt-part-3/140140401. Confidence: medium. For a kick, animate the plant foot, then the hip, then the knee, then the foot, 3-5 frames apart.

M6 NOTHING IS EVER STILL: Loop small secondary motion on every idle element. Use loopOut('pingpong') on 2-key rotation or position moves (the class example is a 15 deg rotation with easy ease). Use wiggle(freq, amp) driven by slider controls, with frequency around 0.5-1 per second. Sources: https://www.skillshare.com/en/classes/motion-graphics-with-kurzgesagt-part-1/631970755 and https://www.classcentral.com/course/skillshare-motion-graphics-with-kurzgesagt-part-2-82026 (medium). My own calm-background values: 2-6 deg or 2-8 px, period 2-4 s, random phase for each element so nothing moves in sync (low).

M7 CONTINUOUS SHOTS, FEW HARD CUTS: I measured full-frame scene changes with an ffmpeg scene score above 0.3. A 2025 video had about one every 12 s (70 changes in 836 s). A 2014 video had about one every 78 s. Put most changes inside one continuous shot instead: a camera push, a pan across a large canvas, or a shape morph. Own measurement of https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PqtggjVAi8M and https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zQGOcOUBi6s. Confidence: medium.

M8 PACING = NEW VISUAL ABOUT EVERY 3 s: About 200 illustrated panels per roughly 10-minute video gives about 3 s per panel. At 155 wpm that is about 8 spoken words per new visual, so plan one new element per clause. Allow a hard scene change at most every 10-15 s. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uFk0mgljtns. Confidence: medium (derived).

M9 CAMERA: Use slow push-ins of 5-15% scale over 4-8 s, and pans across one big illustrated scene (for example, the full pitch drawn as one wide canvas). Ease them with easeInOutSine or a critically damped spring. Never snap the camera. These are my own numbers. Confidence: low.

M10 TRANSITIONS: Plan the 'transitions between ideas' at the sketch stage (source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uFk0mgljtns). Types: zoom into an object so that the next scene appears inside it (ball, then leather panel, then air molecules). Match cut on a shape (the ball circle becomes the sun circle in the sky view). Pan to the next area of one big canvas. Morph a diagram into the next diagram. My own duration: 0.8-1.5 s. Confidence: medium for the practice, low for the numbers.

M11 DIAGRAMS BUILD, NEVER APPEAR: Draw lines and arrows with a trim path (end 0 to 100%). Reveal regions with track mattes and inverted track mattes. Move groups with null objects. Animate path shapes for curves. Source: the Part 1 lesson list at https://www.skillshare.com/en/classes/motion-graphics-with-kurzgesagt-part-1/631970755 (high). My own sequence: the arrow shaft draws in 20-30 frames at 60 fps, then the arrowhead pops in 5-10 frames, then the label pops 4-6 frames later, then numbers count up (low).

M12 PHYSICS MOTION IS NOT EASED (own rule): Move the ball along a trajectory computed from physics, at constant time steps. Do not give the ball in flight a design ease. Put the easing on the camera, the labels and the diagrams instead. Slow motion is fine if it is shown as slow motion. Confidence: own rule for scientific accuracy.

M13 EXITS FASTER THAN ENTRANCES: Entrances take 0.4-0.5 s with a decelerate curve. Exits take 0.2-0.3 s with an accelerate curve. Source for the curve and duration tokens: https://m3.material.io/styles/motion/easing-and-duration/tokens-specs (UI guidance used here as an analogy). Confidence: medium.
narrative_rules: N1 COLD OPEN: Start with a bold claim, often addressed to 'you', in 1-4 short sentences, before any title. Examples: 'Every second of your life, you are under attack.' (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zQGOcOUBi6s), 'You will never leave the solar system. Nobody alive today will.' (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Cyl3X88KEgg), 'Everything we think about aliens might be completely wrong' (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QW_jlUn4gA8). The title card or intro sting comes at about 25-65 s. Measured: 25-33 s at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n-gYFcVx-8Y, 45 s at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PqtggjVAi8M, 65 s at zQGOcOUBi6s. Confidence: high.

N2 PIVOT QUESTION: Close the hook with a short question that frames the video. Examples: 'What happened?' (n-gYFcVx-8Y), 'What IS a memory?' (PqtggjVAi8M), 'Ok but how can this be?' (Cyl3X88KEgg), 'So, what happens in the case of an infection?' (zQGOcOUBi6s). Confidence: high.

N3 SIMPLIFICATION CONTRACT: Tell the viewer openly that you simplify. Examples: 'The human brain is the most complex thing in the universe, so we need to simplify quite a bit.' (PqtggjVAi8M), 'For this video, let's assume the immune system has 12 different jobs.' (zQGOcOUBi6s), 'This was a very, very simplified explanation' (zQGOcOUBi6s). Confidence: high.

N4 'LET'S...' IS RARE: I found 'Let's' framing in a few places. Examples: 'Let's take all the science on exoplanets we have and imagine a perfect world' (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qQW4LTWgtc), 'let's add colours to the jobs' (zQGOcOUBi6s), 'Let's head back to Earth.' (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yDAAlojz8NU). The exact phrase 'Let's start with' did not appear in 14 transcripts I checked. Use it once at most. Confidence: medium.

N5 CHAPTERS WITH TITLE CARDS: Split the video into chapters with 2-5 word title cards spoken or shown on screen. Examples: 'Population Collapse' (n-gYFcVx-8Y), 'Your Brain is Weird Madness' (PqtggjVAi8M), 'Laying the Foundation: Script' (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uFk0mgljtns). Confidence: high. For this film, use one chapter per kick.

N6 SCALE AND PERSPECTIVE SHIFTS: Chain zooms to shift scale. Optimistic Nihilism zooms out in steps: 'a moist speck of dust', then 'one arm of an average galaxy', then the galaxy group, the supercluster and the observable universe (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MBRqu0YOH14). For soccer, use the same chain: foot contact (milliseconds), the ball, the air around the ball, the wall, the pitch from above, the stadium at night. Confidence: high for the device.

N7 GENTLE HUMOUR: Use deadpan understatement, casual slang in serious places, and small pop-culture winks. Examples: 'to protect you from...well...dying' and 'a wild rusty nail appears' (zQGOcOUBi6s), 'Earth ... is actually kind of mid' (8qQW4LTWgtc), 'and video games to finish' (MBRqu0YOH14). On tone: 'I don't think it should be too serious. The videos should be fun, and learning something should be a bonus.' (https://birdinflight.com/en/inspiration/kurzgesagt.html). Confidence: high.

N8 REPEATED MOTIF AND CALLBACK: Plant a phrase or image early and bring it back at the end. 'The loneliest places in existence' comes at 20 s and returns at 503 s (yDAAlojz8NU). 'Personal lore' comes at 28 s and returns at 767-772 s (PqtggjVAi8M). Confidence: high. For this film, plant the image of the opening kick and replay it at the end, now with every force visible.

N9 REFLECTIVE, OPTIMISTIC ENDING: End with a wider thought that comes back to the viewer. Example: 'Life is awfully complicated, but if we take the time to understand it, we'll encounter endless wonders and great beauty.' (zQGOcOUBi6s). Kurzgesagt describes its narration as blending 'rationality and optimism' (https://kurzgesagt.org/what-we-do?visit=videos). Confidence: high. Do not copy the shop or sponsor segment that follows their endings.

N10 NARRATION PACE: I measured 142-169 words per minute over the full runtime of 9 recent long videos (median about 160). Over 14 videos including older ones, the median was about 155. Reflective pieces run slower: 120 wpm for Loneliness (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n3Xv_g3g-mA) and 145 wpm for Optimistic Nihilism (MBRqu0YOH14). Target 150-160 wpm, and drop to about 130 for the ending. Own measurement from English captions, sponsor reads included. Confidence: medium-high.

N11 NARRATOR DELIVERY: Use one calm, warm voice. Kurzgesagt records the narration after the illustration stage. The narrator says: 'It's important to keep the flow, so I try to get one version done and then go back through, retaking paragraphs and sentences'. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uFk0mgljtns. Confidence: high. Use an original voice actor or voice. Never use a clone of Kurzgesagt's narrator.
N12 SENTENCE RHYTHM: Mix punchy fragments with longer sentences. Example: 'the US planned to nuke Israel ... And Panama. And Alaska.' (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h3DCdWyb0cc). Confidence: high.

N13 SCRIPT PROCESS: Research first, then write about a dozen drafts, then get an expert fact-check. Sources: https://kurzgesagt.org/what-we-do?visit=videos and https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uFk0mgljtns ('Writing is the bottleneck'). Confidence: high. For this film, have a coach check each kick technique and a physicist check the airflow and spin claims.

N14 SHOW BEFORE YOU NAME (from the user's request): The user wants the science explained 'without really mentioning' it. So show the effect first (the ball bends, dips or knuckles) and give the cause in everyday words. Name a technical term once at most, and only after the viewer has seen the effect. Confidence: this is my reading of an ambiguous phrase ('scones').

N15 LENGTH PLAN: Kurzgesagt videos run 4-16 min (https://animationexplainers.com/kurzgesagt/). For 3 kicks covered in depth, aim for 8-11 min, which is about 1,250-1,700 words at 155 wpm. Suggested split: cold open 30-45 s, then title, then 3 chapters of 2.5-3 min each, then an ending of 30-45 s. Each chapter runs: mini-hook, then the body mechanics (x-ray view), then the flight (sky view), then how a young player can practise it. Confidence: own plan built on the numbers above.
sound_rules: S1 SCORE LAST, COMPOSED TO PICTURE: Kurzgesagt says 'Every song is original music composed to the finished video to create a unique atmosphere and to highlight the important parts.' Lock the picture first, then write or pick an original score that rises at the reveals. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uFk0mgljtns. Confidence: high.

S2 VOICE FIRST: The Kurzgesagt audio studio aims for 'a rich, immersive experience while maintaining the clarity and prominence of the narration'. Source: https://www.epic-mountain.com/. Confidence: high. My own mix values: duck the music about 10-15 dB under the voice, and let it rise in the gaps between sentences (low).

S3 AMBIENT, ELECTRONIC, ATMOSPHERIC: The studio's soundtracks are described as 'cinematic, electronic, and atmospheric'. Use soft synth pads and slow arpeggios under explanations, and a fuller build for the reveals. Source: https://soundeffects.fandom.com/wiki/Epic_Mountain (secondary). Confidence: low-medium.

S4 SFX LAYER ON ENTRANCES AND MOVES: Kurzgesagt calls sound effects 'the icing on the cake' and says 'try watching a video with headphones if you want to get the full depth of it'. Sources: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uFk0mgljtns (high). A secondary source describes 'soft background tones, deep booms on key words, and futuristic effects': https://10.studio/the-incredible-amount-of-work-behind-kurzgesagts-beautiful-animated-videos/ (medium). Own rules: sync a soft pop or click to the overshoot frame of each primary element, and a whoosh to each camera move or zoom-through. Pan each sound to its on-screen position. Leave background element entrances silent (low).

S5 KICK SOUND PALETTE (own rule): Use a short low thump for foot-ball contact, an airy hiss that follows the ball's spin and speed, a net swish or a post clang, and a far stadium bed that is sparse at night. Use a sub-drop or a moment of silence right before each slow-motion x-ray reveal. Confidence: own design rule.

S6 ORIGINAL AUDIO ONLY: Do not use Epic Mountain tracks from the Kurzgesagt soundtracks (for example https://epicmountainmusic.bandcamp.com/album/kurzgesagt-vol-6-original-motion-picture-soundtrack). Do not use their intro or outro sting, and do not write sound-alike cues. Confidence: high.

easing: STANDARD MOVE (Kurzgesagt 75% influence, derived): cubic-bezier(0.75, 0, 0.25, 1), 50 frames @60fps = 0.83 s. Nearly the same as easeInOutQuart, cubic-bezier(0.76, 0, 0.24, 1), from https://easings.net/.

SOFTER MOVE (After Effects Easy Ease default, speed 0 and 33.33% influence on both keys): cubic-bezier(0.333, 0, 0.667, 1). Source: https://helpx.adobe.com/after-effects/using/keyframe-interpolation.html.

POP-IN WITH OVERSHOOT: cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1) (easeOutBack, https://easings.net/), 0.25-0.4 s total. Alternatively a spring with mass 1, stiffness 200 and damping 16. By my calculation that gives damping ratio 0.57, about 12% overshoot, and settles to 2% in about 0.5 s.
SOFT POP (labels, small icons): spring with mass 1, stiffness 120, damping 14. Damping ratio 0.64, about 7% overshoot, settles in about 0.57 s.
SNAPPY POP (signs, speech bubbles, 5-10 frames @60fps per the Kurzgesagt class): spring with mass 1, stiffness 300, damping 20. Damping ratio 0.58, about 11% overshoot, settles in about 0.4 s.

REMOTION DEFAULT SPRING for reference: mass 1, stiffness 100, damping 10. That gives 16% overshoot and about 0.8 s to settle. Raise damping to remove the bounce. Source: https://www.remotion.dev/docs/spring.
ENTER / DECELERATE: cubic-bezier(0.05, 0.7, 0.1, 1.0) (Material 3 emphasized decelerate), 0.4-0.5 s. Source: https://m3.material.io/styles/motion/easing-and-duration/tokens-specs.
EXIT / ACCELERATE: cubic-bezier(0.3, 0.0, 0.8, 0.15) (Material 3 emphasized accelerate), 0.2-0.3 s. Same source.

CAMERA PUSH-IN / PAN: cubic-bezier(0.37, 0, 0.63, 1) (easeInOutSine, https://easings.net/) over 3-8 s. Or a critically damped spring with mass 1, stiffness 80, damping 17.9 (damping ratio 1.0, no overshoot) stretched to the shot length.
IDLE SECONDARY LOOP: sine or ping-pong loop, period 2-4 s, amplitude 2-6 deg or 2-8 px. Or wiggle(0.5-1, small amplitude) with a separate seed for each layer.
BALL IN FLIGHT: no design easing. Use linear time along a trajectory computed from physics (rule M12).

tools.recommended_stack:
Use Remotion 4.0.529 (React + TypeScript, headless Chrome frame capture, bundled FFmpeg) on Node 26.9.0. Use OpenAI gpt-4o-mini-tts for narration, whisper-1 for word timings, and ffmpeg lavfi synthesis (plus a few CC0 files) for music and SFX.

Pipeline (each step is a script, so a re-run only rebuilds what changed):
1. script.json holds one entry per scene: id, narration text and visual beats.
2. scripts/tts.mjs calls the OpenAI SDK (openai@7.23.0) once per scene with response_format "pcm". It wraps each clip into public/vo/sNN.wav with ffmpeg and caches by sha1(model+voice+instructions+text).
3. scripts/probe.mjs measures each WAV with ffprobe and writes src/timeline.json as [{id, file, durationInSeconds}].
4. scripts/captions.mjs sends each clip to whisper-1 (verbose_json, word timestamps). It converts the result with @remotion/openai-whisper and writes src/captions/sNN.json.
5. scripts/sfx.sh builds pad.wav, whoosh.wav and pop.wav with ffmpeg aevalsrc/anoisesrc into public/sfx.
6. Remotion: Root.tsx imports timeline.json and sizes the composition from the sum of scene frames. Main.tsx is a <Series> of scenes, and each scene holds its own <Audio>. Animations key off word timestamps.
7. Run `npx remotion render`. An optional ffmpeg pass does loudnorm to -14 LUFS.

Why Remotion: it is the only candidate with first-class headless CLI rendering, an audio-driven timeline (Sequence/Series/Audio/calculateMetadata), SVG path tools (@remotion/paths evolvePath/interpolatePath), ready shapes (@remotion/shapes), seeded noise for organic wobble (@remotion/noise), transitions, Google Fonts loading and caption helpers. It is free for an individual. It has an active repo (pushed 2026-09-26, about 60.5k stars).

Kurzgesagt-style flat-vector tips: draw everything as inline SVG with flat fills. Use a rounded Google font through @remotion/google-fonts/<Font> with explicit weights and subsets. Make glows with SVG radialGradient, not CSS filter: blur. Animate with spring()/interpolate() and use noise2D for idle wobble.

Verdict: Remotion 4.0.529 works on Node 26.9.0 (medium-high confidence). One open bug needs a workaround.

1. FIXED: Remotion failed on Node v26.1.0. The extract-zip package broke the Chrome Headless Shell download and left only metadata files. Issue: https://github.com/remotion-dev/remotion/issues/7409 . PR #7423 replaced extract-zip with a vendored and patched yauzl. It was merged 2026-05-18: https://github.com/remotion-dev/remotion/pull/7423 . It shipped in v4.0.463 as '@remotion/renderer: Fix browser download on Node 26': https://github.com/remotion-dev/remotion/releases/tag/v4.0.463 . Thus any version from 4.0.463 up is fine, and 4.0.529 contains the fix.

It crashed in 4-6 of 10 runs on 4.0.529. PR #11680 is pending: https://github.com/remotion-dev/remotion/issues/11679 . Mitigation: never throw in calculateMetadata. Validate script.json and timeline.json in a pre-step script, and keep calculateMetadata a pure sum of numbers.

3. No 'engines' field is set, so npm gives no warning. Node 26 is newer than the CI baseline in the Remotion docs. Smoke-test first with `npx remotion browser ensure` and a 60-frame render (`--frames=0-59`).

4. Fallback if a new Node-26 problem appears. No version manager is installed. Run `brew install node@22` and call `/opt/homebrew/opt/node@22/bin/node node_modules/.bin/remotion render ...`. Or run `npx -y node@22 node_modules/@remotion/cli/remotion-cli.js render ...` (lower confidence: the path of the CLI entry file is not verified).

tools.audio_sync_pattern:
Principle: audio is the master clock. Measure every narration clip first, then derive every frame count from those durations. Never hand-type durations.

A) Measure. Use one of these:
  pcm bytes: seconds = bytes / 48000 (24 kHz x 2 bytes, mono, exact), or
  ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration -of csv=p=0 public/vo/s01.wav
Write src/timeline.json as [{"id":"s01","file":"vo/s01.wav","durationInSeconds":41.37}, ...]. Use WAV, not MP3, because MP3 duration is estimated and has encoder padding.

B) Root.tsx (sizes the composition from the audio):
  import timeline from './timeline.json';
  const FPS = 30, TAIL = 12; // 0.4 s of breath after each line
  const scenes = timeline.map(s => ({...s, frames: Math.ceil(s.durationInSeconds * FPS) + TAIL}));
  <Composition id="Kicks" component={Main} fps={FPS} width={1920} height={1080}
    durationInFrames={1} defaultProps={{scenes}}
    calculateMetadata={({props}) => ({durationInFrames: props.scenes.reduce((a, s) => a + s.frames, 0)})} />
calculateMetadata runs one time before the render and can return durationInFrames, fps, width, height, props and defaultCodec. It can be async. https://www.remotion.dev/docs/calculate-metadata . Keep it non-throwing (see the Node 26 note).

C) Main.tsx:
  import {Series, staticFile} from 'remotion'; import {Audio} from '@remotion/media';
  <Series>{props.scenes.map(s => (
    <Series.Sequence key={s.id} durationInFrames={s.frames} premountFor={30}>
      <SceneById id={s.id} />
      <Audio src={staticFile(s.file)} />
    </Series.Sequence>))}
  </Series>
  <Audio src={staticFile('sfx/pad.wav')} loop volume={0.18} />
<Audio> from @remotion/media is the recommended audio tag. It extracts audio with Mediabunny so the audio stays in sync with the timeline. It has from, durationInFrames, trimBefore/After, volume (a number or a per-frame function), loop, premountFor and playbackRate. https://www.remotion.dev/docs/media/audio

D) Beat sync inside a scene: useCurrentFrame() is local to the Sequence. Convert word timestamps to frames with frameOf = (word) => Math.round(caps.find(c => c.text.trim().startsWith(word)).startMs / 1000 * fps). Then drive spring({frame: frame - frameOf('spin'), fps}) so the ball curls exactly when the narrator says 'spin'.

E) SFX: add <Audio src={staticFile('sfx/whoosh.wav')} from={frameOf('kick') - 4} /> inside the scene. For transition sounds, wrap a presentation with the addSound() helper from https://www.remotion.dev/docs/transitions/audio-transitions .

F) Transitions: <TransitionSeries.Transition> overlaps two scenes and SHORTENS the total (40 + 60 - 30 = 70 frames). https://www.remotion.dev/docs/transitions/transitionseries . Choose one fix. (1) Keep narration on its own top-level <Series> and use TransitionSeries only for visuals, adding the transition length to each visual scene. (2) Use <TransitionSeries.Overlay>, which does not shorten the timeline.

G) Ducking: volume={(f) => narrating(f) ? 0.10 : 0.22} on the music track. Or mix outside Remotion with ffmpeg sidechaincompress.

Loudness pass (YouTube-style -14 LUFS):

- --gl accepts angle, egl, swiftshader, swangle, vulkan or angle-egl. The docs say "On a desktop, angle is recommended". https://www.remotion.dev/docs/gl-options

tools.tts:
PRIMARY: OpenAI gpt-4o-mini-tts. The guide calls it "our newest and most reliable text-to-speech model". Pin the snapshot gpt-4o-mini-tts-2025-12-15 (the current default, the other is -2025-03-20) so re-takes sound the same. https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/text-to-speech , https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4o-mini-tts
- Model ids in the SDK: 'tts-1' | 'tts-1-hd' | 'gpt-4o-mini-tts' | 'gpt-4o-mini-tts-2025-12-15'. https://unpkg.com/openai@7.23.0/resources/audio/speech.d.ts
- Voices (13): alloy, ash, ballad, coral, echo, fable, nova, onyx, sage, shimmer, verse, marin, cedar. The guide says "For best quality, we recommend using marin or cedar". tts-1 and tts-1-hd have only 9 voices.
- instructions: free text that controls accent, emotion, intonation, speed, tone and whispering. It "Does not work with tts-1 or tts-1-hd". Example for this video: "Warm, curious science narrator. Calm wonder with light humour. Steady pace, about 150 words per minute. Short pause after each key fact. Clear, neutral English."
- response_format: mp3 (default), opus, aac, flac, wav or pcm. The guide recommends wav or pcm for the fastest response. PCM is 24 kHz, 16-bit signed little-endian, mono.
- speed: 0.25 to 4.0. stream_format: 'sse' or 'audio'.
- Limits: input max 4096 characters (SDK docstring), and the model page lists a maximum input of 2000 tokens. Rate limit at Tier 1 is 500 RPM.
- Price: $0.60 per 1M text input tokens plus $12 per 1M audio output tokens. The widely quoted estimate is about $0.015 per minute (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing , and the estimate discussion at https://community.openai.com/t/understanding-gpt-4o-mini-tts-pricing-input-characters-cost/1151816). An 8-minute script costs about $0.12, plus re-takes.
- Policy: "Our usage policies require you to provide a clear disclosure to end users that the TTS voice they are hearing is AI-generated". Put a line in the description or end card.

Chunking: send one request per scene (at most about 1,500 characters, about 200 words, about 80 s). Split only at sentence ends. Use the same voice, instructions and snapshot for every scene. Cache by hash, because output is not deterministic. For a pause inside a scene, write it into the text (for example '...') or insert silence with ffmpeg (adelay or apad).
Script sketch (tts.mjs):
  const r = await openai.audio.speech.create({model:'gpt-4o-mini-tts-2025-12-15', voice:'cedar', input, instructions, response_format:'pcm'});
  fs.writeFileSync(`public/vo/${id}.pcm`, Buffer.from(await r.arrayBuffer()));
  // ffmpeg -y -f s16le -ar 24000 -ac 1 -i public/vo/s01.pcm -ar 48000 -ac 1 public/vo/s01.wav
Measure: duration = pcmBytes / 48000, or use ffprobe on the rewritten WAV.

OFFLINE FALLBACK: macOS `say`.
  say -v Samantha -r 170 -f scene01.txt -o public/vo/s01.wav --file-format=WAVE --data-format=LEI16@48000
AIFF works too: `say -v Daniel -o s01.aiff -f scene01.txt`. Insert a pause inline with [[slnc 300]]. The man page lists the file formats AIFF, caff, m4af and WAVE, and a format can take '@samplerate'.
Installed English voices here: Samantha (en_US), Daniel (en_GB), Karen (en_AU), Moira (en_IE), Tessa (en_ZA), Rishi (en_IN), plus the Eddy, Flo, Reed, Sandy and Shelley families. No Enhanced or Premium voices are installed. To add them, go to System Settings > Accessibility > Spoken Content > System voice > Manage Voices, then download (https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/mchlp2290/mac). Downloaded voices then appear in `say -v '?'`. It is not verified whether Siri voices are exposed to `say` (low confidence, assume no). Quality is clearly lower than gpt-4o-mini-tts, so use `say` only for timing drafts.
tools.captions:
Recommended: whisper-1 per scene clip. It is the ONLY OpenAI model with word timestamps: "The timestamp_granularities[] parameter is only supported for whisper-1". gpt-4o-transcribe, gpt-4o-mini-transcribe and gpt-transcribe give no timestamps. https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/speech-to-text
- Call: openai.audio.transcriptions.create({file: fs.createReadStream('public/vo/s01.wav'), model:'whisper-1', response_format:'verbose_json', timestamp_granularities:['word'], language:'en', prompt: sceneText.slice(0, 800)})
- The prompt is limited to 224 tokens. It helps the spelling of terms such as 'Magnus effect' and 'knuckleball'.
- Files can be up to 25 MB. At 24 kHz mono 16-bit (48 KB/s) that is about 8.7 min, so per-scene clips are always fine.
- Price: $0.006 per minute (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing), so the whole video costs less than $0.05.
- Convert: const {captions} = openAiWhisperApiToCaptions({transcription}). This comes from @remotion/openai-whisper 4.0.529 and restores the punctuation that OpenAI strips. It gives Caption[] as {text, startMs, endMs, timestampMs, confidence}. https://www.remotion.dev/docs/openai-whisper/openai-whisper-api-to-captions
- Pages: createTikTokStyleCaptions({captions, combineTokensWithinMilliseconds: 1200}) from @remotion/captions. The text must have a leading space before each word. https://www.remotion.dev/docs/captions/create-tiktok-style-captions . Offset each scene's captions by that scene's start frame. Export SRT for YouTube with serializeSrt().
- Tip: you already know the exact script. Use Whisper only for timings and map the words back to the script text, which fixes misheard words.
Local alternative: @remotion/install-whisper-cpp 4.0.529. The documented recipe is installWhisperCpp({to, version:'1.5.5'}), downloadWhisperModel({model:'medium.en'}), transcribe({..., tokenLevelTimestamps:true}), then toCaptions(). The input must be 16 kHz WAV (ffmpeg -i s01.wav -ar 16000 s01_16k.wav). It builds from source on macOS, and cmake is needed from 1.7.3 up (cmake is installed). https://www.remotion.dev/docs/install-whisper-cpp . The Homebrew whisper.cpp 1.9.4 is not the version the Remotion wrapper was tested with (lower confidence).
tools.music_sfx:
All ffmpeg commands below were dry-run on this machine with `-f null -` and pass. Replace the null output with a file path to use them.

Ambient pad (stereo, detuned chord, slow LFO, soft reverb, 8 min):
ffmpeg -y -f lavfi -i "aevalsrc='0.10*sin(2*PI*110*t)+0.10*sin(2*PI*110.35*t)+0.07*sin(2*PI*164.81*t)*(0.6+0.4*sin(2*PI*0.05*t))+0.05*sin(2*PI*220*t)*(0.5+0.5*sin(2*PI*0.07*t+1))+0.04*sin(2*PI*261.63*t)*(0.5+0.5*sin(2*PI*0.031*t+2))|0.10*sin(2*PI*110.2*t)+0.10*sin(2*PI*109.8*t)+0.07*sin(2*PI*165.1*t)*(0.6+0.4*sin(2*PI*0.043*t+0.5))+0.05*sin(2*PI*220.3*t)*(0.5+0.5*sin(2*PI*0.06*t))+0.04*sin(2*PI*329.63*t)*(0.5+0.5*sin(2*PI*0.029*t+1))':s=48000:d=480" -af "lowpass=f=1400,aecho=0.8:0.6:180|310:0.35|0.25,afade=t=in:d=4,afade=t=out:st=474:d=6,volume=0.8" public/sfx/pad.wav
Change the chord per act by changing the frequencies. Loop it in Remotion with <Audio loop volume={0.18}>.

Whoosh (pink noise, Gaussian envelope, bandpass sweep):
ffmpeg -y -f lavfi -i "anoisesrc=color=pink:amplitude=0.9:d=0.7:r=48000" -af "volume='exp(-pow((t-0.35)/0.13,2))':eval=frame,asendcmd=c='0.0 bandpass f 400;0.2 bandpass f 1200;0.35 bandpass f 3000;0.5 bandpass f 1500',bandpass=f=400:w=1.2:t=o,afade=t=out:st=0.6:d=0.1" public/sfx/whoosh.wav
A simpler version replaces asendcmd+bandpass with highpass=f=250,lowpass=f=4500. A reverse swell: add areverse.

Pop (pitch-drop chirp with exponential decay):
ffmpeg -y -f lavfi -i "aevalsrc='0.8*sin(2*PI*(700*t-2500*t*t))*exp(-t*35)':s=48000:d=0.15" -af "afade=t=in:d=0.003" public/sfx/pop.wav
Tick: aevalsrc='0.6*sin(2*PI*2000*t)*exp(-t*300)':d=0.03 . Ball thump: aevalsrc='sin(2*PI*(120*t-150*t*t))*exp(-t*25)':d=0.25 .

Filter facts: in aevalsrc, '|' separates channels. anoisesrc colours are white, pink, brown, blue, violet and velvet. In asendcmd, ';' separates the intervals. bandpass 'f' is runtime-changeable (the 'T' flag). https://ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg-filters.html

tools.alternatives_considered:
Motion Canvas (@motion-canvas/core 3.17.2, MIT, about 19k stars):
- It has a good generator-based animation API.
- The last stable GitHub release was 2024-12-14 (v3.17.2), then v3.18.0-alpha.0 on 2025-02-16. It is effectively stalled.
- Rendering is UI-driven: "Clicking the RENDER button will initialize rendering". It writes an image sequence that you then encode with ffmpeg. There is no documented headless CLI (https://motioncanvas.io/docs/rendering/).
- Rejected for a scripted pipeline.

Revideo (@revideo/core 0.11.0, 2026-07-10, MIT, about 4k stars):
- It is a Motion Canvas fork with headless renderVideo(), <Audio/> export and parallel workers (https://github.com/redotvideo/revideo).
- It is viable, but its ecosystem, docs and release cadence are much smaller than Remotion's, which releases almost daily.
- Keep it as plan B if the Remotion licence ever becomes a problem.

Python + Pillow 12.3.0 (no numpy, no cairo):
- ImageDraw primitives have no anti-aliasing (https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/issues/5960). Flat vector art needs 3-4x supersampling and LANCZOS downscale per frame, which is slow.
- You must also write easing, path morphing, text layout, the timeline and audio muxing yourself. You would pipe raw RGB frames to ffmpeg (-f rawvideo -pix_fmt rgb24 -s 1920x1080 -r 30 -i -).
- About 7 min at 30 fps is about 12,600 frames. That is feasible with multiprocessing over 16 threads, but the visual quality and developer speed are clearly lower.
- Use it only as a last-resort fallback.

Pick: Remotion 4.0.529. It is headless, audio-first, SVG-native and actively maintained. It is free for an individual and runs on Node 26 after the v4.0.463 fix.
pitfalls: Node 26: use Remotion >=4.0.463 because older versions fail to download Chrome on Node 26 (https://github.com/remotion-dev/remotion/issues/7409). Also make sure that calculateMetadata never throws. Open issue #11679 crashes getCompositions on Node 26.7 when it throws (https://github.com/remotion-dev/remotion/issues/11679).

OpenAI TTS WAV output has a bad RIFF data-size header. ffprobe warns 'Ignoring maximum wav data size' and soxi can report more than 24 h for a 2.8 s clip. Request 'pcm' and wrap it yourself: ffmpeg -f s16le -ar 24000 -ac 1 -i x.pcm x.wav. Or re-mux the WAV before you measure it. https://community.openai.com/t/tts-wav-file-is-corrupted/738642
Do not use MP3 for timing. ffprobe can estimate MP3 duration from bitrate, and encoder padding adds tens of ms per clip, which accumulates over 10+ scenes.
Frame rounding: use Math.ceil(seconds*fps) plus a small tail (about 12 frames). Math.floor cuts the last syllable.

TransitionSeries transitions overlap scenes and shorten the total duration. Narration placed inside overlapping sequences gets cut or doubled. Keep narration on its own Series, or use TransitionSeries.Overlay. https://www.remotion.dev/docs/transitions/transitionseries
The default --jpeg-quality is 80, which gives ringing and banding on flat fills and hard vector edges. Use --jpeg-quality=95, or --image-format=png (slower).

The default concurrency is min(8, cpus/2) = 8 here (https://github.com/remotion-dev/remotion/blob/main/packages/renderer/src/get-concurrency.ts). Run `npx remotion benchmark` with 8, 10, 12 and 14. Too high a value also slows the render.

CSS filter: blur(), drop-shadow, box-shadow and CSS gradients are GPU work, and Chromium disables the GPU in headless mode by default. Kurzgesagt-style glows made with CSS blur can make renders very slow. Use SVG radialGradient or pre-rendered PNG glows, and try --gl=angle (https://www.remotion.dev/docs/gpu).

Calling @remotion/google-fonts loadFont() with no arguments loads every weight and subset. This can cause many requests and render timeouts. Always pass the style plus weights and subsets. Fonts come from Google's CDN, so the render needs internet. For offline renders, use local font files.
All remotion and @remotion/* packages must have the exact same version. Install with --save-exact and check with `npx remotion versions`.

Use Remotion's random('seed') and noise2D('seed', x, y), not Math.random(). Each frame renders in a separate tab, so Math.random() makes objects jitter between frames (https://www.remotion.dev/docs/using-randomness).

TTS is not deterministic and has an input limit of 4096 characters or 2000 tokens. Send one request per scene, cache by hash, pin gpt-4o-mini-tts-2025-12-15, and re-generate only the scenes that changed. Keep the voice and instructions the same for every scene, or the narrator's tone changes between scenes.
OpenAI policy requires a clear disclosure that the voice is AI-generated.

whisper-1 is the only OpenAI transcription model with word timestamps. It strips punctuation, and @remotion/openai-whisper restores it. It can mishear sports terms, so pass the scene text as the prompt (224-token limit) and map the words back to the known script.
createTikTokStyleCaptions needs a leading space before each word in Caption.text. Without it, all words merge into one page.
Hotlinked remotion.media SFX URLs need the network during the render. Some @remotion/sfx items (ding, vine-boom, record-scratch) are not freely licensed. Download only the CC0 items into public/.
Remotion requires macOS 15 or later. This Mac runs 26.5.1, so that is fine. Hardware H.264 (--hardware-acceleration) rejects --crf, so use --video-bitrate instead.
Motion Canvas renders from its browser UI, and its last stable release is from Dec 2024. Do not plan a headless pipeline on it.
